An Arizona mom out in ...
body_text:
NASCAR star Denny Hamlin tells OutKick Outdoors how fishing with professional angler Chris Zaldain has helped accelerate his learning curve and improve his skills on the water.

An Arizona mom out in her neighborhood flying a kite with her 4-year-old daughter a couple of Sundays ago found herself in a fight with a coyote that refused to back down.

The coyote had started nipping at the little girl, according to mom Brittany Cardinal, and before she knew it, mom was swinging her flip-flop at it.

Stock image of woman and girl flying a kite. (Getty Images/iStockphoto)

"We had gone outside because it was windy. And my daughter’s like, 'oh, let's fly a kite,'" Cardinal said, reports AZ Family.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS

A normal activity on a windy Sunday afternoon. That was until mom heard her daughter scream and saw the coyote going after the girl.

"I picked her up and then I started yelling at it, thinking, of course, it’s going to go away, and then it didn't," Cardinal said. "So then I took off my flip-flop, and I was trying to scare it with that by like trying to hit it."

Stock image of coyote wandering around residential area. (Getty Images)

As the mom tried to fight off the coyote and get it to leave them alone, she fell. The coyote then bit her on the face.

ALASKA MOOSE HUNTER MIRACULOUSLY SURVIVES AMBUSH BROWN BEAR ATTACK, SAYS HE 'BLACKED OUT'

"I always hear people say like, 'you don’t feel the pain when like trauma like that happens,' and I mean, I really didn’t feel any pain," Cardinal said of the bite. "I just felt like the pressure of it."

Mom and daughter were eventually able to get away from the feisty coyote and make it back home. Mom had lacerations and puncture wounds on her face from the bite.

THOUSAND OAKS, CALIFORNIA - AUGUST 23: A coyote looks on as it walks on a trail near a residential neighborhood at sunrise on August 23, 2026 in Thousand Oaks, California. (Photo by Kevin Carter/Getty Images) (Getty Images)

Arizona Game and Fish officials have removed several coyotes from the area following the incident and are testing them for rabies. They said that Cardinal did everything you're supposed to do during a coyote attack.

OUTKICK IS NOW ON THE FOX APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

I guess everything except for getting bitten on the face. That I highly doubt is in the protocol. But everything else she did correctly.

Alex Flickinger, public affairs community liaison for Arizona Game and Fish, said, "You fight back, you yell at the animal, be loud with it, throw rocks, whatever you have to do to get that animal to just run off."

title: Vikings say Kyler Murray feeling 'pretty good,' participating in team meetings despite serious concussion
excerpt: The Minnesota Vikings named Kyler Murray their starting QB over J.J. McCarthy. Nick Wright, Chris Broussard, and Kevin Wildes ask if this is the right decision. Plus, they discuss Jerry Jones potentia...
body_text:
The Minnesota Vikings named Kyler Murray their starting QB over J.J. McCarthy. Nick Wright, Chris Broussard, and Kevin Wildes ask if this is the right decision. Plus, they discuss Jerry Jones potentially taking shots at former Dallas Cowboy Micah Parsons.

Kyler Murray’s start to his Minnesota Vikings career went awry on Sunday at U.S. Bank Stadium, as he was knocked out of the game with a concussion suffered on just the third offensive possession for the team.

The hits he took from two Green Bay Packers players were vicious, and after he officially entered concussion protocol, the question became whether he would be missing game time moving forward.

Head coach Kevin O’Connell, though, gave an update on his starting quarterback Monday following the Vikings’ come-from-behind victory to beat their NFC North rival, where he said Murray came into the building feeling "pretty good."

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Kyler Murray of the Minnesota Vikings looks on before a game against the Green Bay Packers at U.S. Bank Stadium on Sept. 13, 2026, in Minneapolis, Minn. (Getty Images)

O’Connell confirmed that Murray is in concussion protocol, but he said that the quarterback was participating in team meetings.

The Vikings will be taking it "a day at a time," he said, while the medical staff makes sure Murray passes each step of protocol.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

In turn, Murray’s status for Week 2’s matchup against the Chicago Bears, who poured 59 points on the Carolina Panthers in their win on Sunday, is up in the air.

However, Vikings fans seeing the initial blow may have thought Murray would not be available next week. Instead, there is hope so long as he clears protocol.

Javon Bullard of the Green Bay Packers reacts after tackling Kyler Murray of the Minnesota Vikings during the first quarter on Sept. 13, 2026, in Minneapolis, Minn. (Getty Images)

Before suffering his injury, which came after Murray tucked and ran before a late slide led to the two defenders sandwiching him on the turf, he went 3-of-5 for 18 yards. He also threw an interception on the very first snap of his regular-season Vikings career, throwing a jump ball after the Packers brought a blitz immediately at the line of scrimmage.

Once Murray was off the field, veteran Carson Wentz, whom the Vikings kept on after serving in a backup role last season, was called upon to lead Minnesota for the remainder of the home opener.

The result was a composed, effective performance from Wentz, who completed 12 of 19 passes for 133 yards and three touchdowns in the 39-22 win.

Lukas Van Ness and Javon Bullard of the Green Bay Packers tackle Kyler Murray of the Minnesota Vikings during the first quarter in Minneapolis, Minn., on Sept. 13, 2026. (Getty Images)

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

Should Murray be unable to play in Week 2, Wentz would almost certainly draw the start for Minnesota, with J.J. McCarthy — the team's first-round pick in 2024 — expected to serve as his backup.

Scott Thompson is a sports writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Australia politics live: Hastie accuses Hanson of avoiding media; Anthony Albanese and King Charles speak
excerpt:
Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Malinauskas still optimistic about steelmaking in Australia

The South Australian premier, Peter Malinauskas, says there is optimism that s...
body_text:
Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Malinauskas still optimistic about steelmaking in Australia

The South Australian premier, Peter Malinauskas, says there is optimism that steelmaking will continue in his state, after the closure of a major blast furnace at Whyalla was announced yesterday.

Speaking to ABC News Breakfast from Whyalla and donned in some hi-vis, Malinauskas says there was disappointment, heartbreak, but also a sense of inevitability when the announcement was made.

He says the plan is to keep all of the remaining workers to continue making steel out of the plant, and that the operation is on track to be sold by the end of the year.

double quotation mark[Whyalla] has the capacity to be a viable operation but it hasn’t been recapitalised. The blast furnace is over 60 years old. It was first built in 1965 and blast furnaces of this age not to be realigned on a frequent basis. This hasn’t been done in 20 years. The fact it’s still going is a miracle. We need to have the plant recapitalised and that’s exactly the plan we have in conjunction with the Federal Government … if we lose this capacity behind me, this country doesn’t have structural steelmaking capacity and we can’t afford that.

There’s also retained optimism about the future of steelmaking in this country through that package, that $1.9bn package on the table as part of the sale process, which is why we’ve got to focus on the big picture here and the long term and make sure we account for the real impacts of yesterday’s decision.

‘Rotten, awful, ugly’: MPs condemn Hanson’s comments on Indigenous Australians

The housing minister says Pauline Hanson punches down on people and her language is rotten and ugly, after comments resurfaced of the One Nation leader saying Indigenous Australians were the “most primitive race”.

Speaking on Sunrise this morning alongside Liberal frontbencher Michaelia Cash, Clare O’Neil warned Hanson against “Americanising” Australian politics and dividing the country.

double quotation markIf Pauline Hanson wants to take us down the road of Americanising our politics, so people in a family who disagree on political issues can’t speak to each other any longer, like, this is the pathway to do it …

We’ve got lots of challenges facing Australia, but we’re not going to solve them by punching down on things that are brilliant about our country. So I think it’s rotten. I think it’s awful. I think it’s ugly.

Cash said she doesn’t agree with Hanson’s comments, but then attacked Labor for not doing more to protect Indigenous children and close the gap, and said the focus should be on action, not Hanson’s comments.

double quotation markI just don’t agree with those comments. But I actually do agree with Senator Jacinta Nampijinpa Price when she says that there are serious issues that do need to be discussed. And these comments shouldn’t be a distraction from them. I mean, why aren’t we closing the gap?

‘She’s been transparent’: O’Neil defends transport minister’s top-tier Qantas membership

Clare O’Neil has defended her colleague, transport minister Catherine King, after it was revealed the latter had accepted a lifetime membership to Qantas’s top-tier membership, the platinum Frequent Flyer rewards.

The status means free entry to Qantas’s first and business class lounges, access to the airline’s VIP team, upgrade priority, extra Qantas points and more. King listed the status on her register of interests on Monday afternoon.

Quizzed on whether the move passes the pub test, O’Neil said “federal politicians … travel an unbelievable amount”.

double quotation markCatherine King has probably been away from her family for a third of the last 25 years. And that’s kind of the extent of this. The important thing is … she made a declaration of it, and she’s been transparent about it.

King attracted scrutiny in 2022 over her decision to reject Qatar Airways’ request to bring extra flights into Australia in a move widely seen as benefiting Qantas.

One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce has been unable to confirm how his party’s sweeping new immigration policy would affect the budget or jobs while declaring they would “deal with it no matter the cost”.

The former deputy PM appeared on the ABC’s second National Forum on Monday evening, which focused on immigration and multiculturalism. He faced backlash from panellists, with journalist and political commentator George Megalogenis claiming One Nation’s plan to cut migration in net terms over three years had never happened in Australian public policy and would “tank the economy” on the scale of the “depression of the 1890s”.

Joyce said “the issue of what it’s going to cost … is contentious” and rejected questioning over why One Nation didn’t consult the parliamentary budget office.

“The Australian people are sort of tired of the fact that you have to go to an economist to come up with policy to help us all better understand what it costs to us,” he claimed, adding it “has to be dealt with” and “we will deal with it no matter the cost”.

Asked if he was worried about what the parliamentary budget office might produce, he replied: “No, I’m not really – because they’re not elected, I am.”

Good morning, Krishani Dhanji here with you. Thanks to Martin Farrer for getting us started.

Migration will dominate parliament again today, after One Nation yesterday announced its policy to cut 750,000 temporary visas over three years – which the major parties said would send the country into a recession.

There’ll also be more reaction to the Whyalla steelworks shutting down a major operation, cutting more than 500 jobs.

It’s going to be a busy one, let’s get stuck in!

‘Multiculturalism is who we are’: Anne Aly

The multicultural affairs minister, Anne Aly, was also on the ABC’s National Forum panel. She said Labor was committed to bringing immigration numbers down in a “manageable way” while ensuring the system both met the needs of Australia and was “fair for those who come here”.

She pushed back at claims immigrants were harming social cohesion, pointing to an Australia she grew up in where “nobody cared what language your mum spoke”.

double quotation markThat’s the Australia that I know. And I fear that that is the Australia that we’re losing … Every time we talk about immigration, multiculturalism, it comes from a deficit point of view.

Social cohesion becomes the burden of people from different countries who have come here and it is their fault, it is their responsibility to socially cohere. The fact is that multiculturalism is who we are. It is part of our identity. It’s who we are as Australia.

Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie has questioned why Pauline Hanson announced One Nation’s immigration policy via a prerecorded video on social media instead of fronting the media.

Appearing alongside Barnaby Joyce on the ABC’s National Forum, he said he backed parts of One Nation’s immigration plan but was concerned about the lack of detail and Hanson’s silence:

double quotation markWe haven’t seen her at all today. And this is someone who wants to be the prime minister of Australia. And she hasn’t had the courage to front the media today and explain the budgetary, the economic and the human impact of these policy changes that she’s suggesting.

His ongoing battle with One Nation appeared to be tempered, however, with him and Joyce largely exchanging niceties, including Joyce claiming in jest, at one point, that they were “back in bed together”.

Chris Bowen has watered down any expectations that a renewed rise in oil prices will lead to the reintroduction of the federal government’s fuel excise relief.

He said Labor was continuing to look “very closely” at the spike, which was prompted after a series of drone attacks forced Saudi Arabia to close its east-west crude pipeline. But he said the federal government had been “very clear” that cutting the fuel excise was a temporary measure.

double quotation markIt’s not the only cost of living measure that we put in place … At the same time, I’m very much focused on ensuring our ongoing fuel supply in this very difficult international circumstance … We’re not going to respond to every daily movement on the world oil price.

Bowen said the situation in the Middle East was “deeply concerning” and confirmed he would be travelling to Saudi Arabia next week to meet with his counterpart, Abdulaziz bin Salman Al Saud.

He was also asked about the appointment of the former opposition leader Sussan Ley to the board of Snowy Hydro, given the Coalition abandoned its commitment to net zero under her leadership and she had blamed Labor’s renewable energy rollout on high energy prices.

Bowen said when he saw an Australian who was “well credentialled, I don’t care how they vote”, and described her as a person of “talent and ability”.

Anthony Albanese spoke to King Charles last night, the prime minister revealed.

Albanese last saw the monarch during a visit to Britain in September last year.

“A privilege to speak with His Majesty King Charles III this evening,” Albanese wrote on social media.

“His affection for the Australian people remains strong. I extended Australia’s best wishes to His Majesty and the Royal Family.”

Good morning and welcome to our live news blog. I’m Martin Farrer with the top overnight stories and then it will be Krishani Dhanji with the main action.

title: Abdul El-Sayed dismisses questions about Hasan Piker ties on 'Face the Nation,' pivots to groceries
excerpt: With 50 days until voters head to the polls, moderate Democrats struggle to find a place within the increasingly left-leaning Democratic Party. Abdul El Sayed's efforts to distance himself from Hasan ...
body_text:
With 50 days until voters head to the polls, moderate Democrats struggle to find a place within the increasingly left-leaning Democratic Party. Abdul El Sayed's efforts to distance himself from Hasan Piker and more are discussed by guest panelists Jeremy Hunt and Michael LaRosa on 'The Faulkner Focus.'

Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed rejected questions on Sunday regarding his relationship with Hasan Piker, saying that the race was not about "a Twitch streamer in California."

CBS News' Weijia Jiang asked El-Sayed on "Face the Nation" about Jewish Michiganders' concerns regarding his ties to Piker, the far-left streamer who has appeared with him on the campaign trail.

"There are Jewish voters in your state who are concerned about your relationship with Piker. You have condemned antisemitism but not called out his rhetoric directly. Why not?" Jiang asked.

JEWISH DEM DEFECTIONS THREATEN EL-SAYED IN MICHIGAN SENATE RACE DECIDED BY RAZOR-THIN MARGINS

Twitch streamer Hasan Piker appeared on the campaign trail with Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo)

Rather than answering the question, El-Sayed deflected, saying that voters were not asking him about Piker and that they were more focused on the issues impacting their daily lives.

"Weiija, with all due respect, this is the third time you’ve asked about a Twitch streamer in California. I’ve done four events in Michigan this week. You know what didn’t come up? Twitch streamers in California," El-Sayed responded. The candidate said that voters would rather discuss grocery prices, healthcare and the environment, among other things.

"I’m not interested in having a conversation about streamers in California because they are not raising the prices of gas and groceries," El-Sayed added.

El-Sayed is not the first Democrat to push back on questions about Piker. Last month, Rep. Debbie Dingell, D-Mich., demanded reporters stop asking her about Piker, saying that "Republicans are trying to make" the race about him.

EL-SAYED TORCHED ONLINE AFTER BRUSHING OFF QUESTIONS ABOUT HASAN PIKER CAMPAIGN TIES: ‘WHAT A PAL’

Michigan Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate Abdul El-Sayed pushed back on questions about his ties with controversial Twitch streamer Hasan Piker. (Emily Elconin/Getty Images)

"I don’t agree with Hasan Piker on a lot of stuff, and I really don’t agree with him on some of the woman things he said. And I’m still trying to figure out, is it the reason he exercises and looks buff is why he has so many followers," Dingell said during a student town hall with El-Sayed and Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md.

Piker has been vocal about his support for El-Sayed, going so far as to call on Democrats to punish those within the party who oppose the Michigan candidate.

"You can't be out here saying like, 'Oh, I'm a centrist Democrat. And I think Abdul is a bridge too far.' That must be punished," Piker said during a stream in August.

While El-Sayed previously appeared with Piker on the campaign trail, he told Semafor in August that he had "no plans" to campaign with the controversial streamer. This came after Piker, who is known for his inflammatory rhetoric and anti-Israel stance, made a remark about Jewish Americans' support for Israel that drew the ire of several Democrats.

"People don't f--- with Israel any longer. And if Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they're singularly invested in Israel, eventually someone will come around and take action not against Israel, mind you, but against American Jews," Piker said during his stream on Aug. 20.

Rep. Hillary Scholten, D-Mich., condemned Piker in a statement, calling him "a hack who thrives on hate, shock and awe because he lacks substance."

ABDUL EL-SAYED PLAYS DOWN HASAN PIKER TIES AFTER STREAMER’S VIRAL ANTISEMITISM FIRESTORM

Hasan Piker, left, listens as Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive candidate in the Democratic primary for U.S. Senate in Michigan, speaks in a green room before a campaign rally, Tuesday, April 7, 2026, at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor, Mich. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo)

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Several other Democratic lawmakers spoke out against Piker after he made the remarks, including Sens. Cory Booker, D-N.J.; Jon Ossoff, D-Ga.; Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich.; and Jacky Rosen, D-Nev.; House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y.; and Reps. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J.; Ritchie Torres, D-N.Y.; Jared Moskowitz, D-Fla.; Brad Schneider, D-Ill.; and Greg Stanton, D-Ariz.

El-Sayed also responded to Piker's comments, and while he did not condemn the streamer outright, he denounced antisemitism and rhetoric that puts the Jewish community in danger.

"I believe all Americans deserve the right to advocate for what they believe without fear of violence. This is particularly true for communities that have been intimidated for their beliefs in the past," El-Sayed wrote at the time.

"My commitment to Jewish safety is the same as my commitment to the safety of my own daughters," he added. "Antisemitism is a scourge, and we need to address it in all its forms. And I stand against any rhetoric that puts the community at risk."

Rachel Wolf is a media and culture reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: US ends limits on coal and gas plant emissions, removing key tool to battle climate crisis
excerpt:
Trump’s EPA strips itself of regulation ability, gutting Clean Air Act in what experts say is a gift to planet polluters

On the heels of the hottest summer ever recorded in the US, the Trump administ...
body_text:
Trump’s EPA strips itself of regulation ability, gutting Clean Air Act in what experts say is a gift to planet polluters

On the heels of the hottest summer ever recorded in the US, the Trump administration has said it will erase any limits on emissions from coal and gas plants that are dangerously heating up our planet.

The US Environmental Protection Agency said it will strip itself of its ability to regulate greenhouse gas emissions coming from power plants under the Clean Air Act, removing a key tool to address the climate crisis.

By erasing any limits on such emissions from coal and gas plants, the Trump administration has severely limited any future administration’s ability to curb this pollution.

The EPA calculated the move will result in 123m metric tons of additional carbon emissions in the next decade, and save power plant operators $370m in direct compliance costs. Lee Zeldin, the agency administrator said the Trump administration is protecting American energy from a “war on coal”.

“Americans will see a decrease in electricity prices, but this is just the beginning,” said Zeldin, who unveiled the reversal of the 2024 carbon pollution standards at a G20 meeting in Houston on Monday.

“We are working to go even further so that American energy can be fully unleashed. Realizing the full potential of American energy means more jobs, lower prices and a more prosperous America.”

The EPA said that greenhouse gas emissions from power plants have “no material impact on global climate change”. This is despite the fact that US electricity generation is responsible for a quarter of the country’s greenhouse gas emissions. If the sector were itself a country, it would be the fifth largest carbon polluter in the world, after China, the US, India and Russia.

Trump, who has called the climate crisis “bullshit” and “a hoax”, earlier this year overturned the foundational 2009 EPA endangerment finding – spurred by a supreme court ruling – that greenhouse gases pose a significant threat to public health and the environment.

This has opened the way for the administration to scrub out any limits on the planet-heating gases that are causing our world to rapidly overheat and worsen deadly heatwaves, drought, wildfires and floods. In February, the EPA eliminated pollution standards for cars and trucks as part of a series of actions Zeldin described as “driving a dagger straight into the heart of the climate change religion”.

Environmental groups immediately vowed to challenge the latest rollback in court. “This is full-throated climate denial while the climate crisis happens in real time and a shocking betrayal of the American public,” said Holly Bender, chief program officer at the Sierra Club.

“The Sierra Club will fight back against this reckless and dangerous proposal with everything we have in the courts, in Congress, and in communities across the country.”

When it issued the latest carbon pollution standards for power plants under Joe Biden’s administration in 2024, the EPA found the rules would slash 1bn tonnes of greenhouse gases by 2047 and deliver $370bn in net benefits.

The rules also would have prevented 1,200 premature deaths and 360,000 asthma attacks in 2035 alone, due to air quality improvements. Under Trump, however, the EPA has eliminated the dollar benefit of saving lives through reduced air pollution in its calculations.

“Every American deserves to breathe clean air, but time and again this administration gives a green light to more pollution at the expense of our health,” said Gina McCarthy, who was administrator of the EPA under Barack Obama.

“Everyone will be affected by their actions, but the most vulnerable among us, our kids and grandkids, will suffer the most. Today’s decision lets the nation’s biggest industrial polluters off the hook by reversing findings the agency itself established.”

Trump has long championed the use of fossil fuels, such as coal and gas, pushing a “drill, baby drill” approach that has opened up more land for extraction while demolishing clean air and water regulations the industry said it found too onerous.

As well as handing out hundreds of millions of dollars in taxpayer funds to prop up coal plants, which have struggled economically in recent years, the Trump administration has sought to directly strangle clean energy projects such as solar and offshore wind.

The latest EPA intervention will probably be significant, if it survives legal challenge, as it will stymie any future attempt to restrict carbon pollution from power plants. It is the latest episode in a decade-long saga over how, or if, the US tames its power emissions.

In 2016 the supreme court knocked down Obama’s clean power plan. A more narrow version, with the parameters set again by the court, was then enacted under Biden.

title: Hochul accused of ‘hit job’ on behalf of teachers’ unions in act of ‘pure censorship’: labor group
excerpt:
Ryan Walters, CEO of the Teacher Freedom Alliance, calls out New York Gov. Kathy Hochul and Democrats for a bill he says equates to "pure censorship."

New York Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul is being a...
body_text:
Ryan Walters, CEO of the Teacher Freedom Alliance, calls out New York Gov. Kathy Hochul and Democrats for a bill he says equates to "pure censorship."

New York Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul is being accused of conducting a "hit job" on free speech on behalf of teachers unions after she signed a law giving the state attorney general the power to fine groups deemed to be engaged in deceptive communications that falsely appear to be authorized by a union.

Hochul signed a law last week prohibiting people and organizations from using deceptive communications that falsely appear to be authorized by a union or union representative. The law, which took immediate effect, allows Democratic Attorney General Letitia James to investigate and sue to stop alleged violations, including those involving out-of-state groups. Courts can impose fines of up to $1,000 per incident.

In response, the Freedom Foundation, a conservative nonprofit that campaigns against public-sector unions, including teachers’ unions, says New York’s new law is a targeted effort to silence its outreach by making its communications vulnerable to government investigations, lawsuits and fines.

CEO Aaron Withe called the law a "hit job." He said the law "isn’t about protecting anyone," adding that it instead "exists because government unions in New York are terrified of an inconvenient fact: when public employees learn they don’t have to pay union dues, a lot of them stop. So instead of making their case to their own members, union bosses ran to their friends in the legislature and got them to write a law that makes speech illegal."

NATION’S LARGEST TEACHERS UNION UNDER FIRE AS CONTROVERSIAL AGENDA PUTS CENTURY-OLD FEDERAL CHARTER AT RISK

New York Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul is taking criticism over a bill she signed last week that empowers the state attorney general to investigate and fine groups deemed to be engaged in deceptive practices against labor union members. (Adam Gray - Pool/Getty Images)

Fox News Digital reached out to Hochul's and James' offices for comment. Fox News Digital also reached out to the New York State United Teachers, United Federation of Teachers and the AFL-CIO for comment.

The law allows James to investigate alleged violations, issue subpoenas and ask a court to block communications deemed deceptive. Courts can impose fines of up to $1,000 per violation, including against organizations outside New York.

The New York State American Federation of Labor and Congress of Industrial Organizations (NYS AFL-CIO) praised Hochul’s decision to sign the bill, which she signed along with two other pieces of legislation related to labor rights. Mario Cilento, president of NYS AFL-CIO, remarked that the law will be "holding individuals accountable for fraudulently claiming to be union representatives."

He said the slate of bills signed by Hochul "put workers first."

In an X post, Hochul similarly framed the bills as prioritizing workers, writing, "Today marks a new day with even more protections, because I’ll never stop fighting for our workers."

"New York State gave birth to the labor movement. Over the last five years, I have continued that legacy by fiercely supporting the men and women of labor," wrote Hochul.

TRUMP UNLOADS ON AOC, MAMDANI FOR LAUGHING DURING SACRED 9/11 CEREMONY AT GROUND ZERO

Attorney General of New York Letitia James, a Democrat, and New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, also a Democrat, attend the New York City Labor Day parade, America's oldest Labor Day Parade, along with members of more than 200 unions and organizations, on Saturday, September 6, 2025, in New York City. (Selcuk Acar/Anadolu via Getty Images)

Meanwhile, the Freedom Foundation has mailed and otherwise contacted New York public employees, including teachers, to inform them of their ability to leave their unions and stop paying dues. Nearly 7,500 New York public employees have used Freedom Foundation materials to cancel their union memberships, including more than 1,400 so far this year, according to the group.

In a statement to Fox News Digital, Withe pointed to the 2018 Supreme Court decision in Janus v. AFSCME, which held that public-sector employees, including public school teachers, cannot be forced to pay union fees for collective bargaining or other speech because that speech can involve political issues protected by the First Amendment.

He said that while the New York law "lets Letitia James fine the Freedom Foundation for outreach the state decides 'impersonates' a union … all we're doing is telling public employees what already gives them: the right to leave their union and stop paying dues."

"This is an anti-speech law aimed at one kind of speaker," said Withe.

He asserted that the New York law was "copied" from a similar measure in Oregon, which the Freedom Foundation is already challenging in the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals. He said his organization will "make the same case here."

Fox News Digital spoke with Ryan Walters, former superintendent of Oklahoma public schools and CEO of Freedom Foundation’s education arm, the Teacher Freedom Alliance. Walters called the New York law an example of "pure censorship and targeting of political opponents by Democrats protecting their union bosses."

INSIDE TEACHERS' UNION MAY DAY 'DRESS REHEARSAL' CRITICS WARN WILL 'GROOM' STUDENTS INTO DEM 'FOOT SOLDIERS'

Ryan Walters speaks with Fox News Digital about TPUSA expansion in Oklahoma and his efforts against teachers' unions (Fox News Digital)

"This is such a canary in the coal mine moment where if New York is allowed to do this - an openly socialist mayor, a governor operating as a tyrant doing the behests of the teachers’ unions - it's going to go on across the country, and our schools will not be able to improve in that kind of environment," he said, adding, "Where New York goes with this is going to be where the other blue states follow."

He posited that the New York law "shows you how important that power structure is for the Democrat party."

"They have to control the school system to continue to control the country," he said. "Despite elections, they still control these education systems at large. That's why the teachers’ unions are enemy number one of progress in this country and why New York needs to be taken on directly for what they're doing."

Peter Pinedo is a politics writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Israel probing Naza film on Gaza for treason, inciting anti-Semitism
excerpt:
Israeli officials have slammed a new documentary film on the military’s conduct in Gaza and called for legal action against the filmmakers and their sources.

Prime Minister Benjamin ‌Netanyahu on Mon...
body_text:
Israeli officials have slammed a new documentary film on the military’s conduct in Gaza and called for legal action against the filmmakers and their sources.

Prime Minister Benjamin ‌Netanyahu on Monday called the documentary, Naza – which alleges that mass ⁠civilian deaths were ⁠routinely built into targeting decisions during Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza – a “shocking” film and accused it of being part of a wave of global anti-Semitic incitement.

Israeli military chief Eyal Zamir has ordered the launch of a legal probe to hunt down sources, which include members of the military and Israeli intelligence with their identities hidden. The culture minister suggested that the government could seek to press treason charges against the filmmakers and others involved.

The documentary, directed by Israeli journalists Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, won ⁠the Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival on Saturday, having received a 25-minute standing ovation when it was screened two days previously.

“It’s shocking. We are fighting global anti-Semitic incitement, and when it comes from within us it is intolerable,” Netanyahu said in a video posted on Telegram.

“And now two Israeli directors ‌portraying the [Israeli military] as war criminals receive applause at the Venice festival.”

Netanyahu’s comments followed a statement from Zamir asserting that the film constituted an attack on the state of Israel.

“Based on what has been published thus far, this is not a film offering criticism of the [military], nor is it an attempt to establish the truth. It is based on blood libels, deliberate distortions of ⁠reality, and grave, false accusations against [Israeli] soldiers and commanders,” ⁠Zamir said.

The military chief has instructed the Military Advocate General, whose legal powers are confined within the military, “to examine and advance possible legal measures concerning the film and those involved in it”.

Culture Minister Miki Zohar stated that he has asked authorities to “investigate how the materials were obtained, who is behind them, and whether in the process of obtaining or publishing them, actions were taken that amount to aiding the enemy during wartime”.

He also said he had requested the Interior Ministry to consider revoking the citizenship of the two filmmakers on account of “treason”.

The film takes its title from an ⁠Israeli military term for expected “collateral casualties” and is built around anonymous interviews with intelligence officers and soldiers involved in the war.

Those interviewed describe how targets in the Gaza Strip were selected and how many civilian casualties were factored into attacks.

“We believe that the denial of a crime is what helps it persist, and this is why it ⁠is especially important for us that Israelis watch this film; it is our country that is doing these crimes,” Abraham said in his acceptance speech at the Venice festival on Saturday.

Gaza health authorities report that more than 73,700 Palestinians, most of them civilians, have been killed in Israel’s devastating war that has left much of the besieged enclave in ruins.

title: NHS doctor sues after 'bearded' trans patient allegedly exposes himself on women's psychiatric ward
excerpt: Texas Children's Hospital's agrees to a $10 million settlement after performing illegal youth gender transition procedures and to open a new detransition clinic. Whistleblower Vanessa Sivadge's testim...
body_text:
Texas Children's Hospital's agrees to a $10 million settlement after performing illegal youth gender transition procedures and to open a new detransition clinic. Whistleblower Vanessa Sivadge's testimony exposed illegal youth gender transition procedures, leading to the major state enforcement action.

A psychiatrist took legal action Thursday against the Greater Manchester Mental Health NHS Foundation Trust in England, alleging hospital officials ignored safeguarding concerns about men who identify as women being admitted to female psychiatric wards despite a landmark U.K. Supreme Court ruling on biological sex.

The Christian Legal Centre, which is representing the psychiatrist under the name "Dr. A," said in a press release that "vulnerable female patients, including survivors of sexual violence, have been detained in psychiatric wards under unlawful NHS policies which allow men to access these wards and intimate places, such as showers, because they merely identify as women."

"The public, politicians and the media need to know that mentally ill men and women are being detained together on mixed-sex wards whilst the NHS pretends its wards are single-sex," Dr. A said in the press release.

The dispute follows the U.K. Supreme Court's unanimous April 2025 decision that the terms "woman," "man" and "sex" in the Equality Act 2010 refer to biological sex. The ruling permits biological males who identify as women to be excluded from certain women-only spaces while leaving existing protections against discrimination based on gender reassignment intact.

FEMALE VIRGINIA OFFICER SUES POLICE DEPARTMENT AFTER ALLEGEDLY SHARING LOCKER ROOM WITH BIOLOGICAL MALE

A senior NHS psychiatrist is suing Greater Manchester Mental Health NHS Foundation Trust, alleging officials failed to protect female patients after allowing biological males who identify as women onto female psychiatric wards. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo)

Despite the ruling, Dr. A claims that her repeated requests about how the NHS Trust was complying with the law were "met with delay, resistance and suggestions that the judgment might be challenged in the European Court of Human Rights."

Dr. A also said that the day after the Supreme Court ruling, the Trust reportedly told staff there would be no immediate changes for patients.

Her claim gained attention after she alleged that a biological male patient who identified as a woman was placed on a women's psychiatric ward where he exposed male genitalia to female patients. According to a report from U.K. outlet The Times, the patient was temporarily moved to a male ward following complaints before being returned to the women's ward.

Dr. A said the incident was described to her by another consultant working at the hospital.

"He said that there had been a man with a beard and full male genitalia who had been exposing himself to female patients and they were unhappy," she explained.

FEMALE INMATE SUES WASHINGTON STATE AFTER ALLEGED ATTACK BY MALE-BORN PRISONER IN WOMEN'S FACILITY

Dr A said a "bearded" transgender patient with male genitalia allegedly exposed himself to female psychiatric patients before being returned to the women’s ward after initially being moved. (Fox News)

Dr. A said she pursued legal action after concluding that her efforts to raise the issue internally over the past three years had not resulted in adequate changes. She filed an Employment Tribunal claim against the NHS Trust alleging unlawful workplace discrimination and harassment over her protected gender-critical beliefs, claiming the Trust ignored her safeguarding warnings and failed to bring its policies into line with the Supreme Court’s ruling on biological sex.

"As a senior doctor, I could not remain silent while women’s privacy and dignity were being compromised. I raised these concerns because I believe every patient has a right to be treated with compassion and to have her sex recognized when intimate care, accommodation and personal safety are involved," she said.

Fox News Digital reached out to Greater Manchester Mental Health NHS Foundation Trust for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

The NHS Trust now acknowledges the Supreme Court ruling on its website and said it is reviewing its existing rules.

"As a result, we are actively undertaking an audit of our policies, procedures and processes in order to reflect this clarification in the law," the Trust said.

MED SCHOOL DEANS COME UP EMPTY IN TENSE HEARING WHEN ASKED POINT BLANK IF MEN CAN HAVE BABIES: 'RIDICULOUS'

The U.K. Equality and Human Rights Commission told Fox News Digital its statutory guidance says transgender women are excluded from women-only services because their sex is male. (Jessica Rinaldi/The Boston Globe)

The Trust's review came as national NHS guidance also remains unresolved. NHS England's current guidance, first issued in 2019, says transgender patients should be accommodated according to their gender presentation, including for toilets and bathing facilities, but NHS England added after the Supreme Court ruling that the guidance is "currently being reviewed."

The existing guidance also states providers should generally have a "zero-tolerance approach" toward mixed-sex accommodation and should protect patients' safety, privacy and dignity.

The Equality and Human Rights Commission pointed Fox News Digital to its new statutory Code of Practice, which took effect in August and outlines how service providers should apply the law to single-sex services.

"In separate or single-sex services, a trans man will be excluded from the men-only service because his sex is female, and a trans woman will be excluded from the women-only service because her sex is male," a spokesperson said.

The EHRC press office also directed Fox News Digital to provisions requiring service providers to consider whether women's safety, privacy or dignity would be jeopardized by sharing a service with men. The guidance specifically tells providers to consider whether women are likely to be undressed, have limited ability to leave or choose an alternative service, or are receiving services connected to male violence against women.

Sonja Shaw, a candidate for California superintendent of public instruction and girls' sports advocate, sharply criticized policies she says put women's safety at risk.

"Sex is real, and girls and women deserve privacy, safety, and fairness, not institutions that pretend otherwise," she told Fox News Digital. "Hospitals putting bearded men who identify as women into female psychiatric wards reads as the next step of a process that has been perpetuated by this perverse political agenda."

"It is the same failure we already see in schools that put biological males into girls’ sports, locker rooms, and bathrooms," Shaw continued. "And it won’t stop until we address the root problem and codify protection for biological women’s right to private and protected spaces. Stop sacrificing women and girls at the altar of ideology. Female psychiatric wards turned into male cosplay zones isn’t healthcare. It’s malpractice against vulnerable women."

CJ Womack is an associate editor at Fox News.

CJ joined Fox News Digital's team in 2026, which highlights the vital role journalism plays in shaping politics and culture. He has years of experience analyzing and reporting on the news media.

CJ graduated from Long Beach State University in 2025 with a Bachelor of Arts in Political Science and a minor in Journalism.

title: Deadly bacteria detected as NYC orders emergency cleaning of cooling towers
excerpt:
Infectious diseases expert Dr. Tyler Evans explains the risks tied to Legionella found in Bronx cooling towers, which symptoms residents should watch for, and when exposure may require medical care.

...
body_text:
Infectious diseases expert Dr. Tyler Evans explains the risks tied to Legionella found in Bronx cooling towers, which symptoms residents should watch for, and when exposure may require medical care.

Health officials ordered the immediate remediation of 10 rooftop cooling towers in the South Bronx after preliminary testing detected Legionella bacteria amid a growing Legionnaires’ disease cluster that has sickened nine people and left one dead.

The New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene issued orders to clean and disinfect the sites. Among the affected structures are cooling towers at major hubs, including Yankee Stadium and Lincoln Hospital.

As public health workers work to clean the equipment, experts note that recurring outbreaks in these neighborhoods highlight deeper systemic vulnerabilities.

NYC LEGIONNAIRES' DISEASE OUTBREAK KILLS FOURTH VICTIM, 76 CASES REPORTED

"When we look at outbreaks of Legionnaires' disease, in New York City, we almost always see it in the Bronx or Harlem," Dr. Tyler Evans, CEO of the Wellness Equity Alliance and former first chief medical officer for New York City, told Fox News Digital.

"A lot of times, we see risk of infections taking place in historically marginalized communities."

New York City health officials ordered the immediate remediation of 10 South Bronx cooling towers — including units at Yankee Stadium and Lincoln Hospital — after detecting Legionella DNA during a cluster investigation that has sickened nine people and caused one death. (New York Yankees/Getty Images)

The department identified the cluster following a surge in cases dating back to late August. Tests confirmed traces of Legionella in 10 of 24 sampled towers, according to city health officials.

PCR (polymerase chain reaction) tests return results quickly, but cannot distinguish between live and dead bacteria. Culture tests to confirm live bacteria can take up to two weeks, prompting city health officials to order immediate cleaning out of caution.

Late-summer weather has compounded the issue. High temperatures create ideal breeding grounds for bacteria inside industrial air-conditioning systems, which add water to the surrounding air, Evans noted.

HEART ATTACKS AND STROKES RISING WITH EXTREME WEATHER EVENTS, RESEARCH SUGGESTS

"Record-breaking temperatures lead to accelerating the risk of the bacteria basically cooking, getting out to become vaporized, and then producing exposure to other people," he said.

Legionnaires' disease, a severe form of pneumonia, cannot be spread between people, nor is it contracted by drinking tap water, the expert noted. Most healthy individuals are not sickened by exposure, but high-risk populations can face severe health consequences.

Preliminary PCR testing quickly confirmed bacterial DNA, but because it cannot distinguish between live and dead bacteria, officials mandated immediate cleanings while awaiting culture test results. (iStock)

"In terms of people ... to be concerned about, it's really older adults — typically 65 and older — or people living with comorbid conditions," Evans said, pointing to underlying factors like diabetes, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) or compromised immune systems.

Health officials urge anyone who has lived in, worked in or visited ZIP codes 10451 and 10456 since late August to monitor their health.

Key symptoms to watch for include high fevers, severe shortness of breath, chest pain and coughing up bloody mucus.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Evans noted that early medical care is crucial, as the illness responds well to standard antibiotic treatments when caught early.

"Infections fall into different buckets — bacteria, viruses, fungi, parasites," he said. "Bacteria are alive. Antibiotics are effective against bacteria because you can kill them, which makes it very treatable."

Legionnaires' disease is a non-contagious form of pneumonia spread through inhaled vapor — not drinking water — that poses the highest risk to adults over 65 and individuals with underlying conditions like diabetes or COPD. (iStock)

While city officials have taken quick action to inspect and clean the structures, Evans emphasized that long-term prevention requires sustained public investment.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"Could we test all cooling towers across New York City on a regular basis during times of risk when it's hotter? Yes," Evans said.

"City health officials do an amazing job, but it costs money. When federal funds are removed from public health, it's very hard to do more when you have less."

Fox News Digital reached out to Yankee Stadium and Lincoln Hospital requesting comment.

Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: Manchester derby VAR officials stood down from weekend Premier League games
excerpt: Matt ‌Donohue, the video assistant referee (VAR) ⁠who ⁠allowed Erling Haaland’s winner in Manchester City’s 1-0 victory over Manchester ⁠United, has not been selected to officiate at any of next ⁠week...
body_text:
Matt ‌Donohue, the video assistant referee (VAR) ⁠who ⁠allowed Erling Haaland’s winner in Manchester City’s 1-0 victory over Manchester ⁠United, has not been selected to officiate at any of next ⁠weekend’s Premier League football fixtures.

Assistant VAR Blake Antrobus has also not been given any assignment after the refereeing body Pro Ref ‌acknowledged in a statement that VAR was wrong to allow Haaland’s decisive goal.

The decision was taken by chief refereeing officer Howard Webb and the management team, with neither ⁠official expected to return ⁠to duty until at least after the international break.

Haaland’s second-half strike was initially ruled out for ⁠offside before being awarded following a VAR review ⁠that determined the Norwegian ⁠striker was onside.

However, the refereeing body later said the VAR had failed to take into ‌account the impact of teammate Enzo Fernandez, who attempted to play the ‌ball ‌from an offside position.

United, who are 13th in the English top flight following the defeat, are next in action when they play Brighton in the League Cup on Wednesday. Their next Premier League game will be played at Fulham on Sunday.

City entertain Norwich City in the cup on Thursday, before hosting Sunderland on Sunday in the league, where they are level on points with leaders and defending champions Arsenal.

title: Goo Goo Dolls' John Rzeznik draws line on politics at concerts: 'I'm not going to lecture you'
excerpt:
Goo Goo Dolls frontman John Rzeznik said he won’t lecture fans about politics at concerts, arguing people from "every political stripe" can come together for the music.

Goo Goo Dolls frontman John Rz...
body_text:
Goo Goo Dolls frontman John Rzeznik said he won’t lecture fans about politics at concerts, arguing people from "every political stripe" can come together for the music.

Goo Goo Dolls frontman John Rzeznik said Wednesday during an "Everything Music" interview with producer Rick Beato that he refuses to lecture concertgoers about politics because fans from across the ideological spectrum come together for the same reason: to see a show.

While discussing why he believes live music remains important during divided times, Rzeznik said political and religious differences are not what matters when he takes the stage.

"I got people, fans, friends from every walk of life, every political stripe, everything," he said. "And I always stress, we got one thing in common because we're living in weird times. We got one thing in common, and that's we're all here to see a show, and I'm not going to lecture people about anything."

Goo Goo Dolls frontman John Rzeznik said he refuses to lecture fans about politics, saying concertgoers from "every political stripe" can come together for the music. (Getty Images)

DOLLY PARTON REFUSED TO PICK POLITICAL SIDES FOR DECADES: ‘I’M NOT IN POLITICS, I’M AN ENTERTAINER’

Entertainment commentator Christian Toto told Fox News Digital that artists can pay a price with their audiences when performances turn into political forums, particularly when celebrity political commentary is already widespread.

"Artists do risk alienating fans when they get on a soap box. That's always been true, but it's even more so today. Why? We're inundated with political screeds, particularly from the rich and famous. In many cases, the arguments being shared are one-dimensional and poorly thought out," Toto said.

"Plus, they're rarely spoken to change hearts or minds," he continued. "The commentary is typically angry and filled with partisan talking points. What does ‘Free Palestine’ mean to someone who questions that community's embrace of violence?"

Entertainment commentator Christian Toto told Fox News Digital that artists risk alienating fans when they turn expensive concerts into political lectures. (Getty Images)

JOHN RICH CLAIMS JELLY ROLL KNEW HE’D LOSE HALF HIS FANS OVER POLITICAL COMMENTS

Toto pointed to the cost of attending major concerts as another reason artists could frustrate audiences by devoting stage time to politics.

"Concert tickets are insanely high in 2026," he said. "Imagine forking over so much money and then, mid-concert, you get a political lecture. Who wants that? Kudos to Rzeznik for understanding that simple truth, one that eludes many ego-driven rockers."

Rzeznik’s approach mirrors comments Rolling Stones frontman Mick Jagger made earlier this year. Fox News Digital reported in July that Jagger viewed his job during concerts as helping audiences forget their problems for a few hours rather than preaching to them.

Rzeznik also criticized AI-generated music as "derivative" while discussing the renewed popularity of the Goo Goo Dolls’ 1998 hit "Iris." (Getty Images)

GOO GOO DOLLS SINGER HOSPITALIZED WITH PNEUMONIA; BAND CANCELS CONCERTS IN SOUTH AFRICA

Explaining his approach to performing, Jagger made clear he did not believe audiences came to see him for political instruction.

"I don't want to lecture them," Jagger said.

Other rock stars have faced a different reception after bringing politics into performances. In June, Bruce Springsteen and The Black Crowes frontman Chris Robinson faced backlash from some concertgoers following political remarks onstage.

Rzeznik told Beato he wants Goo Goo Dolls fans to instead leave a concert feeling better than when they arrived.

"I'm going to play a bunch of songs that, you know, and we're all going to leave here, and we're going to be happier and better for it. That's it," Rzeznik said.

The comments came amid renewed attention for Goo Goo Dolls and their 1998 hit "Iris." The band released a reimagined version of the song with Steve Aoki in March and spent summer touring with Neon Trees. An anniversary edition of the band's 1998 album "Dizzy Up the Girl," which featured "Iris," is scheduled for release Oct. 2.

Fox News Digital reached out to Rzeznik for comment, but did not immediately receive a response.

title: Lindsay Clancy juror denies bias allegations, wants 'conversation started' about women's mental health
excerpt: Paula Devlin, one of 11 jurors on the Lindsay Clancy trial who believed she was not criminally responsible for the deaths of her three children, explains the emotional toll of deliberations. (Rashid U...
body_text:
Paula Devlin, one of 11 jurors on the Lindsay Clancy trial who believed she was not criminally responsible for the deaths of her three children, explains the emotional toll of deliberations. (Rashid Umar Abbasi for Fox News Digital)

If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

WHITMAN, Mass. — An outspoken juror on the Lindsay Clancy murder trial is denying allegations of bias while acknowledging the case gave her a chance to have a "conversation started" on the topic of women's mental health and postpartum-related illnesses.

"We didn't know what was going on outside of that room, but we knew that we had a chance to get a conversation started that could change something, that could maybe stop this from ever happening again," said Paula Devlin, 65, in an interview with Fox News Digital. "I think, that's one of the reasons why we feel — or I feel — so strongly about this is that I hope that no other woman or husband has to go through this."

She made similar comments over the weekend, which prompted allegations that the jury approached the case with an agenda — claims she pushed back against Monday.

LINDSAY CLANCY JUROR SAYS PANEL SAW CASE AS CHANCE TO 'MAKE IT BETTER FOR OTHER WOMEN'

Paula Devlin speaks with a reporter in Whitman, Massachusetts, Monday, Sept. 13, 2026. Devlin was a juror in the murder trial of Lindsay Clancy. (Rashid Umar Abbasi for Fox News Digital)

"We looked at the evidence, and the evidence had holes in the prosecution's case," she said. "In the biggest piece of the whole case, the whole thing was based on mental health. How can you have bias if only women can go through postpartum depression? Only women can go through postpartum psychosis. Only women can deliver a baby. That's not biased. That's just a fact."

JUROR ON LINDSAY CLANCY TRIAL SAYS 'WE LET DOWN LINDSAY' FOLLOWING MISTRIAL

Clancy, a 36-year-old former delivery room nurse, sought help repeatedly, to no avail, Devlin said.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

Then in January 2023, she strangled her three children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months — with exercise bands and tried to kill herself. She survived a fall from a second-story window but was paralyzed.

Callan, left, Dawson and Cora Clancy. The three children were killed at their Duxbury, Massachusetts, home in January 2023. (Lindsay Marie Clancy/Facebook)

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

"I truly, truly in my heart believe that if Lindsay had got the help she really needed, those three children would still be here," Devlin said. "Those five people would still be a family."

Lindsay Clancy, charged with the murder of her three children in Duxbury in 2023, appears in Plymouth Superior Court on Friday, Feb. 20, 2026. (Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images)

LINDSAY CLANCY TRIAL: POSTPARTUM IS REAL, BUT CHILD KILLING DEMANDS ACCOUNTABILITY, VETERAN PROSECUTOR SAYS

A key flaw in the prosecution's case, she said, was that they had no witnesses who would say anything bad about Clancy.

"Nobody could find one bad thing to say about this person, and I would bet my house that those prosecutors looked everywhere to find somebody to be derogatory and say derogatory things about Lindsay," she said. "And nobody could."

PATRICK CLANCY SPEAKS OUT AFTER HUNG JURY IN LINDSAY CLANCY CASE, ADDRESSES PROSPECT OF ANOTHER TRIAL

On January 24, 2023, Clancy fatally strangled her three children in the basement of their Duxbury, Massachusetts, home using exercise resistance bands. She then cut her wrists and neck and jumped from a second-story window in a suicide attempt, leaving her partially paralyzed. (Greg Derr/Pool/The Patriot Ledger)

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

That includes her ex-husband and the victims' father, Patrick Clancy, Devlin added.

Still, she said, she's haunted by the children's faces.

"Those three little faces and just wondering if we missed something, if we didn't ask the right questions of each other, if we could have done better — it's hard not to feel like we failed," she said. "I mean everybody says we didn't fail, but it's hard to not feel that when you're given a task and you don't accomplish it."

body_text:
