title: WWE star Nattie shares insight on The Undertaker’s booking style in AAA
excerpt:
WWE star Nattie talks to OutKick about The Undertaker's impact on the AAA promotion.

The Undertaker ruled the WWE ring for decades as he developed his "Dead Man" persona and put the fear into any of ...
body_text:
WWE star Nattie talks to OutKick about The Undertaker's impact on the AAA promotion.

The Undertaker ruled the WWE ring for decades as he developed his "Dead Man" persona and put the fear into any of his opponents that would step up to him.

Those days are a thing of the past and The Undertaker has since switched his role from fearsome in-ring competitor to one of the creatives behind the AAA promotion in Mexico.

COMPLETE PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE ON OUTKICK

Undertaker looks on during NXT at 713 Music Hall in Houston, Texas, on July 22, 2025. (WWE via Getty Images)

The WWE legend has been among the minds behind AAA’s rise to prominence on the pro wrestling scene. Nattie, a legend in her own right, praised Undertaker for the creative direction he’s undertaken at AAA.

"’Taker is the man. Everybody loves working for ‘Taker. That’s why I think everybody that goes there like Chelsea Green has gone on the record saying, ‘I want to work for ‘Taker.’ She said she would text ‘Taker and ask him please let me do AAA," she told OutKick Dropkick. "And same with Roxanne (Perez), I know she wanted to do AAA.

"‘Taker has really elevated that promotion, along with Jeremy Borash who helps Undertaker run AAA with the family that had run it before WWE stepped in – they still kept management, they still kept people, they still kept the family. But ‘Taker has been involved, WWE has been involved, Jeremy Borash – they just elevated it."

Nattie noted that The Undertaker is different creatively from a Shawn Michaels, who helps run NXT, and Triple H (Paul Levesque), who is the Chief Content Officer for WWE.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Natalya Neidhart attends Build Series to discuss "Total Divas" at Build Studio on Oct. 25, 2017 in New York City. (Steve Zak Photography/FilmMagic)

"And so, the coolest thing about Undertaker is that his style is very different as a booker. It’s very different than Shawn Michaels. It’s very different than Triple H. But it doesn’t mean that any one of them is better than the other," she said. "It just means that ‘Taker has a different style.

"He loves aggression. He loves intensity. He loves selling. I like to say ‘Taker kinda loves violence. He’s just such a cool boss. He’ll give us advice, he’ll give us feedback but he also gives us support and encouragement and he really believes in us. And that’s so important. And he’s communicative. He was helping me for my entrance for last year’s Triplemania. He was helping me with different ideas. He’s the man."

The Undertaker poses in the ring during SmackDown at Wells Fargo Arena on May 20, 2008, in Des Moines, Iowa. (WWE via Getty Images)

AAA wrapped up Triplemania 34 with some massive matches and title changes that will certainly shake up the roster heading into its next show on Saturday night.

Ryan Gaydos is a senior editor for Fox News Digital.

title: Bob Mackie, legendary designer who dressed Cher, Tina Turner and Dolly Parton, dead at 87
excerpt:
Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.

Bob Mackie, the legendary fashion and costume designer known for dressing some of the biggest stars, died Monday. He was 87

"It is ...
body_text:
Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.

Bob Mackie, the legendary fashion and costume designer known for dressing some of the biggest stars, died Monday. He was 87

"It is with a heavy heart that we share the news that Mr. Bob Mackie passed away today," a post shared on his official Instagram read. "He lived his 87 years to the fullest, fulfilling his dream of being a Fashion and Costume Designer, which is all he ever wanted to do."

"His genius and extraordinary designs will live on forever, continuing to bring beauty into this world," the statement concluded.

Cher and Bob Mackie at Diana Vreeland's 14th Annual Costume Exhibit. (Ron Galella/Ron Galella Collection via Getty Images)

Fox News Digital reached out to a representative for additional comment.

Mackie was known for his glittering, theatrical creations that helped define the looks of stars such as Cher, Carol Burnett, Diana Ross, Dolly Parton and Tina Turner.

His career took off after he began designing for Mitzi Gaynor and then landed the job of creating costumes for "The Carol Burnett Show," remaining with the variety series throughout its 11-season run.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Don Ameche poses with Cher, who wears a Bob Mackie evening gown with a feather headdress. (Bettmann/Bettmann)

Among his most recognizable creations was Cher's dramatic feathered ensemble at the 1986 Academy Awards. His work earned him nine Emmy Awards, a Tony Award for "The Cher Show" and three Academy Award nominations.

"Nobody was allowed to even design a halter dress until Cher started wearing them on Sonny & Cher [in the ‘70s], and then all of a sudden they were in everybody’s collection," Mackie previously told People. "And then girls were showing way more skin than they should have, because Cher was showing more skin than she should have. But she looked good in it."

Dolly Parton wears a Bob Mackie design in 1987. (Jerry Fitzgerald/Getty Images)

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Diana Ross and Bob Mackie attend the 20th annual CFDA American Fashion Awards in New York City. (Ron Galella/Ron Galella Collection via Getty Images)

His designs — packed with sequins, feathers, beads and a healthy dose of showmanship — made Mackie one of Hollywood's most recognizable costume designers.

Mackie's work has endured for decades as younger stars have chosen to wear his archival work. Sabrina Carpenter has repeatedly dipped into the legendary costume designer’s archives for major appearances.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

Sabrina Carpenter wears vintage Bob Mackie at the 2024 VMA Awards. (Jamie McCarthy/WireImage)

One of Carpenter’s biggest Mackie moments came at the 2024 MTV Video Music Awards, when she walked the red carpet in a sparkling silver-and-white vintage Mackie gown originally created for Madonna’s 1991 Academy Awards performance.

Before his death, Mackie acknowledged that younger performers such as Carpenter, Miley Cyrus and Zendaya had developed a new appetite for his archival creations.

Miley Cyrus performs on stage wearing Bob Mackie during the 66th Annual Grammy Awards in 2024. (Valerie Macon/AFP via Getty Images)

title: UK politics: Farage hints that Reform’s £72m donations may not be legal under new elections bill - as it happened
excerpt:
In an interview about the donations, he said they are compliant with the law ‘today’

Nigel Farage has hinted that the donations to Reform UK worth £72m might not be legal under the legislation to tig...
body_text:
In an interview about the donations, he said they are compliant with the law ‘today’

Nigel Farage has hinted that the donations to Reform UK worth £72m might not be legal under the legislation to tighten elections law currently going through parliament.

He made the apparent concession in an interview with the BBC in which he strongly objected to the government’s plan to make a new law banning Britons who live abroad, or who have recently relocated to the UK, from giving more than £100,000 a year to political parties retrospective.

It seems likely that the law would apply to Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, the two cryptocurrency billionaires who have each pledged £36m to Reform UK.

In an interview, Chris Mason, the BBC’s political editor, asked Farage if he was sure that both donations were compliant with the law now, and “how we expect it soon to be”.

double quotation markBoth these donations are 100% compliant with the law today. Of that there is no question whatsoever.

Mason pointed out that Farage was saying “today” and he asked if Delo and Harborne were both resident in the UK on 25 March – after which the retrospective restrictions on donations by new arrivals will kick in when the representation of the people bill becomes law.

double quotation markI’m not going to go into their particular details. All I’m going to say is, with the law of the land as it stands, they are both compliant.

Now there is talk, and Angela Rayner was talking about this yesterday, there is talk of them retrospectively declaring donations illegally.

Well, that simply cannot be. If a government was allowed to do this, you know what would happen? There’d be a response the other way. We or the Conservatives would say, right, if you’re going to stop legitimate donors like this, we will then say to the trade unions, you can’t give money. And if you do that, you have collapsed the whole political system.

In fact, there has not just been “talk” of making the cap retrospective. The bill legislating for this has gone through the Commons, and MPs debated amendments creating these exact laws on Wednesday 2 September.

While laws applying retrospectively are rare, they are not unprecedented. Reform UK wants to pass retrospective legislation itself. For example, it plans to abolish indefinite leave to remain as an immigration status, including for people who already have it.

Farage’s position is different from the one adopted by his party over the weekend when Robert Jenrick, the Treasury spokesperson, said that Reform UK was confident the Delo and Harborne donations were “entirely in line with the law as it is and, as far as we know, the law as it’s going to be in the future”.

Nigel Farage has hinted that the donations to Reform UK worth £72m might not be legal under the legislation to tighten elections law currently going through parliament. (See 2.04pm.) For more comment on this story, do listen to the latest edition of the Guardian’s Politics Weekly UK podcast, featuring Pippa Crerar and Kiran Stacey.

Trade unions are set to launch an intervention on Tuesday on political donations after the head of Britain’s trade union movement, Paul Nowak, said the government must act to “stop the super-rich corrupting our politics.”

One of Britain’s steelworks is to come into public ownership after the government said it would take over Yorkshire-based Speciality Steel UK (SSUK).

Westminster’s time is coming to an end, the first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland have said at a landmark summit aimed at putting the UK’s Celtic nations on the path to independence referendums.

For a full list of all the stories covered on the blog today, do scroll through the list of key event headlines near the top of the blog.

Philip Rycroft is former permanent secretary who carried out the government review on the infuence of foreign money on British politics that led to the government deciding to impose a cap on the amount that can be donated by Britons living abroad, and a moratorium on donations in the form of cryptocurrency.

Wider reforms of the donation rules were outside his remit. But, in interviews today, he has said there should be a cap on the amount any person can donate.

double quotation markIt is absolutely true that political parties are essential for the democratic process and they need to raise money from private sources until we get to a point which is, I think a very long way off, when we have significant state funding.

So how do you square the circle? In my view the way you could do that is to have donation caps but to set them at least initially at a really quite a high level, for the sake of argument £1m a year from any individual, corporation or indeed trade union and that would allow the parties still to function without requiring state funding.

Rycroft also that if the government reduced spending limits during election periods, and impose spending limits outside election periods, that would also help because it would “so parties don’t need to raise so much money”.

The Labour MP Phil Brickell has written to the Electoral Commission asking it to investigate if the donations given to Reform UK by Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne worth a total of £72m are legitimate, HuffPost UK is reporting.

One of Britain’s steelworks is to come into public ownership after the government said it would take over Yorkshire-based Speciality Steel UK (SSUK). Alex Daniel has the story.

Ben Quinn is a Guardian political correspondent.

Pete Newman, a former counter-terrorism police commander in London, has been chosen by Reform UK to be its candidate in the upcoming Holborn and St Pancras byelection.

The former police officer has appeared recently in social media posts published by the party’s London mayoral candidate, Laila Cunningham, as it seeks to place crime and policing at the heart of its search for votes in the city.

double quotation markAs a former police detective, it depresses me to see the state of crime and policing in our capital. Residents no longer feel safe and our police officers are struggling to cope.

Police stations are closing left, right and centre, yet Labour don’t care and our Mayor continues to gaslight Londoners over their safety.

I’m standing to ensure that people in Holborn and St Pancras feel safe on their own streets again.

Reform said that Newman was a senior police detective between 2004-2009 at the Met working across London on crime reduction, public safety and counter terrorism security.

In the wake of the 7/7 bombings, he was said to have been charged with leading the response to the aftermath of the attack, specifically leading the Met in Westminster.
 Since retiring from the Met, Reform said Newman has worked as a security and investigative consultant, providing advice and investigative services to businesses.

It has also been announced today that Patrick Stillman, a Liberal Democrat councillor for West Hampstead and outgoing chairman of Camden Lib Dems, will be the Lib Dem candidate in the byelection. And Ewan Cameron, a former Camden councillor and local political campaigner, will be the Conservative representative.

None of these three candidates are seen as having much chance because the byelection is primarily seen as a contest between Labour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali, the leader of Camden Council, and Zack Polanski, the Green party’s leader.

In the Lords debate, Chris Rennard, a former Lib Dem chief executive, said that part of the problem with political donations went back to a decision taken by Tony Blair’s government.

In an attempt to end the “party spending arms race”, Labour imposed a £20m limit on what parties can spend in the 12 months before an election. But that was bigger than necessary – and later increased to £36m by the Tories before the 2024 election, he said.

Rennard said these rules introduced the concept of national spending which could still be targeted at individual constituencies.

double quotation markThis destroyed the concept of the level playing field in constituency campaigning that had applied since Gladstone’s government introduced the Corrupt and Illegal Practices Prevention Act of 1883.

As an example, Rennard said the £72m given to Reform UK “could legally be spent in 72 target constituencies over two years, providing for £1m on national spending in each of them”.

Back in the House of Lords, Theresa May, the former Conservative PM, has said that she particularly welcomes the proposals in the representation of the people bill that will impose a moratorium on parties accepting donations in the form of cryptocurrency.

She said the Bank of England described cryptoassets as “a way of storing value electronically outside of centralised systems and away from regulators”.

She said she had always been sceptical of cryptoassets, and when she served as home secretary she first came across them as “the currency of choice for criminal gangs”. They were also the currency of choice for hostile state actors, she said.

double quotation markIt is absolutely right, I think, that the government is moving to find ways to ensure that cryptoassets cannot be used as donations to political parties, but I simply say this to the government … There are loopholes in what the government is doing because donors are banned from using cryptoassets for donations to political parties, but not to candidates.

I would urge the government to look at this in particular because cryptoassets are used by people who want to avoid anybody knowing what they are doing. And in terms of our democracy and donations to parties or candidates, we actually want the transparency of knowing who is doing that donation, who is making those donations.

Commenting on the revelation about the size of Chris Wormald’s pay-off (see 4.43pm), Alex Burghart, the deputy Tory leader and shadow Cabinet Office minister, said:

double quotation markChris Wormald was just one of many civil servants and advisers fired by Keir Starmer as he tried to save his own skin.

This payout is another appalling waste of taxpayers’ money by Labour.

Whether it’s big payouts for fall guys, or gimmicky giveaways, this government is always happy to spend our money if it thinks it will benefit the Labour party.

Chris Wormald received a pay-off worth almost £860,000 after he was sacked by Keir Starmer as cabinet secretary, the government has revealed.

The figure was first revealed in a story in the Financial Times, and has today been published in the Cabinet Office’s annual report.

Explaining why the award was so high, the report says:

double quotation markThe total is made up of contractual compensation of £332,897 and additional severance of £526,598. The former cabinet secretary elected to take early payment of his pension. The majority of the total severance payment was used to ensure he could access the full value of his pension that would have been due at normal retirement age, rather than it being reduced for early payment.

Wormald was appointed by Starmer – but also sacked by him 14 months later, after Starmer concluded that a more dynamic cabinet secretary would improve the performance of his government. Wormald was replaced by Antonia Romeo.

As the FT reports, the payment to Wormald was signed off by Cat Little, who was then Cabinet Office permanent secretary. She needed a “ministerial direction” to agree the move because it did not comply with normal value-for-money rules.

double quotation markThe proposed award is greater than what Sir Chris Wormald would be contractually entitled to. However, I am informed that a settlement of this level is necessary given that this is a departure from a high-profile, unique role that has been agreed at very short notice.

Denis Campbell is the Guardian’s health policy editor.

The Alzheimer’s Society has lauded Andy Burnham’s history of campaigning to raise the profile of dementia in a statement following the death of his father Roy, who had Alzheimer’s disease.

Michelle Dyson, the charity’s chief executive, said:

double quotation markWe are deeply saddened by the news that Roy Burnham – the prime minister’s father – has died. Kenneth Roy Burnham had been living with Alzheimer’s disease.

The loss of a parent leaves an immeasurable gap in our lives. While every family’s experience is unique, many of us understand the long and often challenging journey that Alzheimer’s disease can bring, not only for the person living with the condition but for those who love them.

The prime minister has been a longstanding advocate for improving the lives of people affected by dementia, often drawing on his father’s experiences. As mayor of Greater Manchester, he supported dementia-focused initiatives delivered with us, including the expansion of our Singing for the Brain programme and ran alongside thousands at the Great North Run for Alzheimer’s Society in 2024.

Most importantly, he has consistently used his voice to highlight the urgent need for social care and dementia care reforms. 
  We send our heartfelt condolences to his family and to anyone else who has experienced the heartache of losing someone to dementia.

In the Lords, Teresa O’Neill, a shadow local government minister, quoted Winston Churchill saying changes to electoral rules should be implemented by agreeement in her speech on behalf of the Conservative party at the start of the elections bill debate.

She said some of the measures in the bill were deeply troubling because they were partisan.

In a reference to the restriction on donations from Britons living abroad, or only recently returned, she said:

double quotation markEven just the perception of partisan, targeted legislation risks breaking down longstanding political conventions and, crucially, trust in the system.

We will all have heard the reports this weekend of crypto donations to Reform UK. It’s our current understanding that these donations would be caught by the overseas contributors cap.

O’Neill asked the minister to clarify exactly who these rules would work, if necessary by letter after the debate.

Sharon Taylor told peers that the government is thinking of doing more to strengthen the “residency requirements” that limit how much Britons can give to political parties if they are not living in the UK.

In her speech opening the debate (see 4.07pm), she said:

double quotation markIn addition to introducing a robust regime that ensures donors contributing above the £100,000 annual cap must demonstrate a genuine and ongoing connection to the United Kingdom, we are considering how we will strengthen the residency requirements, including ensuring the length of time spent in the UK aligns with broader government policy.

In the Lords, peers have just started the second reading debate on the representation of the people bill. Sharon Taylor, a local government minister, is opening on behalf of the government.

She starts by saying she wants to make a reference to the “events of recent times”.

She recalls catching the train early in the morning with tradespeople, public sector workers and small business owners heading into work early and she goes on:

double quotation markIt’s a fundamental principle of our democracy that every one of their votes is exactly equal to the votes of millionaires, crypto bros and industry magnates, and it is that which sits at the front and centre of this bill.

We must put politics back under public control.

We all share concerns about the rise of big money and its ability to dominate public power.

At its heart, this bill is about renewing the foundations of our electoral system so that it remains fair, secure, transparent and accessible in the years ahead.

Rayner ended her speech at the TUC praising Andy Burnham. She said she was glad to hear him “talk about doing things the Labour way”.

And she said, as a former care worker who has campaigned for a better care system, she was particularly pleased about Burnham’s commitment to reform adult social care.

double quotation markAs a former care worker myself, I have waited my whole life for a prime minister to speak about social care the way Andy has, understanding what care workers do and the conditions that they face.

title: Bolsonaro 2.0: Brazil braces for the return of the far right
excerpt:
Neck-and-neck with Lula in polls, Flávio Bolsonaro fires up his base in the bellwether state of Minas Gerais – starting at the scene of his father’s stabbing

A giant banner of Brazil’s incarcerated f...
body_text:
Neck-and-neck with Lula in polls, Flávio Bolsonaro fires up his base in the bellwether state of Minas Gerais – starting at the scene of his father’s stabbing

A giant banner of Brazil’s incarcerated former president Jair Bolsonaro fluttered in the morning breeze as his eldest son, Flávio, touched down at an airfield on the fringe of a city that will soon help decide the future of one of the biggest democracies on earth.

“Brazil is rudderless. Brazil has no president and Brazil needs a president – and that president is Flávio Bolsonaro,” the far-right senator declared as he waded into the flock of supporters who had gathered to welcome him to Juiz de Fora, one of the largest cities in the battleground state of Minas Gerais.

With less than a month before nearly 159 million Brazilians choose their next leader on 4 October, the election appears on a knife-edge, with the incumbent leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and his challenger, Flávio Bolsonaro, neck-and-neck in the polls.

Bolsonaro’s campaign appears to have seized the momentum in recent weeks amid a slew of corruption scandals involving Lula’s son and the supreme court. That has prompted despair among progressives who fear their country could fall back into the hands of a radical rightwing movement that tried to grab power after the then-president, Jair Bolsonaro, lost the 2022 election to Lula.

Last September, Jair Bolsonaro received a 27-year jail sentence for spearheading that botched coup – a verdict supporters insist was unjust. But the ex-president and his accomplices are likely to be freed if his son wins power – a prospect that delights the hardcore Bolsonaristas who turned out to greet Flávio Bolsonaro wearing yellow football shirts and headbands reading: “Lula out!”

“Today is a moment of joy,” said Ulisses Lima, 50, a cybersecurity specialist with a Jesus Christ pendant around his neck. “Flávio represents change. He represents Brazil’s rescue from this socialist abyss we’ve spent so long warning about,” Lima added as supporters waited for the former president’s heir to arrive.

Nearby, another devotee, José Caldeira, fell to his knees and begged for divine intervention to get Bolsonaro out of house arrest. “God, free this nation! Amnesty and freedom for Bolsonaro!” Caldeira bellowed, raising his hands towards the sky.

A third man, Davi Frederico, held a banner celebrating Donald Trump, who has been accused of trying to swing the election in Bolsonaro’s favour through economic and diplomatic pressure. “Make Liberals Cry Again,” it said.

Juiz de Fora, an industrial and university city traditionally associated with the left, is also a key location for Brazil’s hard right. The city’s army headquarters was the launchpad for the 1964 coup that plunged Brazil into two decades of military rule. And it was in Juiz de Fora, on the eve of the 2018 election, that Jair Bolsonaro was stabbed in the gut while campaigning – an attack widely believed to have helped the former paratrooper seal his victory.

Bolsonaro’s shock win ushered in what, from a progressive perspective, were four abysmal years. Destruction of the Amazon rainforest and gun ownership skyrocketed, hundreds of thousands died during a Covid outbreak Bolsonaro was accused of mishandling, and the president’s authoritarian rhetoric and attacks on Brazil’s electronic voting system culminated in the 8 January 2023 riots in Brasília. The supreme court later called those disturbances part of a plot to “annihilate” the country’s democracy.

But the Bolsonaros still enjoy abundant support, and that devotion was visible as Flávio Bolsonaro’s motorcade crept towards the high street where his father was ambushed eight years ago.

“Let’s get the left out! Let’s get these motherfuckers out!” one elderly woman shrieked as the senator passed by on top of a sound truck stamped with the word: “Jesus”. Other fans, many senior citizens, waved Brazil flags from windows or stood on the sidewalk flashing victory signs with their hands.

“Barring some kind of leftwing trickery, Flávio Bolsonaro can already be considered president. All you have to do is take a look at the streets and social media,” claimed Nikolas Ferreira, an influential far-right congressman from Minas Gerais who has more than 9 million TikTok followers.

Alongside the enthusiasm, there were glimpses of the revulsion many Brazilians feel for the former president. One leftwinger took to his balcony with a loudhailer to taunt the Bolsonaristas as they paraded through town. “Trump! Trump! Get my daddy out of jail!” the dissenter jeered in reference to the US president’s attempts to help Bolsonaro escape punishment.

Minas Gerais, a mountainous mining and agricultural region that is larger than France and has 21 million inhabitants, is Brazil’s bellwether state. Since democracy returned in the 1980s, no candidate has won the presidency without triumphing here. In 2018, Jair Bolsonaro beat Lula’s candidate in Minas by more than 1.7m votes. Four years later, Lula reclaimed the state by fewer than 50,000. After landing in Minas last week, Flávio Bolsonaro said he was confident of clawing back the swing state, with one recent poll putting him ahead there.

“[Lula] is a president who you look at and see the past,” the 45-year-old senator said of his 80-year-old adversary. “With Flávio you can be sure that when people look at him, they see a modern government and a government of the future.”

Thomas Traumann, a political analyst who has written a book about his polarised country, said the election was too close to call. “It’s a coin flip,” said Traumann, who believed an unexpected scandal or last-minute “black swan” event could swing the election either way. On Friday, it emerged that Flávio Bolsonaro had been placed under police investigation over suspicions of corruption involving the funding of a big-budget biopic telling the story of the assassination attempt against his father in Juiz de Fora.

For progressive voters, the vision for a Flávio Bolsonaro administration laid out during his visit to Minas is the stuff of nightmares. “I think Flávio Bolsonaro’s presidency is going to be Jair Bolsonaro 2.0,” said Bruno Engler, a Bolsonarista lawmaker from Minas’ capital, Belo Horizonte.

Engler believed a top priority would be zero-tolerance policing, with the younger Bolsonaro pledging an iron-fisted crackdown on criminals his father has compared to cockroaches. “Thugs who don’t surrender will be arrested or neutralised,” Engler vowed, predicting gun laws would be loosened.

Speaking on the street corner where his father was knifed, Flávio Bolsonaro vowed to pack Brazil’s 11-member supreme court with five conservative judges “who are against abortion [and] against drugs”. “We’re going to give the streets back to the Brazilian people … We’re going to lower the age of criminal responsibility. We are going to introduce chemical castration for rapists,” shouted the candidate, who wore a bullet-proof vest.

Those pledges prompted whoops of excitement from the crush of supporters below Bolsonaro’s truck. Dozens ofmobile phones captured the candidate’s every word. But amid the rightwing rejoicing there was fear and trepidation, too.

Lennon César, a law student and leftwing activist who had come to confront Bolsonaro’s fans, voiced incredulity that less than four years after Jair Bolsonaro’s failed power grab, tens of millions of Brazilians seemed poised to vote for his son.

“We were the victims of an attempted coup – and his father was the perpetrator,” recalled César, 28. “It’s terrifying. And the thing that worries me most is that the general public doesn’t really seem to get what’s happening. Brazilians have short memories when it comes to the past.”

As a black, gay man, César felt particular dread at the prospect of a second Bolsonaro presidency, given the patriarch’s hostility to minorities.

César vowed to vote for Lula, Brazil’s first working-class president, calling him the only leader who paid attention to the poor. “If today I’m studying for a law degree it’s because one of Lula’s government programmes allowed me to achieve that,” he said, warning: “These people … might destroy it all.”

A few blocks away, a graffiti artist had spray painted their own message of disapproval on to the facade of Bolsonaro’s Juiz de Fora HQ. “Facists [sic],” it read.

title: Russian strike on passenger train will not deter Ukraine’s backers, Nato chief says
excerpt:
Mark Rutte says attack that narrowly missed Boris Johnson and David Petraeus shows Vladimir Putin’s desperation

The head of Nato has said a Russian drone attack on a train close to Ukraine’s border w...
body_text:
Mark Rutte says attack that narrowly missed Boris Johnson and David Petraeus shows Vladimir Putin’s desperation

The head of Nato has said a Russian drone attack on a train close to Ukraine’s border with Poland would not deter Kyiv’s western backers.

Mark Rutte said the strike on a passenger train showed how desperate Vladimir Putin had become. “He thinks that he can stops us from supporting Ukraine and that he can undermine our unity. He is wrong. Our answer is to increase support,” the Nato general secretary said.

European leaders have condemned the strike in which a Russian drone hit a passenger train on Ukraine’s border with Poland on Sunday shortly after a convoy of high-level diplomats and former leaders had passed through.

The earlier train, which was carrying the former UK prime minister Boris Johnson was running ahead of schedule, may have been the target of the Russian drone strike, Ukrainian Railways has said.

A spokesperson forthe UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, struck a similar note to Rutte, saying the attack “was a futile attempt by Russia to undermine our support for Ukraine. It will not deter us.”

The French foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, said the goal of the attacks was “to intimidate Europeans, discourage and above all divide them”.

The EU’s high representative for foreign and security policy, Kaja Kallas, said the strike “was clearly a message to the western world”. Speaking on the sidelines of an Arctic conference in Finland, she said: “I think the question for us is what do we take from that message? I think we should act the opposite. We should show that we are there for Ukraine and we are not scared off, because otherwise, you know, Russia will just achieve what they want, which is the submission of Ukraine.”

A spokesperson for Kallas added: “We strongly condemn the latest Russian strikes near the Ukraine-Poland border, including the attack against the passenger train,” and referenced a recent EU decision to approve a €6.1bn tranche of the €90bn loan for Ukraine. “We are acting on the front to equip Ukraine better to defend itself, and we will continue to stand firmly with Ukraine and its right to defend itself against Russian aggression,” the spokesperson said.

Overnight attacks across Ukraine involving more than 450 Russian drones and missiles killed at least six people and injured more than 40. Ukraine’s air force said it had intercepted 405 drones and four missiles.

Western Ukraine, which is typically quieter than Kyiv or the eastern frontline zones, was particularly badly hit.

The strikes, which prompted air raid warnings in Poland, came as EU diplomats met in Brussels on Monday for last-ditch talks on the rollover of the bloc’s sanctions against more than 2,600 Russian individuals and entities involved in supporting Vladimir Putin’s war. The sanctions are due to expire on Tuesday but their prolongation is being held up by a dispute about whether to remove an individual from the list.

Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote on Telegram on Sunday: “Ukrainians are fighting every day to prevent these strikes from spreading further into Europe, giving their lives and preventing the aggression from expanding.”

Ukrainian Railways, which operates the line, said a train carrying several security advisers from European countries as well as Johnson and the former Swedish prime minister Carl Bildt, had passed through the border crossing shortly before the drone strike.

The diplomatic train, Ukrainian Railways said, had left ahead of schedule and could have been the target of the Russian drone. Another train, with former CIA Director David Petraeus on board, was still at Yahodyn station when the drone struck, according to the rail operator.

The Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, warned on Sunday that intensifying Russian attacks in Ukraine in the coming weeks could affect Poland, as he chaired an emergency meeting after the Russian drone attacks near the border.

“The coming weeks and months will be a period of very intensive actions on the Russian side,” he said, adding Poland “cannot rule out that this escalation will also affect our territory”.

He added that Poland had been tipped off by its security services, and by intelligence agencies from allied countries, that an attack such as this was likely. “We knew that the Russian plan would include an attempt to disrupt, paralyse, and perhaps even destroy Ukrainian border crossings,” Tusk said.

Multiple injuries including bruising and fractures have been documented by a health service supporting people returned to France under the controversial “one in, one out” scheme.

The pilot scheme, which the French call “one for one”, involves one asylum seeker who crosses the Channel in a small boat being returned to France in return for another in northern France being legally brought to the UK to claim asylum. The scheme is due to end on 1 October.

Samusocial de Paris (SSP) has been commissioned by Île-de-France’s regional health agency to provide healthcare for asylum seekers returned to France in the first eight days after their deportation from the UK, when they are accommodated in a shelter in Paris.

They have documented the cases of 90 returnees between 22 January and 7 June 2026. All are young men, mostly in their 20s and early-30s, who sought sanctuary in the UK after fleeing a variety of conflict zones including Eritrea, Sudan and Afghanistan.

Approximately 1,400 people have been forcibly removed to France by the Home Office since the scheme began in August 2025, although some have subsequently returned to the UK in lorries or small boats.

European leaders joined forces to highlight growing competition in the Arctic, where global warming is opening new shipping routes, governments are vying for vast natural resources and a Russian military buildup is heightening security concerns.

The leaders, mostly from Nordic and Baltic countries, put a spotlight on environmental challenges, economic opportunities and military vulnerabilities at a time of doubts about whether the United States, through Nato, will remain a bulwark against Russia.

“This region has become a geopolitical hotspot,” German chancellor Friedrich Merz told a joint news conference, insisting a new EU focus should complement Nato’s work. “Russia is building up its military capabilities here, and Russia uses its presence for hybrid activities every day.”

Prime minister Petteri Orpo of Finland, which hosted the meeting in the capital of Lapland that’s home to a Santa Claus village, noted “high demand for concrete EU action in the Arctic” and a changing security environment.

“The Arctic has emerged as the central arena of great power competition,” he said.

The two-day gathering that began Sunday comes after a Norwegian seizure of a Russian vessel earlier this month in the remote Arctic archipelago of Svalbard at the request of Ukraine.

Meanwhile, Sweden’s neighbour, Finland, has ⁠joined France’s initiative to extend the reach of its nuclear deterrent through collaboration with partner ⁠European countries, Reuters reported.

In response to US president Donald Trump’s expressions of concern ⁠about the US security commitment to Europe and to the security implications of the Ukraine war, ⁠France in March announced the Forward Nuclear Deterrence Initiative.

“The initiative ​is first and ‌foremost about strengthening European ‌security. It reinforces Europe’s responsibility for its own defence and ‌helps prevent escalation,” Finland’s president Alexander Stubb said in a post on X.

Under the initiative, the French president alone has the authority to decide when nuclear weapons are used, in contrast to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, ‌which has a shared Nuclear Planning Group.

However, it offers joint exercises, the possible short-term deployment of nuclear-capable ​assets on allied territory and deeper consultation.

Finland’s defence minister Antti Häkkänen said in a separate statement that the agreement was a “natural step” after other Nordic countries, such as Norway, ⁠Sweden and Denmark, joined the initiative earlier in the ​year.

Jennifer Rankin in Brussels and Charlotte Higgins and Amy Hawkins in Kyiv

Catching up with other news from across Europe, the head of Nato has said a Russian drone attack on a train close to Ukraine’s border with Poland would not deter Kyiv’s western backers.

Mark Rutte said the strike on a passenger train showed how desperate Vladimir Putin had become.

The earlier train, which was carrying the former UK prime minister Boris Johnson and the former CIA chief David Petraeus and running ahead of schedule, may have been the target of the Russian drone strike, Ukrainian Railways has said.

Early signals are promising for the opposition bloc, as Social Democrats are seemingly encouraged by the Centre party’s openness to talk about the future government.

Foreign policy spokesperson Morgan Johansson said the party’s conditions on not letting fringes control the government (13:53) “sound very good.”

“It’s one of the pieces of the puzzle that needs to be in place to solve this,” he said, quoted by SVT.

“Everyone on this side wants to change the government. That’s the starting point,” he added.

But any formal talks are likely to start only after we know the official results later this week.

Since the party was founded in 1988, the story of the far-right Sweden Democrats (SD) has been one of such continuous growth that a triumph in Sunday’s general election seemed inevitable.

In 2022, they capitalised on electoral gains – and the desperation of right-leaning parties to form a minority administration – and almost made their way into government.

A supporting role in prime minister Ulf Kristersson’s Tidö coalition earned the party, which has neo-Nazi roots, huge influence and mainstream acceptance by the political establishment.

This year’s election had been billed as final confirmation they were no longer pariahs but serious political heavyweights.

Early in the campaign, Kristersson announced that, if his coalition were to win, the SD would take key ministerial positions.

But Sunday’s results suggest the march of the far right into the heart of Sweden’s government has been halted – for now.

Having fallen from Sweden’s second biggest party to third place and, with the right-leaning parties unlikely to be able to form a coalition, the SD appear to have lost their route into government.

The Centre Party is expected to play an important role in any post-election talks.

Although aligned with the opposition, the party made clear this morning that potential coalition partners – including Magdalena Andersson’s Social Democrats – “will need to see the big picture” and not let fringe powers dictate policy.

The party has long been critical of its potential future government partner in the Left Party, which feels emboldened by its strong election result and expected to demand a shift leftwards and its policies to be reflected by any future administration.

The projected result “shows the voters neither want to an economic turn leftwards, not a large role for the [far-right] Sweden Democrats,” party secretary Hannes Hervieu told SVT.

“There is no demand for fringe politics, but a desire for political stability,” he said, adding that the party would bring these points to the Social Democrats.

Curiously, prime minister Ulf Kristersson made similar noises last night about building an alternative majority around centre-right economic policies, but do not read too much into this: it’s still a very long way to go before that means anything more than just early post-election talk.

While the Social Democrats are understandably raring to take a crack at forming the next government, it’s easy to overlook that, despite coming out on top again, the party has actually lost ground since 2022 – recording its lowest vote share since universal suffrage was introduced in 1921.

With 95% of votes counted, the party sits at 28.1%, down more than two percentage points from 2022 (30.3%) and below its previous low of 28.3% in 2018.

Leader Magdalena Andersson was briefly asked about it last night, but waved these questions away, at least for now, as the focus is obviously elsewhere.

But leading Social Democrats are not exactly impressed by Kristersson’s chill approach.

The party’s foreign policy spokesperson, Morgan Johansson, accused him to trying to “cling on” to power, saying it was an “unsightly” behaviour, Expressen reported.

“If [the governing coalition] Tidö no longer has a majority, he will probably have to face the consequences of that.”

But in a stark warning highlighting just how tricky the government formation process is likely to be, Kristersson also said that if all parties stick to their red lines, “Sweden will not have a government.”

It’s clear he has some appetite for exploring a different majority to the red bloc.

Perhaps we should all just channel the Swedish PM, Ulf Kristersson, who essentially said this morning he was “going to take it pretty easy” until the final results are in.

He says there are some conversations scheduled in the meantime – including with fellow coalition leaders this evening – but he essentially wants to see the final results show first.

He also repeats his last night’s suggestion of exploring alternative majorities in the parliament.

One possible option could involve the Centre party switching sides, but it’s not immediately obvious how Kristersson would get them to accept a government with the far-right Sweden Democrats with it.

Senior figures in the Social Democratic party are meeting this morning with party leader Magdalena Andersson to discuss next steps.

The party topped the polls – that is certain – and is most likely to have a first go at forming the next government, but it will have to navigate the complex and often openly contradictory demands of the left-leaning bloc.

It remains to be seen whether they can get the Left Party to work with the Centre Party in particular, given rumbles on both sides about the feasibility of such an alliance.

But today’s doorstep comments suggest there is no rush just yet: all parties will want to wait for the final results on Wednesday or Thursday before committing to exploratory talks.

Party secretary Tobias Baudin confirmed, however, that he has exchanged texts with colleagues in other parties, SVT reported.

Asked about potential differences, he told P1 that he was “completely convinced” the parties would give it out with some “give and take” for all involved.

Hej from Stockholm as the dust settles (a bit) after a hectic election night.

With 95% of votes counted overnight, the left-leaning opposition bloc – led by Magdalena Andersson’s Social Democrats – has widened its lead to three seats, leading 176 to 173 against the reigning centre-right coalition and their far-right partners in Sweden Democrats.

Formally, the result is not settled yet: there is only some 28,600 votes separating the two blocs, with 6% of the votes yet to be counted – and that includes some 200,000 votes expected to come and be counted only on Wednesday.

Still, the Swedish public broadcaster SVT said last night it was 90% confident that the opposition would clinch the victory, even accounting for all the votes yet to be counted.

There is plenty of time for early exploratory talks: the parliament won’t meet until 28 September, when its due to elect a new speaker, and any votes on who could be the next prime minister can only come after that.

But the process of forming the new government could take weeks if not months leaving Sweden in a state of political limbo at a time of unprecedented geopolitical uncertainty in Europe.

No doubt first text messages, frantic WhatsApp or Signals, and phone calls are already exchanged today.

I will be here to cover all this drama for you.

It’s Monday, 14 September 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

title: How Israel systematically dismantles Palestinian life in occupied West Bank
excerpt:
Bethlehem, occupied West Bank – On any given week, Palestinians across the occupied West Bank can experience dozens of what appear to be isolated acts of Israeli violence and suppression.

In early Se...
body_text:
Bethlehem, occupied West Bank – On any given week, Palestinians across the occupied West Bank can experience dozens of what appear to be isolated acts of Israeli violence and suppression.

In early September, Israeli forces killed two teenagers during a military raid in al-Mughayyir, east of Ramallah. Days later in Masafer Yatta, Israeli forces demolished every home in Khirbet al-Tabban, leaving about 70 people, including 30 children, without shelter. In Qusra, south of Nablus, settlers have kept three families under siege inside their homes for more than a month, cutting off their water and power.

In a new report published on Monday, Israeli rights group B’Tselem argued these are not separate incidents. Together, they work towards a single end: Making Palestinian life on the land unsustainable and replacing it with permanent Israeli control. The reality in the West Bank, the group said, is “neither a temporary crisis nor a collection of random human rights violations”.

Instead, it is “an accelerated and explicit phase in an ongoing project of elimination that operates within the Israeli apartheid regime and is driven by a settler-colonial logic of dispossession, displacement, and the establishment of Jewish-Israeli sovereignty”, the publication – called The Elimination Project – added.

Drawing on nearly 2,000 Palestinian testimonies, the report said that seemingly separate Israeli violations are part of what it called “a comprehensive mechanism of elimination”.

By “elimination”, B’Tselem referred to the systematic dismantling of Palestinian society, eroding its institutions, economy, freedom of movement and social life.

The report placed this within what it called the “basic logic of settler colonialism”: Establishing “permanent settler sovereignty over a territory already inhabited by an Indigenous people” by “pushing them out, dispossessing them and dismantling their collective existence”.

It identifies five interconnected fronts through which that process operates: Violence and intimidation, movement restrictions, economic strangulation, social and political destruction, and ethnic cleansing and territorial takeover.

B’Tselem traced that logic to the 2017 “Decisive Plan” authored by Bezalel Smotrich, now Israel’s finance minister. The plan, the group said, gave Palestinians three choices: Accept Jewish supremacy while giving up their national claims, leave, or face violent suppression.

None of this is new, the report argued; the mechanism has run for decades. What has changed is that it has grown far more severe and open, escalating since the current far-right government took office in late 2022 and sharply after the start of the genocidal war against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip in October 2023.

For roughly 3.5 million Palestinians in the West Bank and occupied East Jerusalem, that system is felt in the steady narrowing of daily life: Roads they cannot use, land they cannot reach, and fewer places where they can safely live, work and move.

By December 2025, Israel had at least 925 physical obstacles set up across the West Bank, the most the United Nations has recorded in two decades.

Yusef Kashur, a driver and father of six from Dura, south of Hebron, told B’Tselem that the growing network of gates and checkpoints had turned his work into a “torment”, forcing him onto long, dangerous backroads and to turn down fares he once relied on.

“These drives are exhausting, take a very long time, and the fuel costs so much that I don’t make enough to cover our household needs,” he said.

The restrictions feed a wider collapse. Under an occupation that controls its borders, trade and revenue, the West Bank economy has little room of its own, and it has buckled: Unemployment at the end of last year had roughly doubled to 27.5 percent compared to October 2023, driven in part by the freezing of work permits for about 115,000 Palestinians.

The squeeze is deliberate, the report argued: A family that cannot earn is easier to uproot, and when Palestinians fall back on their own land, the pressure follows them there.

After losing his job inside Israel, Jamil Abu Rayan turned to his grapevines near Halhul, only to find settlers had established an illegal outpost at his main plot. Soldiers also barred him from another plot, calling it “[Israeli] state land”.

He told B’Tselem he lost about 60 percent of his 2025 grape harvest and that he can no longer properly work his land.

Recounting a late January attack in the South Hebron Hills, where entire communities face forcible displacement, Isma’il Khalayleh told the rights group earlier this year that a settler pressed a rifle to his forehead and gave him a deadline: “I’m giving you 24 hours to leave this place.”

Agricultural and grazing outposts have “violently taken control” of nearly 20 percent of the West Bank, according to Israeli settlement-watchdog group Peace Now. More than 1,600 settler attacks were recorded by the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) last year.

The same pressure extends to where Palestinians can build; Israeli authorities make it “virtually impossible for Palestinians to obtain building permits”, according to OCHA, leaving many families who build without them under constant threat of Israeli demolition.

As Palestinian communities are cleared, more illegal Israeli settlements expand. The current government has approved a record 104 new settlements since 2022.

The suppression also extends to the institutions that hold Palestinian society together, with B’Tselem documenting a series of raids and closure orders faced by charities, trade unions and universities.

Ahmad Dweikat told the rights group that in May 2026, soldiers ransacked a Nablus association he co-founded to help women, children and families, confiscating computers and cash, including money set aside for orphans.

Running beneath all of it is the military’s lethal force. B’Tselem counted about 1,087 Palestinians killed by Israeli forces in the West Bank since October 2023, roughly a quarter of them children.

Among them was Jamil Hanani, a 17-year-old boy from Beit Furik who was shot during an army raid on the town. “It’s as if they go out hunting, only they’re hunting human beings,” his father, ‘Atef Hanani, told B’Tselem.

For years, foreign governments have urged Israel to show restraint. That framing misses the point, B’Tselem argued: The violence, closures and demolitions are not failures of the system, but the system working as intended.

Sanctioning an individual settler, reopening a road or freezing a single settlement plan would “leave intact the structure that produces violence, dispossession, and oppression”, it said.

Seen this way, the question is not whether each individual act is an isolated violation, but what they produce together: A steadily shrinking space for Palestinians to live, work, build and remain on their land.

And the West Bank, the report argued, cannot be read apart from Gaza. The two are “different manifestations of the same regime project, directed against Palestinians’ ability to exist as a people”.

title: Ex-CIA director John Brennan subpoenaed in Trump ‘grand conspiracy’ investigation
excerpt:
Subpoena is among a flurry issued in recent weeks as part of DoJ inquiry into alleged conspiracy against Trump

The former CIA director John Brennan has been subpoenaed to testify next month before a ...
body_text:
Subpoena is among a flurry issued in recent weeks as part of DoJ inquiry into alleged conspiracy against Trump

The former CIA director John Brennan has been subpoenaed to testify next month before a Florida grand jury as part of a Department of Justice investigation into whether former law enforcement and intelligence officials conspired against Donald Trump, one of his lawyers said Monday.

Ken Wainstein, an attorney for Brennan, disclosed in a court filing that prosecutors last Thursday presented him with a subpoena for Brennan to appear before a grand jury in Fort Pierce, Florida, on 15 October.

He said he was told that the subpoena relates to a “far-reaching” criminal inquiry examining a loosely defined theory that the government officials who have investigated Trump over the last decade, including over Russia election interference in 2016 and his more recent retention of classified documents at his Mar-a-Lago estate, conspired to deprive Trump of his civil rights. The subpoena to Brennan is among a flurry that have been issued in recent weeks.

Wainstein said he was informed by a prosecutor that Brennan remains a target in a Washington-based investigation into whether he lied to Congress in 2023, a claim the former CIA director and his attorneys have consistently denied. Subpoenas demanding testimony before a grand jury in that false statements probe were issued in spring, then abruptly withdrawn in favor of voluntary interviews.

The subpoena was delivered on the same day that Joe diGenova, the prosecutor who had been leading what is casually known as the “grand conspiracy” investigation, abruptly resigned amid what a person familiar with the matter has described as displeasure from the justice department and White House over the pace and management of the investigation.

The justice department has not publicly announced a replacement for diGenova. The member of the investigative team with whom Wainstein spoke was Kurt Olsen, a lawyer who unsuccessfully pushed the justice department in 2020 to back the Trump’s false claims that the 2020 election had been stolen from him.

The subpoena was disclosed hours ahead of a court hearing in Washington in a lawsuit brought by Brennan. The former CIA director is seeking a court order that would require the preservation of all records from the investigations targeting him, saying such documents would be essential for him to challenge any potential indictment on vindictive prosecution grounds.

title: Texas Democrat Jasmine Crockett under fire for honoring Chris Brown at concert
excerpt:
Congresswoman awarded the convicted abuser and musician a congressional record recognition in Arlington

Democratic US representative Jasmine Crockett is under fire for honoring musician Chris Brown, ...
body_text:
Congresswoman awarded the convicted abuser and musician a congressional record recognition in Arlington

Democratic US representative Jasmine Crockett is under fire for honoring musician Chris Brown, a convicted abuser, with an official recognition at a Texas concert over the weekend.

Crockett, a Texas congresswoman, awarded Brown and R&B musician Usher a congressional record recognition at a performance in Arlington, Texas, on Saturday. Appearing alongside Texas state representative Venton Jones, Crockett said she was there to “honor” Brown and Usher.

“We are experiencing Black joy at the highest level,” she said, according to video from the concert. “And I wanted to make sure we document that at the congressional level. So let’s give it up again for Chris Brown.”

A congressional record recognition is a ceremonial honor in which a member of Congress can enter a specific person or achievement into the official congressional record.

Brown pleaded guilty in 2009 to felony assault against his then girlfriend, music star Rihanna. He also awaits sentencing in a UK incident where prosecutors alleged he hit a music producer over the head with a bottle. Brown pleaded guilty to a charge of “affray” in that case.

Crockett lost the Democratic primary for US Senate in Texas earlier this year to James Talarico, a state representative now running against Republican Ken Paxton in a race that’s considered a toss-up and a key target for Democrats.

Since her loss, Crockett has so far not campaigned with Talarico, with some people online calling attention to her choice not to campaign with the Democratic Senate nominee and instead appear with Brown.

Roxane Gay, the author, wrote on social media platform Threads: “What the hell is (Jasmine Crockett) thinking? This is such a bizarre and unacceptable misstep.” She later added that Crockett didn’t mention voting or endorse candidates in the appearance.

“She just flew on stage and gave a known abuser of Black women (multiple allegations past and recent) a congressional honor,” Gay posted.

Crockett has said she “will be campaigning down ballot” when asked in recent weeks by CNN’s Laura Coates whether she would be campaigning with Talarico, saying she wanted to make sure that people in lower-profile races weren’t getting “overshadowed” by a focus just on the top of the ticket.

Some defended Crockett, saying her appearing with Jones, the state representative, at the concert before thousands of people was using her platform to get voters to turn out for the down ballot.

Crockett did not respond to a request for comment.

title: Country singer Brian 'Nashville' Duckworth, voice behind family band Taylor Made, dies at 56
excerpt:
Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.

Country singer Brian "Nashville" Duckworth has died at the age of 56.

According to an obituary shared by his family, the singer die...
body_text:
Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.

Country singer Brian "Nashville" Duckworth has died at the age of 56.

According to an obituary shared by his family, the singer died at his home Sept. 7.

His family, with whom Duckworth was part of the band Taylor Made, shared in the obituary that, while pursuing a career as a country music star, he "was a devoted dump truck driver for Wolfe’s Excavating," earning him the nickname, "Truck Boss."

They added that "he truly enjoyed" the job "because it allowed him to spend his days outdoors."

"Music was also a special part of his life. He loved to sing and proudly performed with his family band, Taylor Made. Brian never passed up an opportunity to share his voice, earning him the affectionate nickname 'Nashville.'"

DOLLY PARTON'S SISTER REVEALS ‘LAST THING’ COUNTRY LEGEND ASKED OF HER BEFORE DEATH

Country singer Brian Duckworth died at the age of 56 on Sept. 7. (Greg Duckworth Facebook)

Duckworth grew up signing with his brother, Greg, and his sister, Wendy Williams, with the trio coming together in 2008 to form the band I-79 performing under that name for the first time at the Colgate Country Showdown.

They later changed their name to Taylor Made and made a name for themselves with hit songs such as "Things You Don’t Grow Out Of," which reached No. 36 on the Billboard Indicator chart.

He is survived by his wife of nearly 16 years, Tina, his six children, Zach, Ashton, Logan, Kayla, Michael and Matt, as well as his four grandchildren and five brothers and sisters.

"Above all, Brian treasured his family and the special memories they created together," the obituary read. "He also dearly loved his faithful fur family, who were constant companions and brought him great comfort and happiness. Brian’s love of family, music, and the outdoors will forever remain in the hearts of all who knew and loved him."

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Brian Duckworth, right, was in a band with his two siblings, Greg Duckworth, left, and Wendy Williams called Taylor Made. (Taylor Made Facebook)

His niece, Brianna Duckworth Kazner, shared a video on her Facebook account from her wedding, saying she is "having a hard time believing" that is "the last time Taylor Made sang together."

"I grew up watching my dad, Aunt Wendy, and Uncle Brian perform at fairs and festivals until I was finally old enough to join them on a few occasions," Kazner wrote. "As I’ve gotten older and started writing my own music, I knew the guy to call whenever I got creatively ‘stuck.’ He truly had such a way with song lyrics that I knew without a doubt Uncle Brian would pull me out of the songwriter’s slump."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Brian Duckworth, left, with his Taylor Made bandmate siblings, Wendy Williams and Greg Duckworth. (Taylor Made Facebook)

She shared that they recently spoke on the phone, "about a song idea he had," adding, "I can't count the number of times we got to sing together but it will have never been enough."

A cause of death was not stated in the obituary.

Duckworth will be laid to rest at Floral Hills Memorial Garden on Monday.

Lori A. Bashian is an entertainment news writer at Fox News Digital.

title: USA edge Spain to book Women’s Basketball World Cup final against France
excerpt:
The United States will take on France in the final of the women’s basketball World Cup after scraping to a 76-66 semifinal win over Spain in Berlin.

Underdogs Spain, whose best-ever result was reachi...
body_text:
The United States will take on France in the final of the women’s basketball World Cup after scraping to a 76-66 semifinal win over Spain in Berlin.

Underdogs Spain, whose best-ever result was reaching the 2014 final against the Americans, levelled the scores at 58-all at the end of the third quarter against the defending champions on Saturday.

But the experience of the 11-time champions told in the final period as USA outscored their opponents by 10 to seal victory.

Led by 16 points from Breanna Stewart and 13 from Kahleah Copper, USA extended their winning streak at the tournament to 35 matches, a run that dates back to a semifinal defeat by Russia in 2006.

Sunday’s clash with France will be a rematch of the 2024 Paris Olympics gold medal match, which the Americans won by just one point.

“That’s over, you know what I mean? We won that game and that game is over, and this is a completely new game tomorrow,” Stewart told reporters when asked about the 2024 final.

“Everybody has their own things that continue to motivate them … but this is one game to win the gold medal in the World Cup in Berlin, and that’s our entire focus.”

It was another disappointing night, though, for Indiana Fever guard Caitlin Clark, who scored just one point and turned the ball over twice under intense pressure from the Spanish defence.

Spain made a fast start and built an eight-point lead midway through the first quarter.

The Americans found their rhythm and controlled much of the second and third quarters, edging ahead as Copper and Stewart kept the scoreboard ticking over.

But, as they had against Italy, the Americans allowed their intensity to drop, and Spain fought back, finishing the third quarter on a 9-2 run to draw level.

Spain had the 12,650-strong crowd behind them as a stunning upset seemed on the cards, but the Americans stood tall when it mattered, starting the final quarter with a 12-2 burst to regain control.

France advanced to the final for the first time after an 86-64 victory over host nation Germany earlier in the day.

Gabby Williams top scored with 22 points for the Olympic silver medallists, who preserved their unbeaten record at the tournament going into Sunday’s decider in Berlin.

The US-born Williams, who also dished out five assists and recorded four steals, was the constant threat on both ends of the floor for the French.

Admitting she was “on a mission”, Williams told BeIN Sports: “I just want to give it my all.

“You never know when you’ll get an opportunity like this. You don’t know if it’ll be the last one. So, I’m just going to give everything.”

Marieme Badiane told reporters the French would not be daunted by the prospect of trying to stop the American juggernaut.

“We all realise that we can go for the ultimate prize. That’s the goal now. We aren’t stopping here. No one is going to let up.”

Outsiders Germany swept past European champions Belgium in their quarterfinal clash for a first semifinal appearance as a unified country, with East Germany having made the final four in 1967.

France burst out of the blocks early, but the Germans stayed hot on their heels, trailing by just two at the end of the opening period.

France’s quality told as the match went on and they scored nine unanswered points to begin the second half, surging into a 16-point lead.

Alexis Peterson and Emily Bessoir hit threes in the final quarter as the Germans cut the lead to nine to stay within touch, but France pulled away again with a 12-0 run to close out the match.
