title: Abdul El-Sayed touts ‘whole a--’ medical credentials while defending sex changes for children
excerpt:
The Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate candidate argued that medical decisions should be left to patients, parents and doctors, who went to "whole a--" medical school.

Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate ca...
body_text:
The Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate candidate argued that medical decisions should be left to patients, parents and doctors, who went to "whole a--" medical school.

Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed said the government should not restrict sex changes, arguing that "whole a--" doctors like himself should be allowed to make their own determinations for patients' treatment plans.

The remarks came during El-Sayed's Friday rally held at Michigan State University, during which the former Detroit Health Department head responded to a student's question about protecting sex changes. Since launching his campaign, El-Sayed has flaunted that he is a "physician" and, if elected, he would be the first doctor to serve as a Democratic senator in 50 years. However, Fox News Digital previously reported El-Sayed has never held a medical license in Michigan or New York.

"I went to a whole a-- medical school, everybody I graduated with also went to whole a-- medical school," El-Sayed said. "And then ... they went to whole a-- residency. Right? And some of them went to whole a-- fellowship. They took whole a-- exams to provide whole a-- healthcare."

DEM SENATE HOPEFUL’S ‘PHYSICIAN’ CAMPAIGN PITCH UNDER FIRE AFTER LICENSE RECORDS REVEAL KEY GAPS

Abdul El-Sayed (R) answers a question during a press conference at the Michigan Democratic Party State Endorsement Convention in Detroit on April 19, 2026, while communications director Roxie Richner (C) looks on. El-Sayed has never held a medical license in Michigan or New York. (Jose Juarez/AP Photo)

"They are the experts that a patient wants to see when they seek care," El-Sayed continued. "And the decision about what healthcare is necessary ought to be held between a patient — and or their parents if they're under the age of 18 — and their doctor. That's it."

The remarks come as the Trump administration has made major strides in restricting minors' access to "sex-rejecting" procedures, which include hormone therapy and surgeries.

Earlier this week, the Justice Department announced that Mount Sinai had joined other hospitals, like Texas Children's Hospital, the Cleveland Clinic Foundation and Connecticut Children's Hospital, to halt sex change procedures for children after reaching an agreement with the Trump administration.

MEDICAID ENDS FUNDING FOR CHILD SEX-CHANGE PROCEDURES AS TRUMP ADMIN SLAMS 'EXPERIMENTAL' TREATMENTS

El-Sayed has made the promise of Medicare for All — government-run healthcare — as the major selling point of his campaign; he said that even though the government will be covering the bill, it needs to stay out of the doctor's decisions about a patient's treatment plan.

"I don't think the government gets to have a say about what health care is provided in what circumstances and why," El-Sayed said. "And to me, that is the standard on which we decide how we make health care decisions."

THE MEDICARE FOR ALL TRADE-OFFS SOCIALISTS AREN'T TALKING ABOUT, ACCORDING TO EXPERTS

A protester holds a sign in support of sex changes for transgender children outside the U.S. Supreme Court Building in Washington, DC, on June 18, 2025. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

"Not what the government says you can or can't do, but what a patient and/or their parent, if they're under 18, and their provider to decide. That's the most important thing," El-Sayed continued. "And there's a lot of disinformation about us, what we're talking about, when we talk about reproductive rights and when we're talking about health care for the trans folks. But, in the end, the place where the rubber meets the rope is in that clinical room between a patient and a provider, and that to me is the center we should engage on."

El-Sayed argued that Republicans agree with his belief that treatment decisions should be between a patient and their doctor, pointing to the Right to Try Act, which allows terminally ill patients to try experimental drug treatments that aren't yet approved by the Food and Drug Administration after they have exhausted all other treatment options.

"Because conservatives fought for a very long time for this legislation called 'Right to Try' legislation, which is the idea that the government couldn't tell you [that] you couldn't have a certain medication," El-Sayed said.

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION PROBE COULD UPEND WIDELY USED TRANSGENDER YOUTH TREATMENT GUIDELINES

A transgender rights supporter takes part in a rally outside of the U.S. Supreme Court as the justices hear arguments in a case on transgender health rights in Washington, DC, on Dec. 4, 2024. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

"So they agree that the decision about healthcare ought to be between the person and their provider. That's it. So let's use that standard, and keep to that standard, and make sure the government doesn't have the ability to tell you what you can or cannot do with your own life," El-Sayed said.

However, the research on the efficacy of treating individuals with gender dysphoria by allowing them to change sexes with "cross-sex" hormones and puberty blockers is limited.

The World Professional Association for Transgender Health, whose guidelines are used by leading medical associations like the American Academy of Peditatrics, is currently facing a lawsuit from the Federal Trade Commission stemming from allegations that its guidelines misled parents about the "medical consensus and medical necessity, as well as the safety and effectiveness" of sex change procedures.

The FTC has accused WPATH of failing to disclose the side effects associated with some procedures, such as patients experiencing incontinence, erectile pain, mood disturbances, pelvic pain, and vaginal pain stemming from "cross-sex" hormones.

Meanwhile, countries that have socialized medicine have put restrictions in place for minors' seeking sex changes. In England, the National Health Service put a pause on "cross-sex" hormones for 16- and 17-year-olds in March after finding research was "really weak" to support it.

The country already had a ban in place restricting children under 16 years old from taking sex-change hormones.

El-Sayed's office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment regarding his medical credentials.

Elaine Mallon is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business covering national politics.

title: Trump says he would ‘love’ to see unified Ireland and ‘it may as well happen now’ as he visits Dublin – as it happened
excerpt:
This blog is now closed, you can read more on this story here:

Full story: Donald Trump says he would ‘love’ to see united Ireland

Trump has weighed in on the question of Irish unity, saying he woul...
body_text:
This blog is now closed, you can read more on this story here:

Full story: Donald Trump says he would ‘love’ to see united Ireland

Trump has weighed in on the question of Irish unity, saying he would “love to see it unified” and predicting that a united Ireland is “going to happen eventually”.

He suggested it “may as well happen now” and appeared to cast Micheál Martin as the person to help make it happen.

double quotation markWell, I don’t want to cause any problems, but I will tell you I’d love to see it unified.

I have friends on both sides, great people. They’re Irish people. How can they be bad, right?

I’d love to see it unified. I think it would be a great feather in everybody’s cap if that happened. It’s going to happen eventually.

You know what? The way I look at it, it’s going to happen eventually. It may as well happen now.

We’re talking about it and you got the right man over here to get it moving.

But, yeah, I think it would be a fantastic thing.

Now the UK will have something to say about it, obviously. But I think it would be a great thing. I mean, how can it be bad?”

That’s all from us on the US politics blog, thanks for following along. Here is a recap of the day’s developments:

While in Ireland for a two-day visit that combined political meetings with a stop at his Doonbeg golf resort, Donald Trump said he backed Irish reunification. He said he would “love to see” a united Ireland and that it “may as well happen now”. He added that unification would happen eventually and suggested it would be “fantastic”.

His comments prompted a backlash from unionists and UK politicians. Andy Burnham’s position on Irish unification remains unchanged, a spokesperson for the prime minister said. Earlier this week, Burnham said he would stick to the Good Friday agreement “100%” and that there would be no referendum without majority public support.

Similarly, Micheál Martin’s government said Trump’s comments would not change its position, with a spokesperson saying it was committed to the Good Friday agreement and programme for government.

Irish president Catherine Connolly used her meeting with Trump to stress Ireland’s opposition to war and genocide, saying the normalisation of either “can never be accepted”.

Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald called on Trump to apply the lessons of the Northern Ireland peace process to Palestine, urging the US to end arms sales to Israel and “stop facilitating the genocide of Palestinian people”.

The US president also weighed in on the Falkland Islands row, questioning whether Britain would be willing to defend the islands and saying he could potentially help settle the dispute between the UK and Argentina.

Trump said the war with Iran would end “very soon”, possibly after the US midterm elections in November, adding that he expected oil prices to “come tumbling down” afterwards.

When asked about the crisis engulfing the strait of Hormuz, he said: “Everything will work out fine.”

Trump ended his Dublin engagements before heading to Doonbeg, where he arrived at his golf resort for an afternoon of golf and an overnight stay, with the Irish Open taking place on the course.

Our Ireland correspondent Rory Carroll has the full report here:

Trump has landed in Doonbeg, where he will stay overnight and present the Irish Open trophy before returning to Washington tomorrow.

On Trump’s comments on Irish unification, McDonald said they should prompt the Irish government to start preparing for a united Ireland.

Sinn Féin has long campaigned for Irish unification and supports holding a referendum on the issue when the conditions set out in the Good Friday Agreement are met. Under the 1998 peace deal, the Northern Ireland secretary of state should call a referendum if it appears likely that a majority would vote in favour.

“President Trump’s comments on Irish reunification are timely. The taoiseach must now begin planning for a united Ireland,” McDonald said.

In a message to Donald Trump, Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald has called on the US to end arms supplies to Israel and “stop facilitating the genocide of Palestinian people”.

Her party has been a strong advocate for Palestinian rights and has urged for Israel to face greater accountability over its actions in Gaza.

“The US plays a critical role in supporting peace in Ireland. That same commitment to diplomacy and peace must be applied to Palestine,” McDonald said in a post on X.

Donald Trump and his entourage have arrived at Shannon Airport. The US president disembarked Air Force One, shook hands with Irish ministers and waved to the cameras before hopping aboard Marine One, the presidential helicopter, for the journey to Doonbeg.

Garda officers await the arrival of US president Donald Trump at his golf resort in Doonbeg on day three of the Irish Open.

Trump has departed Dublin and is due to arrive in Shannon shortly, before travelling to Doonbeg to spend the afternoon at his golf resort.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has waded into the row over Trump’s Ireland unity comments, accusing the US president of “shooting from the hip” and describing his remarks as “deeply unhelpful”.

double quotation markPresident Trump is shooting from the hip as usual, just like he did with Greenland and Canada becoming the 51st state. This sort of loose talk about the future of democratic countries is deeply unhelpful and creates unnecessary tension. 
  Northern Ireland is part of the United Kingdom. At a time when separatists are in power in Scotland, Wales and NI, we need a Government that will defend the Union clearly and confidently.
  The Conservative and Unionist Party as is our true name will always defend the union. I would like to see the same clarity from Andy Burnham, rather than entertaining the idea of more independence referenda as he did on Wednesday at PMQs.

Irish president Catherine Connolly has issued a statement about her meeting with Donald Trump, saying “war and genocide can never be accepted”.

double quotation markAs President of Ireland, I am very conscious that Ireland and the United States of America are bound by strong ties. This is a deep connection, built over centuries, which allows us to speak openly to one another.

We are in a world facing the existential threat posed by war and climate change, both of which are inextricably interlinked.

I conveyed the strong view of the Irish people that the normalisation of war and genocide can never be accepted.

As a country which has suffered famine, colonisation and the violence of the Troubles, but also the importance of the long and challenging road to peace, I emphasised the unique insight which Irish people can bring to the resolution of conflict.”

A large crowd is gathering in the centre of Dublin to voice their opposition to Trump’s visit to Ireland.

The march is beginning at the city’s garden of remembrance.

Participants are carrying banners and flags, and chanting: “Donald Trump, can you hear? We don’t want you here.”

Northern Ireland’s leading unionist parties, the DUP and UUP, have hit back at Trump’s call for a unified Ireland.

double quotation markPresident Trump knows better than most that elections matter.

Northern Ireland’s constitutional future will be decided by the people of Northern Ireland, not by commentary in London, Dublin or Washington.

Northern Ireland is part of the United Kingdom because that is the settled democratic will of its people.

I am confident NI will continue to choose the UK and the security it offers. As unionists we are not interested in the destruction of our country by joining with the Irish Republic.

TUV leader Jim Allister said Trump “is not the first US president to meddle in the affairs which don’t concern him”.

double quotation markNorthern Ireland is not a pawn in Trump’s fall-out with the UK. Our constitutional future does not depend on him or any other foreign dignitary.

Ulster Unionist Party Leader Jon Burrows MLA said the US president “like anyone else in the world, is entitled to express his view on the constitutional future of another country”, before adding:

double quotation markBut the only people whose decision counts are the people of Northern Ireland.

That is the principle of consent, now enshrined in law through the Belfast Agreement, negotiated and delivered by the Ulster Unionist Party.

America has been, and remains, an important ally, from the Second World War and the global fight against terrorism to the defence of democracy around the world. Their businesses increasingly see that our workforce here is the best in the world.

But when all is said and done, Northern Ireland’s future will be decided by the people of Northern Ireland.

I am confident that we are safer, more secure and more prosperous within the United Kingdom, and that is where we will remain.

Trump has finish his speech at Deerfield, ending on a warm note as he praised Ireland and its people.

“This country is fantastic, it’s just a fantastic place, I love it,” he said.

“I have investments here but that’s not why I love it. I like it because of it’s special people, you have unbelievable people in Ireland.”

Speaking of the Irish people, there have been protests in Dublin against Trump’s visit.

When he was asked earlier about the demonstrations, the US president said: “I didn’t know there was a protest. It can’t be a very big one because we’ve been all over Ireland today already, it’s early in the morning… but I haven’t seen any protest, It’s a friendly protest.”

Back to Trump’s speech, where he has offered his assessment of the Irish people, praising them for their warmth and friendliness before warning they can be “vicious bastards”.

double quotation markYou know they say you can’t generalise about groups of people, countries, but you can. People love coming to Ireland. You know why? Because they love you. They love the people. There’s a friendliness.

There’s also a viciousness and a toughness. Let me tell you, you are some of the most vicious bastards... but when you want to be nice, there is nobody nicer.”

Prime minister ⁠Andy Burnham’s position on Irish unification remains unchanged, ⁠a spokesperson said.

It came after Donald Trump ​told reporters after a ​meeting with Micheál Martin ​in Dublin that unification would “happen eventually”.

During prime minister’s questions on Wednesday, Burnham said he would stick to the Good Friday agreement “100%”.

“I am not aware that there is majority public support for another referendum, and until that changes, there will not be one,” he said.

PA reports that among the gifts Donald Trump received from Irish president Catherine Connolly was a St Brigid’s Cross, traditionally associated with peace, along with a collection of poetry that included Michael Longley’s sonnet Ceasefire.

The symbolism of the gifts is rather hard to miss. As our Ireland correspondent, Rory Carroll, writes in his report ahead of Trump’s visit to Dublin, Connolly was a vocal critic of Trump before becoming president:

double quotation markBefore winning the Irish presidency – a ceremonial post – last year, Connolly was an independent leftwing member of parliament for Galway who protested against Trump’s 2019 visit and more recently assailed him over his positions and policies on Gaza, Iran and other issues. “If we are going to act as an independent sovereign state, a neutral republic, we must use our voice to speak to power and the abuse of power by president Trump,” she said.

Asked in March about the criticism, Trump replied: “He’s lucky I exist.”

title: Taxes wouldn’t fund $5,000 Trump ‘dividend’ if Republicans win midterms, says commerce secretary
excerpt:
Lutnick said $500bn of estimated $1tn needed to fund checks to all US adults could come from new visa program

Donald Trump’s controversial proposal to give a $5,000 “dividend” to all US adults if Rep...
body_text:
Lutnick said $500bn of estimated $1tn needed to fund checks to all US adults could come from new visa program

Donald Trump’s controversial proposal to give a $5,000 “dividend” to all US adults if Republicans maintain control of Congress in November’s elections would not be paid out from US tax revenues, according to the US commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick.

“It’s not tax money,” Lutnick said in an interview with NBC News, adding that the administration could “earn the money that Donald Trump wants to pay out, not from the deficit and not from taxpayers”.

In a speech at the Republican midterm convention rally in Dallas, Texas, on Wednesday, Trump said he would issue the dividends “because of our tremendous strength and success economically” and likened the payment to a one-time, tax-free $1,776 “Warrior Dividend” approved for about 1.45 million US military service members last year.

Trump suggested the dividend, which could cost as much as $1tn if paid out to all Americans, could come in part from tariff revenue.

“If the Republicans win, you win with us, and you get $5,000,” he said, adding that it would be called “the Trump dividend”.

But the proposal has been widely criticized, in part because the US national debt recently surpassed $40tn, up from $10tn in 2008, marking a near 300% increase over 18 years.

Lutnick told NBC that some of the dividend money could come from a planned commerce department program to charge wealthy visitors to the US to pay up to $5m to extend their visas.

“We have a waitlist of more than 100,000 people who want to come,” he said, and calculated that this could raise $500bn. He also cited the government’s $8.9bn investment in chipmaker Intel, which has since appreciated in market value, from $20 per share to $100.

In his comments, Lutnick joined with other administration officials in floating ideas on where the $5,000 checks might come from.

Kevin Hassett, director of the National Economic Council, told Bloomberg TV that the White House is considering a “reconciliation process” in Congress to fund the program.

“We can do it in a fiscally responsible way,” Hassett said. “The bottom line is there are multiple paths to getting it done – don’t underestimate President Trump.”

JD Vance has also suggested tariff revenues would cover the cost and that the payments would not go to wealthy Americans.

However, the supreme court has ruled that revenue raised by Trump’s “liberation day” 2025 import tariffs must be returned, and an earlier proposal to return $2,000 to US taxpayers from tariff receipts was more than the revenue that had been raised, according to the nonpartisan Tax Foundation.

Trump’s $5,000 dividend proposal comes as a recent Associated Press poll found that only about three in 10 US adults, or 32%, approve of how the president is handling the economy, down from 40% at the start of his second term.

title: England survive Pakistan scare to seal 3-0 Test series sweep
excerpt:
Joe Root led from the front as England survived a major wobble to beat Pakistan by eight wickets in the third Test at Edgbaston on Saturday, sealing a 3-0 series whitewash.

The home team, chasing jus...
body_text:
Joe Root led from the front as England survived a major wobble to beat Pakistan by eight wickets in the third Test at Edgbaston on Saturday, sealing a 3-0 series whitewash.

The home team, chasing just 130 to win, were in deep trouble when openers Ben Duckett and Emilio Gay were dismissed in the first over, bowled by Mohammad Abbas.

Root, England’s record runscorer, edged his first ball, bowled by Razaullah, through the slips for four in a nervy start but settled and scored quickly to take the sting out of the situation.

The skipper was given a huge reprieve when he chopped onto the stumps off Mohammad Ali, only for the umpire to signal a no-ball, leaving the bowler distraught.

Root, with Jordan Cox at the other end, had another let-off when he edged an Abbas delivery between first and second slip, with neither fielder moving.

But he reached his half-century off 57 balls with a cut for four, and Cox matched him shortly afterwards.

England reached their target in the 25th over, with Root unbeaten on 62 and Cox 59 not out.

Root, in his second spell as England skipper after the departure of Ben Stokes, admitted his team were not the finished article but said he was delighted with their series win.

“The amount of uncertainty, noise and I guess chaos there was coming into the series, the way the guys have dealt with that – being so clinical with what we’ve had in front of us – and be stood here with a 3-0 win is really pleasing,” Root told Sky Sports.

“It sets us up nicely looking ahead to the start of a new era with (new head coach) Stephen Fleming coming in.”

It is England’s first Test series win since 2024, while Pakistan have now lost 16 of their last 21 games and are bottom of the World Test Championship table.

Root’s men had appeared set for a quickfire win inside three days on Friday before debutant fast bowler Razaullah launched an audacious assault with the bat, clubbing nine sixes as he raced to 81 off 63 balls.

The 21-year-old number nine, who also took four wickets in England’s first innings, put on 121 for the ninth wicket with fellow paceman Abbas (42) as England floundered.

“We had a little bit of pushback yesterday which, in a strange way, was quite a good thing for the group,” said Root.

“Fair play to Razaullah; he made things difficult for us. He played some wonderful shots and made it very difficult to set fields to. He struck the ball nicely – I don’t know how he didn’t pull a muscle, swinging the bat that hard.”

Razaullah’s heroics have changed the mood music, but they came too little, too late for Pakistan, who have endured a miserable series, losing the first Test by an innings and 103 runs and the second by 194 runs.

The tourists sent seven players home after their crushing defeat in the second Test at Lord’s and brought in seven replacements, with Razaullah among them.

They also sacked head coach Sarfaraz Ahmed and assistant Umar Gul as their tour plunged into chaos.

Pakistan made four changes to their side for the third Test, and they put up a fight despite being dismissed for a paltry 133 in their first innings.

Captain Babar Azam admitted his team would have to take stock after a one-sided series.

“Before we came here, we had to think about different things and to decide our team,” he said.

“We had a couple of changes after losing two matches. Playing in England is very difficult. We were trying to do our best in the third match.

“We need to sit down and look hard at our mistakes, decide our playing XI.”

The 3-0 whitewash is a huge tonic for England, who were in turmoil just weeks ago following a series loss to New Zealand and the exits of head coach Brendon McCullum and captain Stokes.

But tougher challenges lie ahead, starting with a Test series in South Africa in December and January, while a home Ashes looms next year.

title: Trump says a unified Ireland would be ‘fantastic’ during Irish visit
excerpt:
United States President Donald Trump has said that a unified Ireland would be “fantastic”, in remarks made during a visit to Dublin that were not welcomed by government ministers in London.

Trump’s c...
body_text:
United States President Donald Trump has said that a unified Ireland would be “fantastic”, in remarks made during a visit to Dublin that were not welcomed by government ministers in London.

Trump’s comments on Saturday came weeks after British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said a referendum on Northern Ireland leaving the United Kingdom was “off the table”.

“Well, I don’t want to cause any problems, but I will tell you, I’d love to see it unified,” Trump told reporters, while sitting next to Ireland’s Prime Minister, Micheal Martin.

“It’s going to happen eventually … I think it would be a fantastic thing,” he said.

“Now the UK will have something to say about it … but I think it would be a great thing,” he added.

Martin declined to respond to reporters’ questions to comment on the US president’s remarks.

Following Trump’s comments, a spokesperson for Burnham said his position on Irish unification remained unchanged.

Responding to questions from members of parliament on Wednesday about a potential poll in Northern Ireland, Burnham said: “I am not aware that there is majority public support for another referendum, and until that changes, there will not be one”.

Under the terms of the 1998 Good Friday Agreement (also known as the Belfast Agreement), a referendum on leaving the UK can be held only at the discretion of the British government.

The accord ended three decades of violence known as The Troubles. The sectarian conflict involved mostly Catholic nationalist paramilitaries seeking a united Ireland, mostly Protestant unionist paramilitaries wanting to remain part of the UK, and British troops.

Gavin Robinson, leader of the DUP, Northern Ireland’s main unionist party, said that Northern Ireland’s future was a matter for its people to decide, not Trump.

“President Trump knows better than most that elections matter. Northern Ireland’s constitutional future will be decided by the people of Northern Ireland, not by commentary in London, Dublin or Washington.”

While polls show a comfortable majority in Northern Ireland favour remaining in the UK, the gap has narrowed slightly since Britain’s departure from the European Union pushed unity higher up the political agenda.

Trump also met Irish President Catherine Connolly, who was elected head of state last year. When Trump last visited Ireland as president in 2019, Connolly, an outspoken politician with left-wing foreign policy views, protested at Shannon Airport in western Ireland.

During Trump’s current visit, some supporters had urged her to speak out against US military actions around the world and defend Ireland’s neutrality.

Anti-war and anti-Trump protests were held in Dublin and some were planned for later in western Ireland, near Trump’s golf course in Doonbeg.

Reporting from the capital, Al Jazeera’s Milena Veselinovic said Dubliners had a “laundry list” of reasons for protesting against Trump’s visit.

“They feel that the Irish government should not be, in their words, rolling out the red carpet for someone like Trump, who they say is a cause of instability in the world and has been enabling Israel’s actions in Gaza … and destabilised the whole of the Middle East.”

Irish people are also protesting against the high cost of hosting Trump, including security, which they say could pay for other things, such as healthcare and social issues, added Veselinovic.

title: Christopher Harborne matches £36m Reform donation of Ben Delo
excerpt:
Party leader, Nigel Farage, ‘humbled’ by contributions from billionaires as Harborne addresses ‘media speculation’

Analysis: donations of £72m make Reform’s prospects both rosier and riskier

The cry...
body_text:
Party leader, Nigel Farage, ‘humbled’ by contributions from billionaires as Harborne addresses ‘media speculation’

Analysis: donations of £72m make Reform’s prospects both rosier and riskier

The cryptocurrency tycoon Christopher Harborne has given £36m to Reform UK, matching a donation from fellow billionaire Ben Delo.

The pledges mean Reform has received a cash injection of £72m in just 24 hours. They are jointly the largest donations made to a UK political party and have intensified calls for restrictions on money received from individual donors.

Reform’s leader, Nigel Farage, said he was “honoured and humbled” by the payments, which come as the party is facing intense scrutiny regarding its funding. Reform said it planned to use the money to hire about 400 campaign managers in target constituencies and was now on an “election footing”.

The Metropolitan police is conducting an inquiry into Reform’s finances and Farage is facing a parliamentary standards investigation into a £5m gift from Harborne, made before he was first elected an MP in 2024. Reform UK and Farage have denied any wrongdoing.

Harborne’s donation was announced on Saturday afternoon. The Guardian understands the money has already been received by Reform.

Bridget Phillipson, the chair of the Labour party, said that Farage couldn’t “buy his way out of the sleaze and scandal he and Reform UK are drowning in – or the multiple police investigations that are ongoing into Reform’s dodgy finances”.

Rachel Millward, the deputy leader of the Green party in England and Wales, accused the prime minister, Andy Burnham, of “flip flopping” on a cap on domestic donations. Burnham, who previously appeared supportive of a cap, has faced lobbying from trade unions who fear restrictions would inhibit their ability to donate to the Labour party.

The Labour MP Stella Creasy tabled an amendment to the representation of the people bill, which is progressing through parliament and has its second reading in the Lords on Monday.

Creasy proposed an annual cap of £100,000 on most domestic donations. Although it attracted the support of 60 MPs from various parties, it was not put to a vote.

“The Labour party urgently needs to find a spine and support a tight cap on donations from individuals,” Millward said.

Duncan Hames, of Transparency International UK, said the donations made “an irrefutable case” for a cap, adding: “At this rate just two people could end up buying our democracy before the next election.”

The campaign group Spotlight on Corruption said the donations could have a “huge and damaging impact” and accused the government of “ignoring the very high risk of the Americanisation of our politics”.

Farage said that Delo and Harborne “know that we are the only party that can turn the country around and win the next general election – thanks to their generosity, we are now able to fight that election on a level playing field”.

Harborne said: “There will be a lot of media speculation regarding this donation. So what do I expect in return for my donations? Nothing. No peerage, no policy change, just a party that is ready for government.

“I have already accumulated enough wealth for the rest of my life. I am committed to putting that to work for Britain and humanity as a whole. I want the same as everyone else in Britain: for my children and grandchildren to have the chance to live happy and productive lives here and be rewarded for their hard work.

“At the next general election, people will have to vote for the party that they think will best get that done and I’m making a donation very clearly to the party that I believe will do so.”

Harborne is a citizen of the UK and Thailand, while Delo recently moved back to Britain from Hong Kong. As part of the new legislation, donations to political parties from Britons living abroad or those who have returned to the country within the past 12 months will be capped at £100,000 a year, with the rules backdated to March.

The Guardian asked Reform exactly how long each has been on the electoral roll. A spokesperson said: “All donations to Reform UK comply strictly with Electoral Commission rules and UK law. Both men are British citizens who are fully entitled to support political change in their own country, despite the establishment’s desperate attempts to silence opposition.”

Their donations have amplified concerns about the influence of “mega donors” on British politics.

Margaret Hodge, a Labour peer and former chair of the House of Commons public accounts committee, said she was “gobsmacked” to hear of Harborne’s donation and said it “reinforces the urgency of us dealing with the issue”. Hodge, who favours a cap, said there was now a “real danger” that British politics could be “captured by rich individuals”.

“There has been a reluctance on Labour’s side to confront this danger because of the trade unions,” she said. “This highlights what a lot of us have been saying – you have to tackle the issue. We can’t leave it alone. Self-interest shouldn’t dominate.”

Many senior Labour figures, including Hodge, believe union funds could be classified as a series of individual donations from members.

“Union members could tick a box saying, ‘I wish to contribute [to the Labour party]’, so it becomes an individual donation, rather than a union [donation],” Hodge said, adding that she believed this would “strengthen democracy” and challenge the power of union leaders.

However, this proposal is likely to be condemned by opposition parties and transparency campaigners.

Shaun Bowler, who runs the campaign group Wake Up GB, has proposed financing political parties through a government funded civic voucher, in which voters could choose to allocate a small sum to the party of their choice.

“The unions funded the Labour party to compete with Conservative funding,” he said. “If you take funding away from the Conservatives and everyone else, it’s a level playing field.”

title: Dr. Drew blasts Ryan Reynolds for calling 1980s a 'brutal' era: 'What happened to fun?'
excerpt:
Celebrity physician Dr. Drew Pinsky tells Fox News Digital why trendy "resets" can hide addiction, not cure it.

Ryan Reynolds has a bone to pick with the 1980s — but Dr. Drew Pinksy isn't buying it.
...
body_text:
Celebrity physician Dr. Drew Pinsky tells Fox News Digital why trendy "resets" can hide addiction, not cure it.

Ryan Reynolds has a bone to pick with the 1980s — but Dr. Drew Pinksy isn't buying it.

The "Deadpool" star recently shared a decidedly un-nostalgic view of the decade, arguing that the passage of time has allowed people to romanticize an era that was far more turbulent than the movies, music and pop culture of the time might suggest.

"What's interesting about when you get far enough away from a time period that's quite distinct, I think there's always a lovely feeling associated with it. It's almost like you pave over all the trauma with, like, puppy dogs and ice cream," Reynolds said during an interview with Variety.

POLITICIAN SPENCER PRATT CALLS OUT ACTOR RYAN REYNOLDS FOR CONDEMNING 1980S NOSTALGIA

Dr. Drew Pinsky challenged Ryan Reynolds’ gloomy assessment of the 1980s and questioned whether the decade was really as "brutal" as the actor claimed. (Getty Images)

"And the '80s was a brutal, brutal time for people. It was a f---ing mess... and people forget that. It was a tremendous strife. Sociopolitical tensions everywhere."

Reynolds pointed to the lingering shadow of the Cold War and the Cuban Missile Crisis, noting that the latter had occurred only a couple of decades earlier.

"So, you know, it's a ... it's a tumultuous period, but you look back at it now, and you're like, 'Oh, yeah. "Top Gun." Cocaine!' Like, 'No!' It was really scary," he said.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Ryan Reynolds attends the "Mayday" premiere on Sept. 1, 2026, in New York City. (Taylor Hill / FilmMagic)

Reynolds made the remarks while promoting his new Apple TV film, "Mayday," a Cold War-era movie set in 1987.

The actor also questioned how future generations will view the current era, suggesting that cultural nostalgia can obscure the realities of the time in which people actually lived.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

His comments sparked a debate on the "Actual Friends" podcast, where celebrity physician Dr. Drew pushed back on Reynolds' assessment.

"I am a Ryan Reynolds fan. I met him way back in the day. People take aim at him all the time. I think he's a great guy," Dr. Drew said.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Dr. Drew Pinsky pushed back on Ryan Reynolds’ take on the 1980s, asking, "What happened to fun?" during the conversation. (Scott Dudelson/Getty Images)

Dr. Drew argued Reynolds was confusing the 1980s with the more turbulent 1970s, describing the following decade as a period of optimism and celebration.

"The '80s was this huge relief that came," he said. "And yes, there was a lot of hatred for Reagan at the beginning, but things went so well it all went away, and it was just one relief, one celebration after another for like eight years."

For Dr. Drew, the debate ultimately boils down to one question: "What happened to fun?"

"The '80s were just flat-out fun. They really were. People were having fun, and we just don't seem to have fun anymore," he said.

Stephanie Giang-Paunon is an entertainment reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Major city eyes crackdown on golf cart tours as furious locals push back
excerpt:
Pauline Frommer, publisher of Frommer's Guidebooks, breaks down how popular destinations are responding to surging visitor numbers.

Backlash is brewing in Rome as tourists are using a new way to navi...
body_text:
Pauline Frommer, publisher of Frommer's Guidebooks, breaks down how popular destinations are responding to surging visitor numbers.

Backlash is brewing in Rome as tourists are using a new way to navigate the crowded cobblestone streets.

Golf cart tours have surged in popularity, with bookings this summer up 147% compared with 2024, according to Tripadvisor data cited by The Associated Press (AP).

POPULAR DESTINATION CRACKS DOWN HARD ON TOURISTS AS NEW LIMITS THREATEN SUMMER GETAWAYS

Critics argue the golf carts are out of control, contributing to illegal parking, heavier traffic and massive crowds.

As many as 500 carts could now be operating on the streets of Rome, Italy, according to AP.

A golf cart used to ferry around tourists is seen near the Colosseum on Aug. 18. The growing presence of carts in the city's historic center is upsetting many local residents.  (AP Photo/Gregorio Borgia)

Supporters counter the carts are quiet, take up less space and produce no exhaust fumes that can discolor historic monuments, the outlet reported.

Pauline Frommer, publisher of Frommer's guidebooks and Frommers.com, told Fox News Digital that Rome's limited public transportation has created demand for another way to get around.

ANGRY LOCALS BLOCK FAMOUS BEACH AS MASS TOURISM PROTESTS ESCALATE AT VACATION HOT SPOT

"There isn't that much public transportation because whenever they start to dig a subway, they come upon a priceless relic and the dig site becomes an archaeological site," said Frommer, the daughter of late travel guidebook pioneer Arthur Frommer.

"Into this void has come a fleet of golf carts."

Rome is moving to regulate golf carts in tourist areas after complaints from locals about the worsening congestion. (NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Frommer said the small vehicles can maneuver through Rome's historic center and narrow streets, making them an attractive option for tourists trying to cover more ground.

The problem, Frommer said, is the sheer number competing for space.

FAMOUS BEACH NOW REQUIRES VISITORS TO RESERVE SPOTS WEEKS AHEAD AND PAY FEES

The Associated Press witnessed hostility firsthand during a late-August ride. A van pulled up alongside a cart, the outlet said.

"You’re in the middle of the road!" the van driver reportedly yelled.

"The road isn’t yours!" the golf cart driver fired back.

A golf cart with tourists travels through central Rome on Aug. 18. (AP Photo/Gregorio Borgia)

Rome's deputy mayor for sustainable mobility and transport, Eugenio Patanè, asked the regional government to give the city greater authority over the carts, according to the AP.

If granted, Rome plans to introduce rules that would limit the number of carts, designate routes for tours and determine which operators can provide them.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"We will be able to regulate this phenomenon that has now become rampant and, in some cases, even worrisome," Patanè told the AP.

The push comes amid a broader debate over how some of the world's most visited destinations can accommodate tourists while preserving everyday life for residents.

On a street in central Rome, a golf cart driver is shown transporting tourists past historic venues.  (AP Photo/Gregorio Borgia)

"Cities around the world right now are struggling with overtourism," Frommer said. "In many of the world's most popular tourist cities, there are more visitors than residents."

Frommer pointed to restrictions on short-term rentals and rules aimed at protecting historic sites as ways major cities have tried to manage tourism.

Limits on golf carts would have an impact on visitors who have difficulty walking.

Rome "has very little public transportation. So for people who have mobility impairments, it can be a difficult city to visit," she said.

A debate rages in Rome about whether golf carts are convenient or chaotic. (AP Photo/Gregorio Borgia)

"For certain types of tourists, yes, this will be a blow. It will mean it'll be harder to get around Rome," she said.

The golf carts have also fueled debate online.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"Unless you have mobility issues and need the golf cart to get around, then please don't," one Reddit user wrote.

"Rome is a living, breathing city, home to millions of us. It's not a theme park for your enjoyment."

A flotilla of golf carts travels past the Basilica of Saint Mary of Minerva in Rome on Aug. 27. (AP Photo/Gregorio Borgia)

Another commenter barked, "Golf carts belong on a golf course or resort, not in an actual city."

Others defended the tours and said they offered an easy way to see the city.

"I did one last week. ... It was around [three] hours and excellent!" one traveler wrote.

The Associated Press contributed reporting.

Kelly McGreal is a production assistant with the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

title: Six Nigerians extradited to US over $6M online romance scam
excerpt:
Alleged members of Black Axe criminal network that swindled US women out of $6m flown from South Africa

Six Nigerian nationals linked to an organized criminal network that allegedly swindled American...
body_text:
Alleged members of Black Axe criminal network that swindled US women out of $6m flown from South Africa

Six Nigerian nationals linked to an organized criminal network that allegedly swindled American women out of more than $6m through online romance scams were extradited to the United States on Friday.

South African police confirmed they were to be extradited earlier on Friday, while local news in Africa confirmed that the Directorate for Priority Crime Investigation, known as the Hawks, facilitated their handover to officials from the US Federal Bureau of Investigation and Secret Service at Cape Town international airport, in collaboration with Interpol South Africa.

The men, who were arrested in the South African city of Cape Town in 2021, face wire fraud and money laundering charges.

They are accused of belonging to a criminal network known as the Black Axe, which Interpol describes as being among criminal groups responsible for a significant share of the world’s cyber-enabled financial fraud, typically through romance, cryptocurrency and investment scams.

According to South African police, the men are alleged to have targeted more than 100 women in the US, defrauding them of more than $6m through online romance or love scams.

Among the alleged victims were pensioners and businesspeople who were reportedly targeted through sophisticated online relationships.

“Through the coordination of Interpol South Africa, the six will today be transported from a correctional facility in Cape Town to Cape Town international airport, where they will be handed over to officials from the FBI and the United States Secret Service, who arrived in South Africa this morning,” said police spokesperson Katlego Mogale.

A recent operation by Interpol targeting west African organized crime groups led to the arrest of 58 people and the identification of 263 suspects linked to various criminal networks involved in similar crimes, the multinational police body said last month.

The operation aimed to disrupt money laundering, identify high-value targets, seize assets, and support arrests and prosecution.

In South Africa, authorities raided seven locations in the city of Johannesburg linked to a syndicate that ran romance and investment scams targeting retirees in English-speaking countries.

In that operation in South Africa, police arrested 39 people, seized $2.67m and froze more than 250 bank accounts, Interpol said.

title: Jeremy Thomas, British producer of The Last Emperor and Sexy Beast, dies aged 77
excerpt:
An outstanding figure in the UK film industry, Thomas was noted for collaborations with directors including Bernardo Bertolucci and David Cronenberg

Jeremy Thomas, the distinguished British producer ...
body_text:
An outstanding figure in the UK film industry, Thomas was noted for collaborations with directors including Bernardo Bertolucci and David Cronenberg

Jeremy Thomas, the distinguished British producer of films including Sexy Beast, High-Rise and the multi-Oscar-winning The Last Emperor, has died aged 77.

A representative for Thomas said he died on Friday “peacefully, at his country home in Oxfordshire, surrounded by his family and loved ones”.

Thomas, who started producing feature films in the early 1970s, was known for forging strong creative relationships with acclaimed auteurs, producing a string of films directed by the likes of Nicolas Roeg, David Cronenberg and Bernardo Bertolucci.

The Last Emperor, directed by Bertolucci, was an early triumph for Thomas, winning nine Oscars including best picture. He went on to become a major figure in the British film-making establishment, including a spell as chair of the British Film Institute and winning a Bafta for outstanding British contribution to cinema.

Born in 1949, Thomas’s father, Ralph, was a prolific film director whose work included the popular Doctor in the House series starring Dirk Bogarde, and his uncle Gerald Thomas directed all 30 of the Carry On films. Thomas started out as an assistant editor, working on the Jimmy Cliff thriller The Harder They Come and Ken Loach’s Family Life, before gaining his first producer credit on Mad Dog Morgan in 1976, with Dennis Hopper as the 19th-century Australian outlaw of the title.

Thomas was quickly into his stride, making Bad Timing, Insignificance and Eureka with Roeg, The Shout with Jerzy Skolimowski and Merry Christmas, Mr Lawrence with the Japanese master director Nagisa Oshima. The success of The Last Emperor, which Thomas had to finance independently, consolidated his status as a leading figure in British cinema, and he subsequently concentrated on prestige projects including The Sheltering Sky and Little Buddha (both with Bertolucci) and Naked Lunch (with Cronenberg).

Thomas then suggested to Cronenberg he should direct JG Ballard’s Crash, and the resulting film was enormously controversial, resulting in local authority bans in several areas in the UK. Following this, Thomas’s films included riskier propositions, such as Sexy Beast, directed by Jonathan Glazer, an adaptation of Alexander Trocchi’s Young Adam, by David Mackenzie, and Terry Gilliam’s bizarre corpse comedy Tideland. Later highlights were Jim Jarmusch’s vampire fantasy Only Lovers Left Alive, another Ballard adaptation, High-Rise, directed by Ben Wheatley, and Tale of Tales and Dogman from the Italian director Matteo Garrone.

In 2019 Thomas was the subject of a documentary by Mark Cousins, who accompanied him on his car drive from the UK to the Cannes film festival for another Garrone film, Pinocchio; it screened there in 2021. Thomas also directed one film himself: All the Little Animals, starring Christian Bale, which was released in 1999. His most recent film, Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo, directed by Takashi Miike, is due to premiere at the Toronto film festival on Monday.

title: Texas vs Ohio State is more than a rematch: A BBQ-fueled collision between college football power brokers
excerpt:
Be sure to catch Trey's reporting on X @TreyWallace and at OutKick.com

AUSTIN, Texas – The anticipation has been brewing since last year's dud of a game in Columbus. The rematch is set for Saturday n...
body_text:
Be sure to catch Trey's reporting on X @TreyWallace and at OutKick.com

AUSTIN, Texas – The anticipation has been brewing since last year's dud of a game in Columbus. The rematch is set for Saturday night in Texas, as Ohio State makes the 1,234 mile trek to Austin for a rematch with the Longhorns.

But more importantly, Steve Sarkisian will have his 'semifinals aren’t good enough' mantra tested by a Buckeyes team looking to make another Big Ten statement in what is now "SEC Country."

While the offseason has been filled with questions surrounding whether this is the year Arch Manning takes the next step in becoming one of the best quarterbacks to come out of Austin, the bigger question is whether both Texas and Ohio State can justify spending over $40 million on their 2026 roster.

LSU PRESIDENT WADE ROUSSE ENDS LANE KIFFIN'S SEC SHOWDOWN, BUT THERE IS STILL RELATIONSHIPS TO MEND

In reality, the storylines write themselves when it comes to what happens on the field. Will this turn into a shootout in Austin, or will both defenses rise to the occasion to limit both Manning and Julian Sayin?

Either way, we're in for a show on Saturday night.

Texas Longhorns will face Ohio State on Saturday night in Austin. (Via: Trey Wallace. OutKick)

And, there will be thousands of Ohio State fans in town to witness the next chapter of this convenient rivalry. It didn’t take very long for the first Buckeyes to be seen, at least by me, on their way to Austin for this Top-5 showdown.

Sitting at the gate inside the Nashville airport, waiting to board my flight to Austin, the trash talking had already begun.

"Look, I know you're headed to Austin, but I just wanted to tell you all 'Go Buckeyes' and I hope the ride back is a bit longer," a Southwest gate agent said over the intercom.

What more could you ask for? Trash talking by the guy who is scanning our plane tickets is the perfect way to get this weekend started.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Head coach Ryan Day of the Ohio State Buckeyes looks on during the first quarter against the Ball State Cardinals at Ohio Stadium on Sept. 5, 2026, in Columbus, Ohio. (Diamond Images/Getty Images)

In all honesty, the more entertaining part came on the actual plane. Sitting two-seats over from a fan donning an Ohio State pullover, the Buckeye started explaining how much it was costing him for this college football adventure that would have him meeting up with four of his friends a little later than expected, thanks to a three-hour delay in the Music City.

How much was this Airbnb that would become their Buckeye fortress over the next three days?

"In all, it was around $22,000 for the entire house," the Ohio State fan told me while sitting in the 23rd row of a Southwest airline flight. "Add on another $3,000 for tickets, and we darn sure better be headed home with a win."

Brandon Inniss and Jeremiah Smith of the Ohio State Buckeyes celebrate after a three-yard touchdown catch by Smith during the second quarter against the Ball State Cardinals at Ohio Stadium in Columbus, Ohio, on Sept. 5, 2026. (Diamond Images/Getty Images)

He was only half-kidding, most likely questioning his financial decisions if Ohio State left Texas with a loss, or somehow the ridiculously expensive housing turned into a nightmare. I will say, judging by the rentals I then had to look up on the site following his oddly truthful explanation of expenditures, his group would at least have a nice Alaska king to sleep on over these next three days.

I'll enjoy my sleep at the $237 a night hotel that the company luckily procured through some fantastic booking tactics on my part.

Think of the party scene in this town as a tamed Bourbon Street, though I did my best to stay away from the raucous environment that I was told was coming after the 11 p.m. CT hour on both nights.

Sorry, I'm at the age where the body starts shutting down around 8 p.m., and my brain had already hit a wall around two hours earlier. I just can't keep up with these kids nowadays, and I have zero shame in admitting that.

But, from the bustling music to the strong smell of marijuana pumping from the streets, it was pretty obvious as to why this town is such a tourist attraction. The restaurants were one of a kind, though we usually don't give out free advertisements around here.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Terry Black's BBQ, in Austin, Texas (Via: Trey Wallace. OutKick)

title: Death toll from Philippines ferry fire climbs to 35, with dozens still missing
excerpt:
The ferry caught fire near tourist hotspot Coron on Wednesday

The Philippine Coast Guard says it has recovered 30 bodies from the wreckage of a ferry that caught fire this week, bringing the total de...
body_text:
The ferry caught fire near tourist hotspot Coron on Wednesday

The Philippine Coast Guard says it has recovered 30 bodies from the wreckage of a ferry that caught fire this week, bringing the total death toll to 35.

More than 130 people were on board the MV June Aster when the blaze erupted on Wednesday as it neared its destination at the tourist hotspot of Coron, after departing from Manila.

Forty-three people were rescued, with many receiving treatment in hospital, and searches continue for more than 50 people who remain unaccounted for.

The country's coast guard says more bodies remain on the boat, which they were unable to board until Friday due to toxic fumes and lingering heat.

In a press conference, coast guard spokesperson Commodore Noemie Cayabyab said most bodies had been retrieved from the sleeping area of the boat, which had been making a 22-hour journey.

"Agencies are currently undertaking the proper recovery and identification of the remains in accordance with established procedures," Cayabyab said.

"We recognise the grief of the families affected by this tragic incident."

Earlier, the coast guard said preliminary interviews with the survivors suggest that the fire started in the cargo hold. Some passengers were not wearing life vests, they noted.

A survivor who was hauled to safety on a rescue boat told the BBC he had heard frantic cries onboard when the fire erupted, and was trampled by panicked people as he tried to escape.

The Philippines' maritime authority is investigating the circumstances surrounding the incident.

The ferry, built in 2002, held valid safety certificates and passed an enforcement inspection in March, but investigators are looking into potential manifest discrepancies, cargo loading integrity, and crew emergency response protocols, the Palawan Daily reported.

The vessel was carrying 117 passengers and 17 crew members.

Atienza Interisland Ferries, the vessel's operator, has pledged full cooperation with the inquiry.

"Our hearts remain with the affected families, and we will not rest until all individuals are accounted for," the company said in a statement on Thursday.

title: Arrest made over the death of black woman found hanged from tree in Mississippi
excerpt:
Warning: This story contains distressing details

Police in the US state of Mississippi have arrested a man in connection with the death of a black woman found hanged from a tree, and say they could s...
body_text:
Warning: This story contains distressing details

Police in the US state of Mississippi have arrested a man in connection with the death of a black woman found hanged from a tree, and say they could soon take more people into custody.

Tasia Fortune's body was found in the lot of an abandoned home in Jackson in August, but police only announced they were treating her death as a possible homicide earlier this week.

"That arrest today is an important development in this investigation, but it is not the conclusion," Jackson Police Chief RaShall Brackney said on Friday. "This case remains active."

Fortune's death has worried locals in Jackson, a majority-black city in a state with a history of racial violence and lynching.

During Friday's news conference, Brackney said the medical examiner had confirmed Fortune's cause of death was homicide and said there would be a murder charge.

She identified the suspect as Jarques Ratliff, 51, and said there was an "association" between Ratliff, who is also black, and Fortune, but would not elaborate further.

"Additional arrests will be pending as our investigators continue to follow the evidence," Brackney said, adding that they had interviewed 15 people in the case.

Fortune's mother, Christy Spivey, told the BBC that she cried when police called  to update her about the arrest, saying:  "I guess I do feel like a little sigh of relief...like a little bit of peace just come over me."

"I just hope that they've got the right person," she added.

The arrest of a suspect followed weeks of what Spivey and residents in Jackson described as relative silence and inaction from local officials.

Combined with the grim nature of Fortune's death and Mississippi's history of racial lynchings, the lack of information about the case had left the community in shock and fear.

Spivey earlier told the BBC she had tried contacting Jackson police several times over the last two weeks, leaving multiple voicemails, and had not heard back.

Brackney addressed the family's frustration on Friday, saying: "We have been in constant contact with the mother and the stepfather, as well as the biological father, throughout this case."

A letter Spivey wrote to officials about the limited communication and speed of the investigation was read during a public city meeting on Tuesday - moments before Jackson police made the announcement about a possible homicide.

"I'm kind of like in awe," Spivey said. "Like, I can't believe it. That was quick."

Earlier this month, Fortune's death was described by a member of the US Congress as part of a pattern of "possible modern-day lynchings".

More than 50 members of Congress this week sent a letter, external to the FBI and justice department, saying they were "extremely alarmed by reports of black people found hanging from trees in numerous states" and calling for an independent investigation into the deaths of black Americans.

"The series of deaths raise significant suspicion of foul play given the role of lynching in our nation's history," it states.

So far this year there have been at least 10 reported hangings of black people in the US, they said, adding that there were more than 70 lynchings documented between 2000 and 2025.

Mother demands answers, weeks after black woman found hanging from Mississippi tree

title: North Korea fires ballistic missiles off eastern coast, Seoul says
excerpt:
North Korea has fired ballistic missiles towards the sea off its eastern coast, according to South Korea’s military.

South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) said that it detected several missiles l...
body_text:
North Korea has fired ballistic missiles towards the sea off its eastern coast, according to South Korea’s military.

South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) said that it detected several missiles launched from North Korea’s eastern coastal area of Wonsan about 5:20am on Saturday (20:20 GMT on Friday), which flew about 250 kilometres (155 miles). It added that it is closely exchanging information on the launches with the United States and Japan.

South Korea’s presidential National Security Office said it held an emergency security meeting with the Defence Ministry, the JCS and other relevant agencies following the launch.

The US Pacific Command said North Korea’s launch event does not pose an immediate threat to US territory or to its allies, adding that Washington remains committed to the defence of South Korea and its other allies in the region.

The missiles were launched a day after South Korea concluded five days of joint maritime drills with the US and Japan that were focused on North Korea.

Hours after the exercises began on Monday, North Korea’s defence minister, Kim Song Gi, criticised the exercise and warned North Korea was capable of taking “strong and reflective countermeasures from the standpoint of power”.

Late last month, North Korea slammed plans for the so-called Freedom Edge exercises in international waters off South Korea as a “threat” to Pyongyang and other countries in the region.

The North also fired a barrage of missiles into the sea on August 20, despite an overture from US President Donald Trump, who said he planned to meet this year with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

The August launch from the nuclear-armed North came as South Korea and the US held a shorter edition of their annual Ulchi Freedom Shield military exercises, following an order from Trump to scale back the drills.

The order from Trump, who called the exercises “inappropriate and hostile” towards North Korea, alarmed US allies in the region.

Pyongyang has long condemned US-South Korea joint exercises as rehearsals for invasion, often staging missile launches around the drills.

title: US rapper Lil Durk found not guilty of murder-for-hire scheme
excerpt:
Prosecutors accused musician, born Durk Banks, of putting bounty on fellow rapper in retaliation for friend’s killing

Chicago rapper Lil Durk has been acquitted of all charges in a murder-for-hire sc...
body_text:
Prosecutors accused musician, born Durk Banks, of putting bounty on fellow rapper in retaliation for friend’s killing

Chicago rapper Lil Durk has been acquitted of all charges in a murder-for-hire scheme, in which a man was fatally gunned down in 2022.

Prosecutors had accused Lil Durk, born Durk Banks, of putting a bounty on Atlanta rapper Tayquian Bowman’s life in retaliation for the 2020 shooting death of Banks’s friend, fellow Chicago rap star King Von.

The state alleged that associates of Only the Family, Banks’s alleged criminal enterprise and record label, tracked Bowman to a gas station in West Hollywood in 2022, where they opened fire on his car. Bowman’s cousin, Saviay’a Robinson, was fatally shot in the ambush.

Kacey Hester, who said he had been a shooter in the attack, testified, according to Courthouse News, that Banks probed for details on the ambush: “Did somebody get hit? How many times did you shoot? What did you do?”

Banks’s defense attorneys cast doubt over the reliability of Hester’s testimony, saying he was seeking a more lenient sentence.

The rapper’s defense team also sought to portray Kavon Grant, Banks’s former assistant, whose cousin died after an altercation with Bowman’s entourage, as the mastermind of the 2022 shooting.

Prosecutors rebuffed the lawyers’ notion. “No one is saying he was the one on the ground with a gun in his hand in Los Angeles, but you know this story doesn’t happen without him, and it doesn’t make sense without his leadership,” assistant US attorney Ian Yanniello reportedly said.

The Friday federal jury verdict brought an end to a highly publicized case that drew loyal fans and celebrity supporters to the downtown Los Angeles courthouse.

Banks’s legal woes are not over yet. He is due to appear in court for a second trial on a racketeering charge.

“While we are disappointed with the jury’s decision regarding Durk Banks, AKA Lil Durk, we look forward to presenting our evidence at his second trial, scheduled for 5 October, when he will face racketeering murder and firearms charges,” said first assistant US attorney Bill Essayli.

Speaking to Politico yesterday, Chip Roy, the Republican US representative from Texas, openly questioned how the government would pay for it. “Well – I would like to know how they would plan to pay for … back of envelope … well over $1tn,” he said.

Former representative Marjorie Taylor Greene, a staunch Trump ally turned critic, said on X: “$5,000 for the peasants will be in the mail after the election only if you vote Republican, along with those DOGE and tariff money checks.”

We’re wrapping up our live coverage for the day. Here are today’s key developments in US politics:

The US marked the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks. Ceremonies and remembrances were held across the country in tribute to victims.

In New York City, a memorial ceremony took place that included all living former presidents, as well as mayor Zohran Mamdani, former mayor Rudy Giuliani and vice-president JD Vance.

Donald Trump spent the day in Washington, where he attended a ceremony at the Pentagon. Trump used his speech to honor the lives lost in the September 11 attacks, but also to defend his administration’s ongoing war in Iran.

Defense secretary Pete Hegseth similarly linked the war in Iran with 9/11 at his speech during the Pentagon ceremony.

Trump also bizarrely posted a video to Truth Social of his message from the January 6 attack on the US Capitol building, in which he told supporters to “go home” while also promoting election conspiracies.

The CIA meanwhile declassified more than 70 presidential intelligence briefs regarding al-Qaida and its leader Osama bin Laden. The documents included a 1998 brief that warned the terror group “may fly an explosive-packed airplane into a US city”.

Longstanding Fox News anchor Maria Bartiromo, who abruptly split from the network this month, gave her first comments since the departure – promising to reveal her next moves soon.

Jon Husted, the Republican senator in Ohio, fired his political director after the aide was discovered to have used a photo of Nazi SS soldiers in his Facebook profile picture.

Trump departed for Ireland, where he will be for a two-day visit largely focused on golf.

Donald Trump is now en route to Ireland for a two-day visit and is set to touch down in Dublin tomorrow morning. He’ll meet with Ireland’s president, Catherine Connolly, a leftwing politician with a history of strongly criticizing Trump.

House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform chairman James Comer, a Republican representative from Kentucky, announced Friday he will move forward with a resolution to hold billionaire Leon Black in contempt of Congress.
  Black, a private equity investor and client of Jeffrey Epstein, has been in a weeks-long fight with the congressional oversight panel as it investigates Epstein’s abuses and operations. Comer has accused Black of not complying with the committee’s subpoenas.

“It doesn’t matter how wealthy, powerful, or connected you are, no one gets to pick and choose which lawful congressional subpoenas they will obey. Rather than provide the American people with answers about his relationship with Jeffrey Epstein, Leon Black has chosen to hide behind litigation by suing me and the Committee in an attempt to obstruct our investigation,” Comer said in a statement.

An attorney for Black defended the investor and accused Comer of retaliation for Black’s lawsuit against the committee that argues it does not have the authority to compel him to turn over non-disclosure agreements.

“These transparently retaliatory actions by Committee Chairman James Comer in response to our legitimate and constitutionally protected litigation are outrageous and continue his pattern of overreach,” said Susan Estrich, a lawyer for Black. “We intend to vigorously pursue our lawsuit against the committee and chairman James Comer individually for abusing their power by unlawfully bullying and destroying legal protections of private citizens.”

Ohio senator Jon Husted has fired his political director after the aide was found to have used a photo of Nazi SS soldiers as his Facebook profile picture. The campaign for Husted, a Republican, told The Washington Post that the senator had decided to “part ways” with 25-year-old Stephen Woytek after the photo was discovered.

“While he denies negative intent, his social media activity displays a complete lack of judgement and disregard for its impact on others,” Husted’s campaign spokesperson told the Washington Post regarding Woytek. 
 The incident is one of several recent cases where young Republican staffers have been discovered affiliating with pro-Nazi content online.

Maria Bartiromo has pledged “to be back soon w[ith] my next moves” in her first comments since her abrupt departure from Fox News on 3 September.
  In a social media post on Thursday, Bartiromo – who had anchored at Fox for more than 12 years – said: “I want to thank all of my friends, followers, and supporters for all the kind words.

“I am so grateful for the outpouring of love this past week on social media & through texts. I love you all and I promise to be back soon w[ith] my next moves.”
  The post contained a picture of a rainbow emerging from clouds over water.
  Media reports on 4 September said Fox dismissed avid Donald Trump supporter Bartiromo for divulging the conservative network’s editorial guidance to the president’s administration. But her lawyer quickly and sharply denied that Bartiromo was fired by Fox, issuing a statement dismissing reports that the network had terminated her “irresponsible” and “absolutely and unequivocally false”.

A Republican political action committee affiliated with Donald Trump has reserved $74m in advertising this week, Reuters reported. The No Going Back Pac plans to pour money into close House and Senate races in battleground states, including in Michigan, where Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed is in a tight contest with Republican Mike Rogers.
  The president has vowed to spend heavily on midterms as his approval rating sinks to record lows and Republicans face the prospect of losing key races.

Donald Trump posted a video message on Truth Social that he originally issued on January 6, 2021, as his supporters stormed the US Capitol building. The message includes the president falsely stating that the 2020 election was “stolen from us” while instructing those at the Capitol to “go home in peace”.
