This is all a headache for central bankers, as high oil prices create inflationary pressures through the economy. Later today, MPs in London will question Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey, and colleagues, about their recent decision to hold the Bank Rate at 3.75%.

MPs are likely to question witnesses on the potential inflationary impact of the ongoing war in Iran and how the MPC considers recent developments in AI, the committee says.

title: Low turnout threatens Commons vote on assisted dying, say MPs
excerpt:
Backers seek support for second attempt to get law through House of Lords after ‘undemocratic’ rejection last year

MPs on both sides of the assisted dying debate have voiced fears about turnout affec...
body_text:
Backers seek support for second attempt to get law through House of Lords after ‘undemocratic’ rejection last year

MPs on both sides of the assisted dying debate have voiced fears about turnout affecting the vote on Friday, when the bill returns to the Commons for its second attempt to become law.

Those who back the change in the law have been emphasising the “undemocratic” nature of the bill’s rejection by the House of Lords after it was talked out by a handful of peers after passing the House of Commons. The bill fell despite multiple days of debate from peers because of the number of amendments tabled in the Lords.

Several former cabinet ministers and ministers say they intend to speak out on the bill now they are freer to express their views, especially on the conduct of the Lords.

The private member’s bill – originally sponsored by Kim Leadbeater – has been revived by the Labour MP Lauren Edwards. It had passed last year by a majority of 23 in the Commons.

In an article for the Guardian, Edwards said the bill was “the most pressing, progressive reform of this parliament. But it was blocked in the Lords earlier this year by a small minority of peers, led in part by ex-Tory ministers such as Thérèse Coffey and Mark Harper”. She said the Lords should not be “allowed to frustrate the will of the elected chamber a second time”.

Edwards said she rejected some accusations from Labour MPs that she was reopening divisions in the party at a moment when there was a chance to re-unite it now that Andy Burnham had replaced Keir Starmer as prime minister.

“Exactly the reverse is true. MPs have already made their decision. In a democracy, we settle our differences by voting on them. Last time, opponents in the Lords prevented a vote taking place on the bill’s provisions,” Edwards said.

“Other major social changes such as a woman’s right to choose and gay rights were bitterly contested at the time. But once passed, the reforms were quickly accepted and ceased to be controversial.

“It is time to do the same and give terminally ill people the choice to exercise some control over the manner of their deaths. We owe it to them, and to the vast majority of voters who support them, not to sit back and allow a minority of unelected peers to stand in their way.”

Backers of the bill have stressed that MPs should see the vote as a moment to assert the Commons’ decision-making power, rather than re-run the arguments.

Jo Stevens, the former Welsh secretary said: “I’ve always supported the principle of assisted dying. I have constituents and friends who desperately wanted one and a constituent who I helped after they were arrested for escorting someone who chose an assisted death at Dignitas.

“I and many other MPs, including MPs who didn’t support the bill, are furious at the outrageous behaviour of a small number of unelected peers who went against the will of the Commons. Many of these are former MPs who should know better, especially former ministers who were rejected by the electorate.”

However, several MPs said they believed it was the pro-side that was finding it hardest to convince MPs to stay and vote on Friday. “No one has changed sides, but the numbers are going to be tighter because people are absent,” one MP said.

Two MPs who voted in favour of the bill are no longer in parliament: Starmer, who quit as an MP last week and is yet to be replaced; and the former Makerfield MP Josh Simons, who was replaced by Burnham, who has said he will abstain.

Other high-profile supporters of the bill, including the cabinet minister Louise Haigh, minister Ian Murray and former chancellor Jeremy Hunt, have written to constituents previously saying they were uneasy about using the Parliament Act to pass the law. The act would come into force, within certain conditions, if the Lordswere to reject the bill a second time.

title: UK-US trade could suffer as a result of sanctions for illegal Israeli settlements, American ambassador warns – UK politics live
excerpt:
UK to reassert support for Palestinian rights and a two-state solution in move drawing criticism from US and Israel

UK to adopt tougher stance on Israel with illegal settlements trade ban

Good morni...
body_text:
UK to reassert support for Palestinian rights and a two-state solution in move drawing criticism from US and Israel

UK to adopt tougher stance on Israel with illegal settlements trade ban

Good morning. It is hard to understand Labour/leftwing politics in the UK at the moment without reference to Israel and Gaza. Keir Starmer’s popularity with some progressive voters slumped in part because he was seen as unwilling to do enough to channel the anger they feel about how Israel is treating Palestinians – even though last year he took the historic step of formally recognising the state of Palestine. Quite a lot of what Andy Burnham has done in his early days as PM has had a “continuity Starmer” flavour, but today the new government will take a bold step that will recast the UK/Israel relationship, acting where the Starmer administration just dragged its feet.

In a statement to MPs, Ed Miliband, the new foreign secretary, will announce that Britain is banning trade with illegal Israeli settlements on the West Bank. Patrick Wintour has the story here.

For years, successive governments – Labour and Conservative – have condemned the decades-long expansion of Israeli settlements on Palestinian land on the West Bank – while doing precious little about it. But with Benjamin Netanyahu’s government escalating the process, Miliband will tell MPs that action is necessary now to stop the prospect of a two-state solution (Israel living alongside a viable Palestinian state) being killed off for good.

As Patrick reports in his story, Miliband is not giving pro-Palestinian supporters everything they are asking for. Quite what impact the measures will have on Israel remains to be seen. But it is still a big shift in policy. And, conveniently for Labour, it is coming just a day after the party moved the writ for the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, where what was a safe Labour seat is under threat from the pro-Palestinian Green party.

But the move isn’t without risks. The Conservatives argue that anything that jeopardises Israeli security cooperation with the UK could increase the terrorism risk to Britons. There are concerns that any government policy that stigmatises Israel is likely to heighten antisemitism. And there have been warnings that Israel and its allies – particularly the US – could retaliate.

This morning Mike Huckabee, the US ambassador to Israel, has said exactly that. In an interview, he told the Today programme:

double quotation markI don’t know if [the British government is] really aware of the implications and how it’s going to affect Brits.

For example, 25% of pharmaceuticals that are used in the UK are made in Israel. Are they willing to give those up? It looks like they are.

Are they willing also to do great damage to any Brits who are doing business in a number of states in the US?

I don’t know what all of the national sanctions or repercussions or retaliations will be from the US. [That] hasn’t been announced yet. But I do know that there are a number of states – let me mention one, one of the largest US states, Florida – it has a law that if this action is taken, then Brits will not be able to do business with any company or business in Florida.

Huckabee – a very rightwing Republican and former governor, who like most US ambassadors was appointed because he was close to the president – went even further at the weekend, accusing the UK government of “Jew hate”.

I will post more from his interview soon.

11.30am: John Healey, the chancellor, takes questions in the Commons.

Noon: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.

After 12.30pm: Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, makes a statement to MPs about his plan to impose a ban on trade with illegal Israeli settlements.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

A Labour MP has warned that the proposed ban on trade with illegal Israeli settlements on the West Bank could increase the risk to British Jews.

In an interview with the Today programme, Peter Prinsley, vice chair of Labour Friends of Israel, said:

double quotation markMy fear is that opponents of Israel won’t distinguish between Israeli government policy, Zionistic political philosophy, and British Jews.

As far as they’re concerned, the whole thing’s the same, and I think it carries a real risk of increased chances of attacks on the British Jewish community. Which is exactly what I said to Ed Miliband when I was asked to see him two or three nights ago.

Prinsley also said he thought it was a mistake for the government to announce the ban now, only weeks before the election in Israel on 27 October. He explained:

double quotation markI think the timing is terrible. I think we need to wait for the result of the Israeli election, and then we need to have another think.

We must do whatever we can to preserve the two-state solution, and I think the behaviour of the presently-elected Israeli government is really outrageous in this respect. I have a horrible feeling that what we’re doing will not only embolden the present government of Netanyahu, but has the capacity to influence the election itself, which is on a knife edge.

The Conservatives have described the proposed ban on trade with illegal Israeli settlements as “performative posturing”. Chris Philp, the shadow home secretary, used the phrase on the Today programme when he was asked about the announcement coming today.

double quotation markWe think it’s performative posturing.

It’s very difficult to distinguish goods that come from the West Bank area versus the rest of Israel. So practically, it’s very difficult to implement.

It also risks damaging an important security relationship because we do rely, the UK relies, on Israel for vital information and intelligence about terrorist threats.

But I would also like to say, that said, we do oppose the building of settlements on land which is Palestinian, whether that’s sponsored by the Israeli state or simply allowed to happen, because we do think a two-state solution is the right solution, and building settlements on Palestinian land is obviously wrong.

The full details of the ban have not been announced. But the Foreign Office has not challenged the accounts of what Ed Miliband is expected to say later today.

title: Indonesia airports reopen after volcanic ash disrupts thousands of flights
excerpt:
Indonesia has reopened its main airport in Jakarta and four others that had been closed ⁠due to volcanic ash from Mount Anak Krakatau.

The five airports reopened on Tuesday after authorities cleared ...
body_text:
Indonesia has reopened its main airport in Jakarta and four others that had been closed ⁠due to volcanic ash from Mount Anak Krakatau.

The five airports reopened on Tuesday after authorities cleared volcanic ash from critical infrastructure.

The disruption affected more than 340,000 travellers and approximately 2,900 flights.

Videos shared on social media by Soekarno-Hatta international airport in Jakarta showed firefighters and firetrucks clearing runways and other operational facilities covered by ash.

Transport Minister Dudy Purwagandhi said it may take “a bit” longer for flight schedules to return to normal.

“We ask for a little patience from passengers and the public, as we will be carrying out inspections to ensure that these aircraft are fit to fly,” Dudy told reporters at the airport.

“The first departing aircraft was a cargo plane,” Dudy said. “We will be operating these aircraft, but before we do so, we want to ensure their airworthiness. So, it may take a bit of extra time.”

Anak Krakatau, which had a major eruption on Saturday, sits in a strait between the islands of Java and Sumatra.

The volcano erupted at least three times on Tuesday morning alone, according to the head of the national Geology Agency, Lana Saria.

“The impact is not as big as the previous eruptions, but we’ll continue to monitor,” the head of the Geology Agency, Lana Saria, told the Reuters news agency.

Anak Krakatau is one of about 130 active volcanoes in Indonesia, which straddles the “Pacific Ring of Fire”, a highly seismically active zone where different plates on the Earth’s crust ‌meet to create a large number of earthquakes and volcanic eruptions.

An outburst in 2018 partly collapsed the volcano’s crater, which triggered a tsunami along the coasts of Java and Sumatra, killing more than 400 people.

title: One Nation’s Warren Pickering admits to illegal drug use and says he is ‘no angel’ in extraordinary press conference
excerpt:
Victorian One Nation leader says his actions ‘hurt people I loved, and I will live with that forever’

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or ...
body_text:
Victorian One Nation leader says his actions ‘hurt people I loved, and I will live with that forever’

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The Victorian One Nation leader, Warren Pickering, has admitted he “made mistakes” in his 20s, including using ecstasy, methamphetamines and marijuana, losing his licence multiple times for drink driving and hurting people he loved.

But he has denied claims by his ex-partner, published by The Australian, that he smoked ice – also known as crystal meth – in front of children and said he was considering legal action against the publication at a press conference on Tuesday. Guardian Australia and the ABC were barred from attending the press conference.

Accompanied by James Ashby, One Nation’s national director, and his daughter and stepson, Pickering said he was “no angel” as a young man and used illegal drugs in his 20s.

“Never would I have ever said that I was somebody who was a drug addict. I did use them … as a young man and I’m not proud of that,” Pickering said.

He listed ecstasy, methamphetamine, speed and marijuana, but denied using ice or smoking it while his children were home.

“No, I did not,” Pickering said, when asked directly.

Pressed by a reporter about whether he had used ice, Pickering said “ice is not on that list.”

When the reporter said methamphetamines are ice, Pickering replied: “Well, speed”.

“Look, guys, I’m clearly not as familiar with the terms … as you would like me to be,” he said.

Pickering also confirmed he lost his driver’s licence three times for drink driving.

“I believe I lost my licence for drink driving as an 18-year-old, and again as a 20-year-old, and then probably a decade later, I believe they were low-level drink driving,” he said.

Pickering said his actions “hurt people I loved, and I will live with that forever”. But he said he had “changed his life dramatically” for the sake of his daughter and three stepsons, stopped using drugs and joined the Australian defence force, which he said gave him a sense of purpose.

“That’s what inspired me to engage in the political sphere to provide service to community in a different way, post-service,” he said.

Ashby also spoke, telling reporters a handwritten note from Pickering published by The Australian, which references “sexual deviance”, was in relation to “behaviour that involved the couple’s open relationship”.

“They opened that relationship to a third person, and at the same time, Mr Pickering was exploring his own sexuality,” Ashby said.

Pickering said he was “working with the lawyers” to get the stories “taken” down and was receiving advice about possible defamation action.

Reporters from The Australian were able to attend the press conference at Crown Casino. However, reporters from both Guardian Australia and the ABC were asked by Ashby to leave after identifying the media outlet they worked for.

title: Ukraine’s prosecutor general resigns after corruption allegations as Russia resumes strikes on Kyiv – Europe live
excerpt:
Ruslan Kravchenko leaves post after his offices were searched at the weekend, as Moscow renews attacks after pause for peace talks

Ukraine’s prosecutor general, Ruslan Kravchenko, resigned from his p...
body_text:
Ruslan Kravchenko leaves post after his offices were searched at the weekend, as Moscow renews attacks after pause for peace talks

Ukraine’s prosecutor general, Ruslan Kravchenko, resigned from his post over corruption accusations that saw anti-graft officers search his offices at the weekend as part of investigations into illegal call centres, AFP reported.

In a statement, Ruslav Kravchenko has denied he was involved in the alleged scheme, and said his resignation was a “political decision” as he wanted to avoid his position being used “as an instrument of political confrontation.”

His decision to step down poses another challenge for Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy after tricky summer which involved a government reshuffle and a political crisis linked to his controversial decision to sack popular defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov.

The latest political crisis comes as Russia has resumed its attacks on Kyiv after a brief pause over the weekend intended to facilitate peace talks with senior US representatives.

“It was a complex attack that the Russians tried to plan to cause as much harm to life as possible – ballistic missiles, cruise and anti-ship missiles, and jet-powered shaheds. There is significant damage to residential buildings and other civilian infrastructure in the capital,” Zelenskyy said this morning.

At least two people died in the attack, and 10 were injured. Further attacks were also reported in Dnipro, Kharkiv, Sumy and Zaporizhzhia.

Elsewhere, I will keep an eye on the latest from Germany as the fallout from the Saxony-Anhalt election continues, and on reports from France about thieves stealing four works of French impressionist painter Auguste Renoir during a night heist at a museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer.

It’s Tuesday, 8 September 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

Iceland summoned the US ambassador for talks last night after US president Donald Trump posted on social media an AI-generated map of the US, Canada and other countries, which appeared to include Iceland as the US territory.

Icelandic national broadcaster RÚV reported that the ambassador was told that the post was “completely inappropriate.”

The map also included Greenland as the US territory, despite being posted just hours after the EU unveiled a €200m investment package for the territory in an apparent attempt to strengthen its ties with the bloc (Europe Live, Monday).

The number of people injured in this morning’s attacks on Kyiv has gone up to 12, local authorities said.

Two thieves have broken into a museum dedicated to the French impressionist painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir in southern France, stealing four artworks and dropping one as they fled, the mayor has said.

“This morning, two individuals broke into the Renoir Museum and stole four works of art,” said Bryan Masson, the far-right mayor of the town of Cagnes-sur-Mer.

“Spotted thanks to the town’s video surveillance cameras, the two individuals fled, abandoning one of the stolen paintings as they ran,” he said, adding that his office estimated the value of the stolen works at €9m (£7.7m).

The museum was opened in 1960 in the painter’s last home before his death in 1919. Its collection includes objects and furniture that belonged to Renoir, including his easel and wheelchair, as well as portraits, landscapes and nudes painted by the artist.

The mayor said it took five minutes for the authorities to respond. “The museum alarm went off at 5.48 am. At 5.53 am, just five minutes later, our municipal police were on the scene,” he said.

The theft comes less than a year after eight items valued at around €88m were stolen during a daylight robbery from the Louvre in Paris. The four suspected Louvre robbers have been arrested, but the stolen items have not been found despite extensive searches by French investigators in the Paris region, and exchanges with police in Belgium, Italy and beyond.

Art thieves in ‌Europe are committing more violent robberies and specialist gangs have ​been replaced by ad-hoc opportunists recruited through social media, Europol said last month.

Separately, European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen has condemned the presence of senior Serbian officials at yesterday’s funeral of Bosnian Serb war criminal Ratko Mladić, saying it showed “a failure to confront a dark chapter in Europe’s recent history” and questioned Serbia’s alignment with the EU.

Mladić, who died last week, was buried with military honours in after a memorial service attended by tens of thousands of people and led by Porfirije, the patriarch of the Serbian Orthodox church.

In a statement this morning, von der Leyen said:

“The images from Ratko Mladić’s funeral yesterday in Belgrade were shocking. Ratko Mladić was a convicted war criminal. He was responsible for genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity. He died while serving a life sentence for the Srebrenica genocide and other crimes.

The elements of official support and the presence of some senior Serbian officials at the funeral are deeply regrettable. They demonstrate a failure to confront a dark chapter in Europe’s recent history and contradict the values underpinning Serbia’s path towards the European Union.

Our thoughts are with all the victims of the crimes committed in the countries of former Yugoslavia.”

title: Ban on neo-Nazi White Australia party is ‘authoritarian’ and breaches constitution, high court hears
excerpt:
Lawyers also argue commonwealth does not have the power to ban a political party, as the high court ruled in 1951 over attempt to ban the Communist party

Follow our Australia news live blog for lates...
body_text:
Lawyers also argue commonwealth does not have the power to ban a political party, as the high court ruled in 1951 over attempt to ban the Communist party

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Lawyers for an outlawed neo-Nazi political party have argued anti-hate laws passed after the Bondi terror attack rely on the opinion of a politician and are “authoritarian in nature”.

The White Australia party, formerly known as the National Socialist Network (NSN), was designated as an illegal hate group in May after the Australian Security and Intelligence Organisation passed on its recommendation to the home affairs minister, Tony Burke.

The listing means that activities including supporting, funding, training, recruiting and joining the group constitute a criminal offence with a maximum penalty of 15 years in prison.

The far-right nationalist party is challenging the ban at the high court over two days this week, with its lawyers arguing the law breaches the implied freedom of political communication and that handing the decision to Burke breaches the separation of powers.

Lawyers also argued the commonwealth does not have the power to ban political parties, citing a major cold war-era high court ruling in 1951, which overturned a ban on the Communist party of Australia.

If successful, the ruling could wind back the laws that have also banned the Islamist group Hizb ut-Tahrir.

On Tuesday, the group’s barristers, Peter King and Shahed Sharify, argued a total ban on the party was akin to using a “sledgehammer on a nut”.

The arguments centre on proving part 5.3B of the criminal code – which allows the federal police minister to recommend to the attorney general that a group is listed as a prohibited hate group – is invalid.

Sharify argued the law’s breach of implied freedom of political communication was “authoritarian in nature” and suggested it could be used to ban any political party where its members had threatened or engaged in a hate crime with the assistance of the organisation.

The barrister said the banning of hate groups was determined by a politician, based on an opinion with no judicial fairness to appeal that decision.

Sharify said the law’s purposes would be better served by handing that decision to a judge rather than a “busy minister who flicks through a brief and decides in two hours”.

Acting for the government, Brendan Lim, denied the laws could be used for the “illegitimate purpose of quelling political competition”.

Groups can be listed if it is considered “reasonably necessary to protect the Australian community or part of the Australian community against social, psychological, physical or economic harm”.

Under the rules, Burke must receive advice from the head of Asio recommending that an organisation be considered for listing. The home affairs minister must then receive written agreement from the attorney general and brief the opposition leader.

Unlike the terrorist group listing, a listed hate group cannot make a de-listing application.

The government is also expected to defend the anti-hate laws by arguing the party is not a political party but an arm of White Australia, itself a rebranded version of NSN.

“Forming a political party was a calculated attempt to secure legal protection for members engaging in openly racist and anti-Semitic speech,” the commonwealth said in written submissions.

Members of the White Australia party sat in the front of the courtroom’s public benches, including its leader, Tom Sewell.

The 33-year-old was sentenced in June to a community corrections order – which includes 200 hours of community work – for behaving in an offensive manner in public.

A Melbourne magistrate had found the neo-Nazi leader emulated “Nazi thugs of 1930s Berlin” when he used “appalling racial slurs” during a stunt outside a Chinese consulate.

Former 2GB and 2UE radio host has denied 22 indecent assault and sexual touching charges

body_text:
Former 2GB and 2UE radio host has denied 22 indecent assault and sexual touching charges

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A friend of Alan Jones who has denied witnessing an alleged assault in a Mosman restaurant has agreed in court that he sent the broadcaster a text message saying “if you need me to refute any lies, I of course will”.

Under cross-examination by prosecutor Georgina Wright, the witness agreed he was a loyal and “very good friend” to Jones and the two men shared an “unbreakable bond”. He said he once sent Jones a text saying the “love of my life has always been you”.

Wright said in the Downing Centre local court on Tuesday: “And you told the defendant ‘if you need me to refute any lies, I of course will’?”

The witness has told the court he can’t recall being at the lower north shore restaurant at a lunch hosted by Jones in 2008.

“I don’t recall ever having lunch in the Mosman area,” he said.

“I have never seen Mr Jones do anything inappropriate. I have not ever, ever seen him do anything sexually inappropriate, ever.”

Jones has been charged with 20 indecent assault charges and two counts of sexual touching involving six men. The 85-year-old had pleaded not guilty.

The prosecutor, Wright, said on Tuesday: “And you’re more concerned with loyalty to Alan Jones than with answering the prosecution’s questions truthfully in this trial, aren’t you?” 
 “I answered every question that you’ve asked truthfully,” the witness replied.

Earlier in the trial, another guest at the Mosman luncheon alleged a victim known as complainant C looked “distraught” while sitting next to Jones, who had his hand under the table.

C has testified that Jones instructed him to sit next to him and spent the entire lunch with his left hand under the table either on his leg or on his penis over his pants.

The witness on Tuesday told the court he messaged Jones in late 2023 after journalist Kate McClymont’s article containing allegations against the former 2GB host was published in the Sydney Morning Herald.

The text message said: “Everyone who loves you are right behind you, and we’re not going anywhere. These people are sick. The support you have is amazing and your loyal friends will always be there for you xx. We’re not going anywhere x.”

Asked by Wright who he was referring to as “sick”, the witness said: “People of the left that have always hated Mr Jones.”

The witness agreed he had described McClymont as “cunt”, a “bitch” and “evil”. He also called her a “low breed” and admitted he had a very negative view of her investigative reporting.

After initially telling Jones McClymont had contacted him but he would not be returning her call, he told the court he did speak to the journalist briefly after Jones asked him to do so. He said he told McClymont he had not witnessed anything inappropriate. “It didn’t happen and I was happy to tell her,” he said.

Text messages read out in court showed the witness referred to allegations of inappropriate behaviour by Jones as a “bullshit witch hunt”.

The witness agreed that he had told Jones that working with him for years on the breakfast program were the best years of his life. He told the court he was very proud because Jones was “one of the great broadcasters of history”.

The witness agreed he sent a text to Jones stating: “I still can’t believe I am close to the greatest broadcaster there’s ever been.”

Wright added that the witness had called Jones in another message “the greatest influence” and a “brilliant mind”.

The witness’s evidence was delayed by two days after the prosecution sought leave to cross-examine him as an unfavourable witness. It is the prosecution case that he was tailoring his evidence to “assist” Jones by denying he saw anything happen between Jones and C at the lunch. Other witnesses have told the court he smirked and made jokes about C being groped by Jones under the table.

The trial before judge Glenn Walsh continues.

title: Billionaire Chris Rokos, who paid £330m in tax last year, to quit UK
excerpt:
Hedge fund tycoon is latest financier to exit amid fears among super-rich over tax rises

The hedge fund billionaire Chris Rokos is poised to leave the UK, the latest in a string of high-profile exits...
body_text:
Hedge fund tycoon is latest financier to exit amid fears among super-rich over tax rises

The hedge fund billionaire Chris Rokos is poised to leave the UK, the latest in a string of high-profile exits among Britain’s super-rich.

The founder of Rokos Capital Management is preparing to move his residency to Greece, and will open an office in Athens as part of the move, according to Bloomberg.

He joins a number of billionaires who have left the UK, which many have blamed on the abolition of the non-dom regime, as well as higher tax on private equity investments, inheritance and capital gains.

Rokos, who founded his firm in 2015, was ranked third in the Sunday Times’s annual list of top taxpayers in the UK, paying an estimated bill of £330m in 2025. He has a net worth of about $4bn (£2.96bn), according to Bloomberg’s billionaires index.

This year he also made a record £190m donation to the University of Cambridge to fund the creation of the Rokos School of Government.

Rokos, who went to a state primary school before being offered a scholarship to Eton college and studying maths at Oxford, said at the time that he “would like to give something back to Britain”.

The publicity-shy tycoon and former Tory donor has spent much of the past decade presiding over one of England’s most expensive home renovations ever, of the 200-room Tottenham House mansion near Marlborough in Wiltshire, adding a tennis pavilion and private cinema in the £175m revamp.

Greece offers a 15-year high-net worth investor regime, which requires individuals to invest at least €500,000 ($430,000) in real estate, businesses or shares based in Greece within three years of applying for the tax status. In exchange, they can pay a flat tax of €100,000 a year on their income earned abroad.

His exit comes after the chancellor, John Healey, who will present his debut budget in October, said in his first big speech on Monday that he wanted to see Britain “as a country of wealth creation”.

Andy Burnham has previously expressed support for higher taxation on wealth, although in July signalled that he would not increase such taxes immediately after becoming prime minister.

There have been several high-profile exits from the UK after the Conservative chancellor Jeremy Hunt laid out plans to overhaul the non-dom system in 2024. They include Shravin Bharti Mittal, an heir of one of India’s richest families; Nassef Sawiris, an Egyptian investor; and Richard Gnodde, a veteran Goldman Sachs banker.

Gnodde left for Milan, while Sawiris is reported to be resident in Italy and Abu Dhabi. Mittal listed the United Arab Emirates as his residency after previously naming the UK in an official registry filing.

The Labour government brought in a new regime last year, under which foreign income and gains are subject to UK tax after four years rather than the previous 15. A new residence-based system means also that their global assets are subject to inheritance tax after 10 years.

While there have been several high-profile moves, the extent to which higher tax has triggered an exodus of wealthy people is not yet clear in official data. The latest provisional figures show a modest 0.5% decline in the number of non-domiciled residents in the tax year ended in April last year, at 73,400.

Other European countries have created tax regimes designed to draw in rich foreigners, including Italy, which has proved a popular destination owing to its flat tax of €300,000 on foreign-sourced income.

A representative for Rokos was approached for comment.

title: Tokyo tourist hotspot bans short-term rentals amid surge in complaints
excerpt:
Shinjuku ward targets accommodation in residential areas and near cultural sites as locals complain visitors disposing of rubbish improperly and being too noisy

A neighbourhood in Tokyo popular with ...
body_text:
Shinjuku ward targets accommodation in residential areas and near cultural sites as locals complain visitors disposing of rubbish improperly and being too noisy

A neighbourhood in Tokyo popular with foreign tourists will ban visitors from using thousands of short-term rental accommodations after a slew of complaints about behaviour.

In the latest sign that Japan’s patience with mass tourism is wearing thin, Shinjuku ward – home to the notorious Kabukicho nightlife district and the world’s busiest railway station – will prevent visitors from using private lodgings in residential areas and near schools and important cultural sites, Japanese media reported this week.

The measure, to be introduced through a local ordinance, could encourage other local authorities to follow suit. Shinjuku, with a regular population of more than 350,000, is home to 3,775 private lodgings – or minpaku – the largest number anywhere in Japan.

While tourism has boosted sectors of Japan’s economy and raised the country’s profile overseas, the surge in visitor numbers has created tensions with residents in popular destinations such as Tokyo, Kyoto and Osaka.

Shinjuku ward believes the measure will affect as many as 2,000 lodgings in residential areas – almost half the total, according to the Mainichi Shimbun. The number of minpaku residences in Shinjuku has almost tripled since 2022.

Reports said officials had been forced to act after receiving more than 1,300 complaints from residents in the 12 months to March. Many cited disruption caused by visitors who did not dispose of their rubbish properly, made too much noise and smoked in areas where it is banned. There have also been reports of trespassing.

Officials said temporarily revoking the licenses of renters whose tenants misbehaved would not address residents’ concerns. “Even if we crack down on badly behaved operators, the number of complaints remains the same,” a ward official told the Japan Times. “So we decided it’s better to change the ordinance.”

Authorities did not single out particular operators for the ban. But it is likely to affect those using popular companies such as Airbnb.

An Airbnb spokesperson told the Guardian: “Shinjuku has been an important partner to us, and we take residents’ concerns seriously. Home sharing works best when residents, hosts and guests can all live well alongside each other, and that is what we want to help the ward protect.

“We would welcome the chance to work with the ward on measures that target the problem more precisely - a prohibition across residential zones would close thousands of registered homes affecting compliant and responsible hosts, while leaving untouched the unregistered operators behind much of the disruption residents describe.

“We believe there is a version of this ordinance that protects residents’ quality of life without closing responsible, licensed hosts, and we want to help find it.”

The ward will ask for members of the public to give their feedback on the proposal next month, with a view to submitting revisions to the ordinance in February. It also plans to reduce the number of days per year that minpaku in residential areas can be rented out from 180 to 120.

Authorities in Kyoto – where tourists flock to view temples and shrines, rent kimono and photograph traditional geisha entertainers – limit minpaku operations in residential areas to just 60 days a year, during the off-peak season between January and March.

“Residents are concerned that their communities could be falling apart,” Kyoto’s mayor, Koji Matsui, said earlier this year. “We have strengthened the oversight of operators, but that is not enough. We need to go further,” the Asahi Shimbun quoted him as saying.

A record 42 million people visited Japan last year, spending a combined ¥9.5tn ($62bn) – also an all-time high. The government has set a target of 60 million visitors by 2030 – a goal critics say will exacerbate “tourism pollution”.

Authorities near Mount Fuji have introduced climbing fees and imposed a daily visitor cap in an attempt to reduce overcrowding on Japan’s highest mountain. In February, the town of Fujiyoshida, a popular Fuji viewing spot, decided to cancel this spring’s cherry blossom festival, citing a rise in disruptive behaviour by tourists.

The mayor, Shigeru Horiuchi, said the decision had been taken to “protect the dignity and living environment of our citizens”.

title: Real’s Mbappe embraces Ballon d’Or talk after historic World Cup goals
excerpt:
Real Madrid striker Kylian Mbappe says it is natural for people to consider him a potential Ballon d’Or winner this year after his World Cup exploits.

The France captain scored 10 goals at the tourna...
body_text:
Real Madrid striker Kylian Mbappe says it is natural for people to consider him a potential Ballon d’Or winner this year after his World Cup exploits.

The France captain scored 10 goals at the tournament this summer to win the Golden Boot, with his country finishing fourth. He has netted 22 in the competition, making him the World Cup’s all-time top scorer.

Mbappe, 27, has not yet won the prestigious trophy given to the world’s best player.

“I think that when you play for Real Madrid, which is the best club in the world, naturally people associate you with that kind of award, they associate you with collective awards, individual awards,” Mbappe told reporters.

“A lot of people, when they see me in the street, talk to me about the Ballon d’Or, a lot of people talk about me as a possible Ballon d’Or winner … Of course, I made a lot of history this summer in the most important competition in sport, but we’ll see.

“I have the feeling that it’s a good year for that, but there’s still a long time to go, and people are free to vote for whoever they think is the best player in the world.”

Since joining Real Madrid in 2024, Mbappe has scored huge quantities of goals, but the club has failed to win a major trophy.

On Tuesday, the record 15-time European champions host Inter Milan in the Champions League in the first match of the league phase.

During Mbappe’s first two years at Madrid, the team has appeared unbalanced, with many star names, including the Frenchman and Brazilian winger Vinicius Junior, widely considered not to be contributing enough to the team effort – in contrast to Ousmane Dembele at Paris Saint-Germain and Raphinha at Barcelona.

“We have to improve,” admitted Mbappe. “But I could play dumb and tell you that I score more goals than [Dembele and Raphinha], and that they need to score more goals to be like me.

“Everyone is different, but I want to do things intelligently and say that of course I have to improve and all that, but I don’t like comparisons because I think I do a lot of things that others don’t do.”

Real Madrid coach Jose Mourinho recently said he would prefer if Mbappe scored fewer goals but also worked hard to help the team win titles.

Mbappe said he would accept lower numbers if it led to trophies, but noted they were not mutually exclusive.

“I’d take 30 goals with titles, yes, but… for me it’s an absurd debate,” said Mbappe.

“I always want to score goals and win titles … you don’t have to choose, you can do both things.”

Veteran Portuguese coach Mourinho led Inter to Champions League glory in 2010 at the Santiago Bernabeu before he departed to take over at Real Madrid.

Despite his history with the Italian side, whom he steered to the treble that year, the coach said that only mattered before and after, but not during the match.

“There aren’t many [people] left from my time, but it’ll always be a pleasure to see people, even if I don’t know them, but people who defend Inter, before and after,” said Mourinho.

“During the game I want to win, they want to win, and there won’t be time to think about things from a wonderful past.”

Inter coach Cristian Chivu started the 2010 final playing under his opposite number on Tuesday at the Bernabeu.

“Mourinho is a special person, and I was lucky to have encountered him,” said Chivu, who described the Portuguese as a “winner”.

“There are few in the world like him,” continued the Romanian coach.

“He showed it here but at other big clubs too. I’m sure Real Madrid will have a great season.”

Mourinho wants his Madrid players to bounce back from their first defeat of the season, 1-0 at Real Betis on Friday in La Liga.

“I want to win. I could tell you I want to play well, but I don’t want to play well like we did against Betis and lose,” added Mourinho.

title: Australia’s classroom disruption among worst in world, prompting calls for ‘digital detox’
excerpt:
Public school students are the equivalent of two and a half years behind their independent peers, as global report shows decline in reading and maths

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily ne...
body_text:
Public school students are the equivalent of two and a half years behind their independent peers, as global report shows decline in reading and maths

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Public school students are more than two years behind their independent counterparts and Australia’s classroom disruption remains among the worst in the world, a global report has found.

The 2025 Programme for International Student Assessment (Pisa) results, released on Tuesday by the Australian Council for Educational Research (ACER), tested the literacy of 15-year-olds in 91 countries, including Australia. The tests have run every three years since 2000.

The latest report found Australia’s year 9 students were continuing a long-term national decline in performance, particularly in mathematics and reading, despite maintaining above-average OECD results. It also pointed to continuing gender divides in performance.

ACER research director, Dr Jonas Bertling, said Australia remained a “strong international performer” that was placed “well above the OECD average” but the full story was “a little mixed”.

He pointed to “persistent challenges”, including a steadily falling trend in the three Pisa testing areas – mathematics, reading and science, as well as persistent inequalities.

“We see a decline that is different for different genders in reading and in math. And we see that there are uneven outcomes by socioeconomic backgrounds,” he said.

“The disciplinary climate also still needs attention, so we’re not quite where we want to be as a nation. We’re really standing high, but I think we have some strengths to build on.”

Students in government schools recorded a mean score about 50 points lower than independent schools across science, reading and maths – equivalent to two and a half years of study behind. The federal government has reached a deal with states and territories to fully fund public schools for the first time – but not until 2034. Low funding has been blamed for a steady exodus from the sector.

The latest results also found gender differences in performance were persisting, with more female students reaching the proficient standard and exceeding in reading than males and the converse in maths. Performance in science was similar for both genders.

Australia’s disciplinary climate had improved compared with a record low in 2015 but remained poor, ranking behind 68 countries and better than just 11.

Noise and disorder in the classroom was reported by 41% Australian students as occurring often, compared with the global average of 31%, and 39% said their peers got distracted by using digital resources compared with the OECD average of 28%.

Australia is among 58% of countries that have banned smartphones in schools, indicating other tools, such as laptops and tablets, are causing distractions.

The federal education minister, Jason Clare, said Pisa results pointed to the “need to wind back the amount of screen time in schools”. “A bit of a digital detox,” he said.

“These results and Pisa over the past show us students who use screens a lot score lower than those who don’t.”

The last Pisa test, undertaken in 2022, saw Australia’s students climb into the top 10 of OECD countries, despite continuing the national dip. Australia’s 2018 results were the nation’s worst performance to date, due to narrowing gaps between its average results and the OECD average, particularly for mathematics.

Australia is now ranked 11th for science and reading and 17th in mathematics, which is largely stable compared with the 2022 results. The OECD gap between Australia and other nations had widened in all domains, with students around a year ahead of average in science and reading and six months ahead in mathematics.

The 2025 tests were the first time Pisa introduced a new category, learning in the digital world, which required students to demonstrate their use of digital tools to solve problems, including generating online models. Australia ranked lower than seven countries and 32 points, or around one and a half years, above the OECD average.

East Asian nations including Singapore, Japan, South Korea and participating Chinese regions performed the best overall globally, while Estonia also ranked highly. Australia scored higher than the US in science, mathematics and reading but below the UK and New Zealand. It also ranked above Canada in reading.

The shadow education minister, Julian Leeser, said the results should be a “wake-up call” for the federal government.

“This is the sharpest drop in maths and reading scores in a decade,” he said. “What we need is a rigorous curriculum, effective teaching methods and discipline in the classroom.”

title: England’s teenagers outperform peers in most countries in maths, reading and science
excerpt:
OECD test sees results dip in almost all member nations and warns of ‘digital distractions’ eroding academic skills

England’s teenagers are outperforming their peers in most countries in maths, readi...
body_text:
OECD test sees results dip in almost all member nations and warns of ‘digital distractions’ eroding academic skills

England’s teenagers are outperforming their peers in most countries in maths, reading and science, according to an international survey that warns of “digital distractions” eroding academic skills around the world.

The Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) programme for international student assessment (Pisa), which last year tested 760,000 15-year-olds in 91 countries and regions, found that results dipped in almost all of its members compared with previous years, with the exception of England and a handful of others.

England’s steady performance helped move the UK into the top 10 international rankings as other countries dropped out, with Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland recording results slightly lower than in previous years.

While England’s biggest improvement came in science, it was its performance in reading that stood out, putting it ahead of Australia, the US, Finland and France, and with only the scholastic powerhouses of Singapore, Taiwan and the combined Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu and Zhejiang regions in China performing significantly better.

Prof Mary Richardson of University College London, the lead author of the Pisa reports for Wales and Northern Ireland, said: “Despite the international trend of declining performance in reading, we found 15-year-olds in England, Wales and Northern Ireland to be reading just as well as they were in 2022.

“In science and maths, we also saw good performances, particularly for pupils in England and Northern Ireland, where scores were above the international average.”

Georgia Gould, the schools minister for England, said: “We are determined to build on these positive results and go further so all young people leave school with strong literacy and numeracy. And we want to take on the areas where England performs less well – how far pupils feel like they belong and value school. The next leap forward will come from pupils engaged and excited to be at school.”

Laura Trott, the shadow education secretary for England, said it was “bonkers” for the government to move away from the academic emphasis that was proving to be so successful in England’s schools.

Trott said: “Focusing on academic outcomes increases opportunity. It beggars belief that Labour wants to reduce standards. In doing so, the most disadvantaged will be worst hit as they will lose out on the most opportunity.”

The OECD’s overall analysis was gloomy, saying that “learning outcomes have stagnated or declined in many countries, in some cases for well over a decade”.

It highlighted the international decline in reading scores as “most concerning”, with average scores falling by double digits across OECD members since 2018. The organisation said the results implied that a majority of 15-year-olds in 2025 had performed at a level previously expected of 14-year-olds.

The OECD’s analysts stated: “The long-term declines in performance suggest deeper structural issues within education systems, with challenges at the school and system level. These include changing attitudes towards reading, the impact of digital distractions on students and rising levels of absenteeism.

“Overall, the data suggest weaknesses in how education systems are adapting to social, technological and economic change.”

Andreas Schleicher, the OECD’s director for education and skills, said while the negative impact of the Covid pandemic was a common explanation, the downturn in reading skills had emerged before the pandemic.

“We cannot say for sure but declining levels of reading for enjoyment and the shift towards digital reading – skimming social media feeds and rapidly processing information – may be compromising the ability of students to engage with complex texts and data,” Schleicher said.

Schleicher noted that while some uses of digital devices for learning were beneficial, those countries where devices were allowed for leisure at school saw “substantially lower” student performance.

“This raises questions about whether devices such as smartphones – designed to maximise a user’s attention – are compatible with sustained academic attention,” Schleicher said.

A report on Scotland’s performance, produced for the Scottish government, said that the 2025 result “presents a mixed but more positive picture”, with performances in science, mathematics and reading little changed since 2022.

But the report concluded: “Scores remain significantly below those achieved in several previous cycles, and a substantial proportion of pupils, particularly in mathematics, did not reach the OECD baseline proficiency level.”

Màiri McAllan, the education secretary for Scotland, said: “While recognising the positives, these results also underline the need for change in certain areas.”

title: Russia strikes Kyiv as three-day pause during US envoy visits ends
excerpt:
Russia has struck Kyiv after a three-day pause in attacks on the Ukrainian and Russian capitals expired, following a visit by two US envoys that yielded no tangible progress towards peace.

Two reside...
body_text:
Russia has struck Kyiv after a three-day pause in attacks on the Ukrainian and Russian capitals expired, following a visit by two US envoys that yielded no tangible progress towards peace.

Two residential buildings were damaged by Russian air raids early on Tuesday, city officials in Kyiv said. Drones hit buildings in the capital city as well as in the Boryspil and Fastiv districts on the outskirts of Kyiv, according to the State Emergency Service of Ukraine.

An air raid alert, published by the Kyiv city military administration, urged residents to take shelter due to the threat of an “enemy” drone attack.

Following the reported attacks in Ukraine, Russian regional Governor Roman Busargin said a Ukrainian drone attack injured several people after hitting civilian infrastructure in Saratov, nearly 1000km from Moscow. The number of casualties from both incidents remains unconfirmed (621 miles).

Russia and Ukraine pledged to halt strikes on each other’s capitals for three days as Washington dispatched envoys to Moscow and Kyiv. However, fighting continued elsewhere.

Attacks paused after leaders Vladimir Putin of Russia and Volodymyr Zelenskyy of Ukraine announced the ceasefire during the visits by US President Donald Trump’s envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, to Moscow and Kyiv over the weekend.

Russia’s state news agency TASS confirmed that the three-day suspension Putin had ordered for his forces expired on Monday evening local time.

Witkoff and Kushner held talks with officials in Moscow and Kyiv regarding ending the conflict. Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov called the more than three-hour meeting in Moscow on Saturday “highly useful”.

After talks with Ukraine’s Zelenskyy, Witkoff said: “We’ve had a very meaningful discussion, substantive, important, and we are very encouraged, and we look forward to continuing this as long as it takes.”

Witkoff also raised the prospects of reviving three-way negotiations to end the war.

A White House official told the Reuters news agency that the next steps regarding the war, which Russia began with a full-scale invasion of its neighbour in February 2022, would be announced in the coming weeks.

title: Yemeni forces launch counteroffensive against Houthis, vow to retake Sanaa
excerpt:
Yemen fighting escalates as gov’t forces launch air strikes on Houthi targets

Forces loyal to Yemen’s internationally recognised government have launched counterattacks against the Houthi rebels, wit...
body_text:
Yemen fighting escalates as gov’t forces launch air strikes on Houthi targets

Forces loyal to Yemen’s internationally recognised government have launched counterattacks against the Houthi rebels, with officials saying they aim to recapture the capital, Sanaa, more than a decade after the Iran-backed Houthis seized it.

Major-General Samir Al-Sabri, Yemen’s deputy defence minister, said in remarks broadcast on state television on Monday that “the decision has been made to retake Sanaa”.

The announcement came as fighting intensified in the provinces of al-Bayda and al-Jawf, seen as the main gateway to the capital. The Houthis said seven people were killed in a strike on a prison in al-Hazm in al-Jawf.

The renewed hostilities mark one of the most serious escalations since a United Nations-brokered truce in 2022 halted large-scale fighting in a war that began after the Houthis took Sanaa in 2014. The capture of the capital prompted a Saudi-led military intervention the following year.

Diplomats had hoped the truce in 2022 would evolve into a durable political settlement, but those efforts have faltered amid regional tensions triggered by the war launched by the United States and Israel against Iran.

Fighting in Yemen resumed in July, when government forces struck the Houthi-controlled airport in Sanaa, blocking the landing of an aircraft from Iran. Then last week, the Houthis launched a major offensive, trying to advance through western Taiz and southern Hodeidah, towards the port city of al-Makha and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait in the Red Sea.

Earlier, the Houthis had declared a blockade against Saudi vessels transiting the waterway.

That strait is a vital corridor for shipping between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. It has taken on new significance for Saudi oil exports since Iran began restricting passage through the Strait of Hormuz at the outset of the US and Israel’s war on the country.

Ahmed al-Shalafi, Al Jazeera’s Yemen affairs editor, said Yemeni government forces appear “to have absorbed the initial shock” of the rebel offensive “and expanded the fighting across several fronts, partly to stretch Houthi forces and increase pressure on them”.

He said the fighting was mainly concentrated west of Taiz and south of Hodeidah on Thursday, but has now spread to the provinces of al-Dhalea, Marib, al-Jawf and al-Bayda.

“Al-Jawf is particularly important because it borders Saudi Arabia and connects towards Saada, the Houthis’ main stronghold,” he said. “Al-Bayda is strategically significant because it lies at the centre of Yemen and connects eight governorates – four in the north and four in the south.”

The fighting has resulted in hundreds of casualties.

The World Health Organization said on Monday that nearly 900 people have been killed or wounded since Thursday, with the majority in Taiz and along the western coast. It said an estimated 21,000 people – roughly 3,000 families – have been displaced from Taiz alone.

Health officials say the casualty count is expected to rise further.

Rashad al-Alimi, the head of Yemen’s Saudi-backed Presidential Leadership Council, claimed sweeping gains against the Houthis on Monday, crediting government forces with advances in al-Jawf, al-Bayda, Taiz and Hodeidah.

“Our armed forces will continue to carry out their constitutional duty until state institutions are restored and their authority extends over the entire territory of Yemen,” al-Alimi said in a statement. He accused the Houthis of choosing escalation over peace, warning that the group would bear full responsibility for the consequences of its actions.

Majid al-Nuzaili, a spokesman for Yemen’s government-aligned forces, said on Monday that the objective of the campaign was to “liberate Yemen from the grip” of the Houthis “and restore Sanaa as a capital for all Yemenis”.

He also warned civilians to avoid several major roads leading into Sanaa, saying the alert applies to routes connecting the capital with Marib and al-Jawf, including roads through Nihm, Sirwah, Mahliyah and al-Hazm.

The media centre of the Yemeni government-aligned forces reported carrying out several air attacks against Houthi positions west of Taiz on Tuesday. Earlier, they had claimed attacks on Yatma in al-Jawf and said their forces were “engaged in intensive battles” against the Houthis in the province.

The media centre said Yemeni government-aligned forces had also advanced to the outskirts of Dhi Na’im district in al-Bayda.

For their part, the Houthis said they repelled a large-scale advance by Saudi-backed forces towards the al-Labanat mountains in Yemen’s al-Jawf province.

In a post on X, Mohammed al-Farah, a member of the Houthi political bureau, claimed dozens of fighters were killed or wounded and that Houthi forces also targeted reinforcements in al-Jawf with several ballistic missiles.

He said the strikes destroyed or damaged dozens of vehicles and armoured vehicles, and claimed that commanders were among those killed or wounded.

Al Jazeera could not independently verify the claims by the Houthis or the Yemeni government.

title: Barnaby Joyce says he’s not ‘Jesus Christ’ and admits One Nation has not modelled super policy in fiery interviews
excerpt:
Jim Chalmers says One Nation’s superannuation policy is ‘an absolute shambles’

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Bar...
body_text:
Jim Chalmers says One Nation’s superannuation policy is ‘an absolute shambles’

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Barnaby Joyce, One Nation’s Treasury spokesperson, says his party has not modelled the potential impact on retirement incomes and inflation from his party’s plan to give millions of households early access to their super savings in his second combative interview in two days.

The morning after telling the ABC’s 7.30 program that he “was not Jesus Christ” and so could not be expected to know everything, Joyce on Tuesday ridiculed any suggestion that One Nation’s proposal should have included the economic analysis that typically accompanies major policy proposals.

“Is there an implication beyond it being their money? Do you model the money you get paid at the end of the week?” he asked rhetorically.

The New England MP also told ABC Radio National on Tuesday that the lack of any guardrails around who could access their super early and for what purpose was not an issue as “people are not stupid” and would not take their money out of super unless it made financial sense.

“If they believe … that the alternative of getting their money to pay for their rental, to pay for their house payment, would be to leave it where they’re getting a spectacular return in their super … then most people who have a brain between their ears will do precisely the latter and leave it in the investment of superannuation,” he said.

Under One Nation’s proposal, Australians who pay rent or a mortgage – so roughly 9 million households – would be given a choice to divert a portion of their superannuation to their take-home pay for up to three years.

The full 12% compulsory super contribution would still be paid by employers but 3% could be paid directly to the account holder by their super fund, and still taxed at the lower 15% rate.

Modelling by the Super Members Council, which represents the not-for-profit super sector, suggested the average worker would be $25,000 poorer by retirement were One Nation’s scheme implemented.

The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has savaged One Nation’s plans, telling a meeting of Labor’s caucus that the plan was a threat to the compulsory super rules.

“Once you lose the principle of universality, the policy starts to disappear,” he said.

“If you watch [the Joyce interview], it’s clear that the policy has not been thought through.”

Jim Chalmers, the treasurer, attacked the super policy as “an absolute shambles”.

“They haven’t been able to tell us: what does this mean for pension spending? They haven’t been able to tell us: what are the broader economic implications of this superannuation advice from One Nation? This is a shambles from beginning to end.”
