title: Bolivian blast death toll rises to 7, rescuers search for missing soldiers
excerpt:
The death toll from explosions at a military base in Bolivia has risen to seven, as rescue teams continue searching for people still missing three days after the blasts.

Bolivian army Commander Hecto...
body_text:
The death toll from explosions at a military base in Bolivia has risen to seven, as rescue teams continue searching for people still missing three days after the blasts.

Bolivian army Commander Hector Alarcon said on Monday that seven people remain unaccounted for after the explosions at a military barracks in Viacha, about 30km (20 miles) southwest of La Paz.

“Our priority remains finding our comrades who are still missing and providing answers to their families as soon as possible,” Alarcon said.

Health Minister Marcela Flores said 84 people have been treated since the explosions, with 31 still in hospital.

The blasts happened on Friday afternoon in an area of the military facility used to store pyrotechnic material. Authorities had previously said the site was used to hold confiscated fireworks, grenades and TNT-based explosives.

The cause remains under investigation, but President Rodrigo Paz said the explosions appeared to have been an accident linked to the improper handling of explosives stored at the base.

Prosecutors in Viacha have opened an investigation into possible manslaughter and other crimes, while investigators are also looking into how the explosives were stored.

“Our Armed Forces are reviewing their protocols, and everything needed to provide greater safety, not only for enlisted personnel and officers, but also for nearby residents living close to military bases,” Paz said.

He announced a period of national mourning and urged Bolivians not to politicise the tragedy.

The explosions sent debris flying through the surrounding area, tearing roofs from buildings and uprooting trees, affecting dozens of homes. Footage posted on social media showed windows shattering and thick black smoke rising from the military facility.

Residents living nearby were evacuated to a temporary shelter after the blasts. Defence Minister Ernesto Justiniano said on Saturday that it was not yet safe for some residents to return because the shockwave had damaged homes.

Many of those initially reported missing were young conscripts aged 18 and 19 completing Bolivia’s mandatory military service. At least two of those confirmed dead were also first-year conscripts.

Former President Evo Morales has criticised Paz’s government over its response, accusing it of mishandling the disaster and calling for the matter to be taken to the International Criminal Court.

title: Alleged killers of Australian surfers and American friend go on trial in Mexico
excerpt:
Three men on trial for killing Jake and Callum Robinson and Jack Carter Rhoad in Baja California in 2024

The alleged killers of two Australian surfers and an American at a Mexican surfing hotspot in ...
body_text:
Three men on trial for killing Jake and Callum Robinson and Jack Carter Rhoad in Baja California in 2024

The alleged killers of two Australian surfers and an American at a Mexican surfing hotspot in 2024 have gone on trial in the border resort where the three were murdered.

The Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33, respectively, and their 30-year-old American friend Jack Carter Rhoad were shot dead after being robbed in Mexico’s violence-hit Baja California.

They were camping in a remote beachside area when they were attacked. Their bodies were found hidden on a cliff.

The Robinsons’ parents travelled to the port city of Ensenada for the start of the trial.

“It’s about representing our sons, being here for them. I know they want us to be here,” Martin Robinson told reporters as he entered the court with his wife, Debra.

“We want to find out what happened. We want to find out why,” he said.

The girlfriend of one of the accused was sentenced to 20 years in prison last year after admitting she had instigated the robbery.

The crime sparked outrage and sadness in Australia and the United States.

Callum Robinson played professional lacrosse in the US. His brother Jake was pursuing a career in medicine. Rhoad was killed a few months before he was due to marry.

Other foreign tourists have previously been targeted in criminal attacks on Mexico’s Pacific coast.

Two Australian surfers were murdered in 2015 while traveling through the north-western state of Sinaloa.

title: Gaza: Genocide in Real Time?
excerpt:
Gaza examined through occupation, blockade, mass killing and the genocide case before the ICJ.

Gaza, seen through the legal and political framework of genocide, as allegations are argued in real time...
body_text:
Gaza examined through occupation, blockade, mass killing and the genocide case before the ICJ.

Gaza, seen through the legal and political framework of genocide, as allegations are argued in real time before international courts. This episode traces how decades of occupation, blockade and repeated wars created conditions of confinement, dependency and dehumanisation long before the war that began on October 7, 2023. It explores how displacement orders, siege tactics, destruction of infrastructure, and AI-assisted targeting have shaped the scale and pattern of killing and destruction. Drawing on testimony, military analysis and legal argument, the episode follows how Palestinian victims, Israel, and third states frame the intent and nature of the violence, and why the International Court of Justice has warned of a “plausible risk” of genocide without yet ruling on its commission. It asks what this unfolding legal battle means for accountability, future deterrence and the people of Gaza themselves.

title: Erika Kirk reflects on first year of grief after Charlie Kirk's assassination in NYT essay
excerpt:
Fox News Chanley Painter reports the latest on the preliminary hearings in the Tyler Robinson murder trial. Fox News contributor Donna Rotunno also provides her take during Fox & Friends First.

Erika...
body_text:
Fox News Chanley Painter reports the latest on the preliminary hearings in the Tyler Robinson murder trial. Fox News contributor Donna Rotunno also provides her take during Fox & Friends First.

Erika Kirk explained why simply getting "through the next 15 minutes" has been a critical step in getting through the first year since the tragic assassination of her husband Charlie Kirk.

Kirk, who took over leadership of Turning Point USA (TPUSA) following the fatal shooting of her 31-year-old husband at Utah Valley University on Sept. 10, 2025, penned a New York Times guest essay headlined, "What I’ve learned about grief," that was published on Monday.

Kirk said the first 24 hours after her husband was assassinated felt "like a fever dream," and she told Second Lady Usha Vance that she didn’t know how she would move forward. The wife of Vice President JD Vance then offered words that are now "seared into" Kirk’s heart.

JD VANCE'S WIFE USHA DETAILS HOW CHARLIE KIRK'S DEATH INFLUENCED DECISION TO HAVE FOURTH CHILD

Erika Kirk penned a New York Times guest essay about grief as the one-year anniversary of the tragic assassination of her husband approaches.   (Dimitrios Kambouris/Getty Images)

"You know when you’re on an airplane with your kids, and you’re going to land in 15 minutes, but the kids are going crazy, screaming, throwing things, and then the plane lands, and the kids relax, and everything is fine again? That’s how it will be. Just get through the next 15 minutes," Vance told Kirk, according to Kirk’s guest essay.

Kirk explained that things like seeing his toothbrush and towel in their shared bathroom were tough, but she constantly thought of Vance’s advice.

"I stood in the doorway of our bedroom. I turned on the light and walked toward his side of the bed. I stared at his pillow and wondered how long a person’s scent can last in sheets. I stood there in silence, replaying all of the completely ordinary mornings we woke up there together. I wasn’t ready to be there, so I turned off the light and crawled into bed with my 3-year-old daughter. Just get through the next 15 minutes," Kirk wrote.

"For months, I avoided my bedroom. I told myself it was OK to confront the pain gradually and to sit with each memory as it came to me," she continued. "The first Saturday without a love note from him passed. His 32nd birthday. My birthday. Thanksgiving. When I put the Christmas tree together wrong, it made me realize that being a widow means old traditions will need to make room for new ones. The wave crashes on me again and again. Every time, just get through the next 15 minutes."

The CEO of the conservative nonprofit listed other family milestones that her beloved late husband had missed, and she eventually realized their young daughter was also "surviving her own little crashing waves."

Erika Kirk speaks during the memorial service for her husband, political activist Charlie Kirk at State Farm Stadium on Sept. 21, 2025, in Glendale, Arizona. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)

"Grief is strange. Time continues even when every part of you wants it to pause or, better yet, rewind. But the people we love who have passed on would not want us to spend the rest of our lives trying to rewind. At first, I needed to survive the next 15 minutes. Over time, I’ve realized that Charlie would want me to live them," Kirk wrote.

"Occasionally, I’m asked whether I’m angry at God. I say no. My husband was one of one. I was blessed to be his wife, and I understood his assignment here on Earth, which he more than fulfilled. He wanted people who felt lost to know the everlasting hope he found through faith and the sense of meaning and purpose that can fill the deeper longings we so often try to satisfy elsewhere," she added. "To the world, he was Charlie Kirk. But to me, he was the love of my life. To our children, he was the center of their world."

Kirk believes that it’s easy to struggle to understand God’s plan after losing a loved one and faith is truly tested when "bad things happen."

HOW CHARLIE KIRK INSPIRED HIS MENTOR'S FIGHT TO DEFEND REALITY

Charlie Kirk was assassinated Sept. 10 during an outdoor event at Utah Valley University.  (Trent Nelson/The Salt Lake Tribune/Getty Images)

"True faith means accepting that we won’t get every answer and finding peace in that," Kirk wrote. "I have seen extraordinary good born out of something unimaginably evil. I have watched people return to faith in droves, reconcile with their families and forgive old wounds because of Charlie. I know my husband is in heaven, but I ache for him to be here. Still, I can stand and say without a shadow of a doubt that God is good."

She wrote that the wave still comes, but it is different a year later and she even welcomes it, as "a moment the grief makes Charlie feel impossibly close." Kirk believes grief is universal," doesn’t care whom you voted for" and never truly goes away.

"I am learning that grieving Charlie and living life at the same time are part of the rhythm of grief. I can miss him with every part of me and still laugh with our children. I can have a broken heart and still experience joy," Kirk wrote.

"If you are living through grief, I won’t tell you what to feel or that tomorrow will be better than today. I will tell you what a dear friend told me: Just get through the next 15 minutes," she continued. "One day, maybe when you least expect it, you’ll start to see that those 15 minutes hold more than just grief. The grief is there, always, but so is the beautiful gift of life."

CHARLIE KIRK'S FAMILY COMES FACE TO FACE WITH ACCUSED ASSASSIN FOR FIRST TIME

President Donald Trump greets Erika Kirk, widow of Turning Point USA founder Charlie Kirk, during a public memorial at State Farm Stadium in Glendale, Arizona, on September 21. (Patrick T. Fallon/Getty Images)

Psychotherapist and author Jonathan Alpert told Fox News Digital that the second lady provided strong advice.

"One of the hardest parts of grief is that your mind races ahead, filling you with anxiety. How am I going to do this for the next year? How am I going to raise my kids without this person? What are holidays going to look like? How do I build a life I never expected to be living? Suddenly you’re trying to solve the rest of your life at the worst possible moment.Sometimes you really do need to shrink the window and just get through the next 15 minutes," Alpert said.

"Resilience isn’t pretending you’re fine. It’s being able to hurt and still live your life," he added. "Erika’s piece shows that those two things can exist at the same time."

TPUSA did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Charlie Kirk founded TPUSA to promote conservatism on college campuses nationwide. He was speaking before more than 2,000 people at a TPUSA event in Orem, Utah, when he was assassinated, leaving behind Erika and their two children.

Fox News Digital’s Michael Sinkewicz contributed to this report.

Brian Flood is a media editor/reporter for FOX News Digital. Story tips can be sent to brian.flood@fox.com and on Twitter: @briansflood.

title: Ritzy Miami steakhouse manager held on ICE detainer after mom found stabbed to death
excerpt:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A Miami steakhouse manager allegedly emerged from his luxury apartment covered in blood and clutching a knife before t...
body_text:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A Miami steakhouse manager allegedly emerged from his luxury apartment covered in blood and clutching a knife before telling police he had acted in self-defense after his mother was found stabbed to death inside.

Stefano Eduardo Cremasco-Cicero, 36, told officers, "I was defending myself," after Miami police were called to the Brickell high-rise early Friday, according to an arrest report obtained by WPLG.

Cremasco-Cicero is charged with second-degree murder with a weapon, Miami-Dade County jail records show.

KARMELO ANTHONY STAYS SILENT AS ANALYSTS WARN DEFENSE FACES UPHILL BATTLE IN TRACK MEET STABBING TRIAL

Stefano Cremasco-Cicero is being held without bond on a second-degree murder charge and an ICE detainer. (Miami-Dade County Corrections and Rehabilitation)

Officers were dispatched at about 4:47 a.m. for an "unknown request for police assistance," according to the outlet.

Officers found Cremasco-Cicero in the lobby with blood on his hands, clothing and shoes, the outlet reported.

He allegedly directed officers upstairs to the apartment.

Inside the apartment, police found his mother lying behind the front door with multiple apparent stab wounds, according to WPLG. Miami Fire Rescue pronounced her dead shortly after 5 a.m.

FLORIDA MAN ACCUSED OF KILLING MOM AND BURNING BODY BECAUSE SHE ‘WANTED TO BE CREMATED’

Cremasco-Cicero was reportedly found in the lobby with blood on his hands, clothing and shoes. (WSVN)

Authorities have not publicly identified the woman or disclosed her age. Police said she was visiting from Mexico and staying with her son.

The unusual chain of events began when a food delivery driver arrived at the building and encountered Cremasco-Cicero in the lobby, according to the report.

He allegedly opened the door for the driver and asked her to call 911. Cremasco-Cicero ultimately placed the call himself but handed the phone to the woman so she could give the dispatcher the building information, WPLG reported.

The driver noticed blood on him as they waited for police, according to the outlet. When she tried to return his phone, he allegedly refused to take it, and she later handed it to responding officers.

THE SURVEILLANCE CAMERA ON YOUR STREET CORNER: LAWFUL SPYING OR CONSTITUTIONALLY PROBLEMATIC?

Investigators then turned to surveillance video and building access records to piece together what happened in the hours before police arrived.

Police were called to a high-rise in the Brickell neighborhood of Miami early Friday. (WSVN)

Surveillance video showed Cremasco-Cicero and his mother returning to the building together at about 10:32 p.m. Thursday, according to WPLG. They were reportedly alone in the elevator.

COURTNEY CLENNEY'S DEFENSE INSPECTS KNIVES AT CENTER OF ONLYFANS MODEL'S MURDER CASE AHEAD OF TRIAL: REPORT

At about 4:26 a.m., surveillance video allegedly captured Cremasco-Cicero entering an elevator wearing a white shirt, khaki pants and white shoes that appeared to be covered in blood. Police said he was carrying a knife.

He allegedly dropped the knife after stepping out of the elevator, picked it back up and rode another elevator upstairs, according to the report.

Investigators said Cremasco-Cicero later reappeared in a different, long-sleeved blue shirt and walked out of the building while using his phone. He returned minutes later and sat on a couch in the lobby before flagging down the delivery driver, WPLG reported.

Cremasco-Cicero’s wife, who was in France at the time, told detectives that his mother had been staying with him at the time of the incident, according to local reports. (WSVN)

Police said Cremasco-Cicero had small cuts on his hands and blood residue on his body and clothing. Crime scene investigators photographed him and collected his clothes, according to the outlet.

5 REASONS MORE AMERICANS ARE CUTTING OFF THEIR OWN PARENTS, ACCORDING TO PSYCHOLOGIST

After obtaining a search warrant, homicide detectives allegedly recovered several kitchen knives with blood on them, blood-spattered shirts, broken glass and a broken wine bottle from the apartment, WPLG reported.

Cremasco-Cicero’s wife told detectives she was in France attending a wedding when the killing happened, according to the report. She said her husband and his mother had not been close since his parents divorced and that he had recently been under stress while preparing to open a restaurant in Coconut Grove.

Stefano Cremasco-Cicero is seen sitting for an interview with WSVN-TV about his restaurant in July. (WSVN)

The Miami Herald identified Cremasco-Cicero as the U.S. operating manager of the high-end 1986 Steakhouse in Miami.

The arrest report identified Cremasco-Cicero as a Miami resident through an investor visa, according to WPLG.

Miami-Dade Corrections records reviewed by Fox News Digital show Cremasco-Cicero was booked Friday night and is being held at the Turner Guilford Knight Correctional Center. The records list no bond, a domestic-violence designation and a hold for immigration authorities.

The jail record does not provide additional details about the immigration hold.

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson confirmed to Fox News Digital that Cremasco-Cicero is an illegal immigrant.

"On August 5, 2026, ICE lodged a detainer for Stefano Eduardo Cremasco Cicero, a criminal illegal alien from Mexico, charged with homicide," the DHS spokesperson said. "We are calling on Florida to honor our detainer. His claims will be heard by an immigration judge and he will receive due process. This administration will not ignore the rule of law."

"Under President Trump and Secretary Mullin, if you break the law, you will face the consequences," the spokesperson added. "Criminal illegal aliens are not welcome in the U.S."

A motive for the killing remains unclear.

Fox News Digital reached out to the Miami Police Department, the Miami-Dade Clerk of Courts and 1986 Steakhouse for additional information.

Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

title: Serbian government sets up snap vote with call to dissolve parliament
excerpt:
Serbia’s government has proposed the dissolution of parliament, paving the way for early elections.

‌Prime Minister Djuro Macut announced the call in Belgrade on Monday. The move to a snap election i...
body_text:
Serbia’s government has proposed the dissolution of parliament, paving the way for early elections.

‌Prime Minister Djuro Macut announced the call in Belgrade on Monday. The move to a snap election is seen as a bid to tighten the rule of President Aleksandar Vucic after nearly two years of anti-government unrest.

Parliamentary elections were not due until December next year, but Vucic on Monday announced plans to hold a vote in late October, with speculation rife that he will seek to move into the role of prime minister.

The early election will test how secure a grip on Serbian politics Vucic still enjoys. The veteran authoritarian leader has run the country as president or prime minister for 12 ⁠years.

However, massive and persistent anticorruption demonstrations, following the killing of 16 people when a concrete canopy collapsed at a railway station in 2024, have presented him with his sternest challenge yet.

The student-led protest movement has long demanded early elections.

“If we want to mitigate tensions in society there is no better way than to ask people,” Macut said as he announced the dissolution call.

“Serbia has faced protests, blockades, deep divisions, problems in education and heavy pressure on institutions,” he told ministers. “For some time, parts of the public have been calling for early parliamentary elections,” adding that “a responsible government never ignores such demands.”

Vucic is expected to set ⁠a date for elections in the coming days. According to the constitution, between 45 and 60 days must be allowed for campaigning.

The president has already said that the vote will be held on either October 18 or ⁠25.

The election would allow Vucic, whose Serbian ⁠Progressive Party nominated on Saturday to run for prime minister, to try to reassert his authority.

The ‌opposition and demonstrators accuse Vucic and his allies of violence against political opponents, rampant corruption, ties with organised crime and ‌stifling ‌media freedoms. The president and his circle have denied any wrongdoing.

Vucic’s opponents have condemned the fact that Serbia’s bid to join the European Union has stalled. The president has instead worked on maintaining close ties with Russia and China.

Vucic has faced additional EU pressure in the past week over public homage to war criminal Ratko Mladic, the former Bosnian Serb army commander, who was buried as a hero in Serbia on Monday despite his United Nations court conviction.

title: Rob Lowe says Tom Cruise was his ‘nemesis’ in the fight for blockbuster roles
excerpt:
The host of FOX’s "The Floor" told Fox News Digital that he advised his son to create his own content.

Rob Lowe had plenty of competition for blockbuster roles in the 1980s and ’90s – and one Hollywo...
body_text:
The host of FOX’s "The Floor" told Fox News Digital that he advised his son to create his own content.

Rob Lowe had plenty of competition for blockbuster roles in the 1980s and ’90s – and one Hollywood heavyweight repeatedly stood in his way.

"That dastardly Tom Cruise was always a nemesis," Lowe told the New York Post.

"I remember reading ‘Jerry Maguire’ ... and they were like, ‘Tom Cruise.’ I also remember reading ‘Top Gun’ and going, ‘Oh, this movie is going to be f---ing massive,'" he recalled. "They were like, ‘Tom Cruise.'"

'BLUE LAGOON' STAR CHRISTOPHER ATKINS SAYS ALCOHOL COST HIM ICONIC 'FOOTLOOSE' ROLE BEFORE GETTING SOBER

Rob Lowe revealed that Tom Cruise was a recurring "nemesis" who beat him out for blockbuster roles including "Top Gun" and "Jerry Maguire." (Pool Denize-Pelletier/Gamma-Rapho via Getty Images)

Despite losing out on what he considered to be big roles. Lowe found his stride as a core member of the Brat Pack. He starred in several career-defining films of the Brat Pack-era, including "St. Elmo's Fire," "The Outsiders," "Class," and "Oxford Blues."

Yet one major piece was missing from Lowe’s ’80s résumé – a coveted role in a John Hughes movie.

Lowe admitted he was never in the running for the coming-of-age hit "Ferris Bueller’s Day Off."

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Despite those setbacks, Rob Lowe found success as a key member of the Brat Pack in films including "St. Elmo’s Fire," "The Outsiders" and "Oxford Blues." (Frank Edwards/Fotos International/Getty Images)

"No, that’s a big regret," he said, noting Hughes was not interested in casting Lowe for the role that went to Matthew Broderick.

"John Hughes never got what I was selling," Lowe explained.

"I met with John once, and it’s not like he didn’t have a lot of parts I could have done," he added. "When you really look at it, there were more than a few parts, multiple parts in some movies. Never, phone never rang."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Rob Lowe also opened up about his regret over never landing a role in John Hughes’ iconic movies, including "Ferris Bueller’s Day Off" and "The Breakfast Club." (Nancy Moran/Sygma via Getty Images)

Decades later, Lowe has come up with his own explanation for why Hughes never came calling.

"I have a theory about it; I think I was actually already too well known," Lowe said.

"John put in people who [weren’t] already well known," he explained. "He made people well known. At least that’s what I tell myself to make myself feel better for not getting a role in ‘The Breakfast Club.'"

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

The actor later built a lasting career through roles on "The West Wing," "Parks and Recreation" and other film, television and streaming projects. (Getty Images)

Lowe's early movie roles established him as a teen heartthrob, but he later built a remarkably durable career spanning film, network televisio and streaming projects.

A major second act came with his role as Sam Seaborn on "The West Wing," which earned him Emmy and Golden Globe nominations. He later showed off his comedic side as the relentlessly upbeat Chris Traeger on "Parks and Recreation."

title: Judge denies ousted Stars and Stripes journalists effort to reverse Pentagon's firings
excerpt: Erik Slavin, the recently ousted editor-in-chief of the military newspaper Stars and Stripes, spoke with Fox News Digital about his lawsuit against the Pentagon, alleging his firing violated First Ame...
body_text:
Erik Slavin, the recently ousted editor-in-chief of the military newspaper Stars and Stripes, spoke with Fox News Digital about his lawsuit against the Pentagon, alleging his firing violated First Amendment rights.

A federal judge Friday denied a request from the trio of ousted Stars and Stripes journalists to reverse the Pentagon's firing of them.

U.S. District Judge Trevor McFadden denied a temporary restraining order filed by Stars and Stripes publisher Max Lederer, editor-in-chief Erik Slavin and reporter Lara Korte, claiming they "ultimately fail to carry their significant burden to show that they are clearly entitled to a preliminary injunction."

In a joint statement to Fox News Digital, the three journalists expressed their disappointment with McFadden's decision but insist it's not the "final judgment."

"We are reviewing the decision with our attorneys and considering our next steps," Lederer, Slavin and Korte said. "We continue to believe that the Pentagon should not be able to fire journalists for speaking out against censorship and defending the editorial independence of Stars and Stripes."

FIRED STARS AND STRIPES SUE PENTAGON, ALLEGE RETALIATION AND FIRST AMENDMENT VIOLATION

A federal judge ruled in favor of the Pentagon in denying an effort to block the firing of three Stars and Stripes journalists. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)

"This case is not primarily about the three of us. It is about whether the servicemembers who swear to defend the Constitution, and the military families who serve alongside them, can rely on a free and independent press. It is also about whether the military and civilian journalists at Stars and Stripes can do their jobs without fear of retaliation," they added.

Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell touted the legal win on social media.

"The court applied settled Supreme Court law: public employees do not receive First Amendment protection when they speak with the government’s voice," Parnell wrote on X. "The record showed these interviews were arranged with supervisor involvement, conducted at Stripes workplaces, and presented the speakers in their official titles, discussing the paper they run. That is government speech, not private-citizen speech."

"Stars and Stripes is a Department of War publication funded to inform the military community," Parnell continued. "The Department has both the authority and the responsibility to ensure it remains focused on the force — warfighting, readiness, and the men and women who serve — rather than becoming a platform for airing employee grievances. We will follow the law and complete the personnel process."

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION SUBPOENAS NY TIMES JOURNALISTS IN GRAND JURY LEAK PROBE TIED TO AIR FORCE ONE REPORT

Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell praised the judge's ruling on X. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)

Last month, the Pentagon fired the journalists from the military newspaper over alleged insubordination. In return, they filed a lawsuit alleging retaliation and violation of their First Amendment rights.

The firings stem from Slavin and Korte's unauthorized participation in a July "CBS Sunday Morning" segment about the Pentagon's efforts to overhaul the paper and Lederer's refusal to fire them at the direction of Pentagon leadership.

According to the lawsuit, the trio allege Pentagon leadership "understood these interview statements expressed personal opinions, and therefore took no immediate action, despite their displeasure" and that it wasn't until Stars and Stripes published its report on the alleged strife aboard the U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln that the Pentagon's stance had shifted.

The lawsuit notes that Pentagon leadership demanded Lederer to fire Slavin and Korte just one day after the report was published.

Listed as the defendants in the lawsuit are the Pentagon, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, Parnell and his principal deputy assistant Andrew Brey.

Stars and Stripes editor-in-chief Erik Slavin was fired by the Pentagon for alleged insubordination after he participated in an interview on "CBS Sunday Morning." (Screenshot/CBS News)

In an interview with Fox News Digital, Slavin insisted the Pentagon never explicitly stated how he and Korte were deemed insubordinate for the CBS News interview, noting that he had given many other media interviews without having to seek authorization from Pentagon leadership.

"This isn't about me. It's not about three jobs. It's about whether servicemembers and their families are gonna have access to independent news and information and news that they can trust," Slavin said. "And it's my concern for our staff that they might face further retaliation if they make statements along the lines of 'Hey, we work for Stars and Stripes and we provide independent news.' So this is about protecting an institution, in my mind."

Joseph A. Wulfsohn is a media reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to joseph.wulfsohn@fox.com and on Twitter: @JosephWulfsohn.

title: Kenya minister warns foreigners against 'misusing' visas to trade
excerpt:
Trade Minister Lee Kinyanjui says foreign nationals must comply with the law

Kenya's trade ministry has warned foreign nationals that visa-free entry into the country does not grant them the right to...
body_text:
Trade Minister Lee Kinyanjui says foreign nationals must comply with the law

Kenya's trade ministry has warned foreign nationals that visa-free entry into the country does not grant them the right to work, as the government vows to shut down unlicensed small businesses run by migrants.

President William Ruto had set today as the deadline for foreigners operating small-scale businesses to cease work.

Hundreds of people have gathered at Burundi's embassy in Kenya as they rushed to get documents, after the embassy had earlier said it would offer emergency free travel documents to citizens who want to go back home.

It is unclear how many foreign nationals are involved in small-scale trading or how many would be affected by the crackdown.

In a statement, the trade ministry said there was a "deliberate misuse of visa applications by some visitors", adding that some entered Kenya as investors or tourists but then got involved in business activities in breach of their declared status.

"Owing to the high number of foreigners involved in the retail and local trade sectors, there is therefore a need to align their activities and ensure compliance with work permit provisions," Trade Minister Lee Kinyanjui said.

Last week, Ruto said that Kenya remained open to foreign investment, but it could not be "that a person comes from China or elsewhere to be a hawker or open a small shop".

He argued that investors should create jobs and expand production rather than compete with Kenyans in small businesses.

Ruto's comments sparked mixed reactions, with some critics describing them as a populist move that risked stoking xenophobia. Government officials deny the allegation.

Burundi's Foreign Affairs Minister Edouard Bizimana said in a post on X that "Kenyans in Burundi were living peacefully but if the hate speech against Burundi continues things will certainty change".

"Kenya government is responsible for the lives of Burundians living in Kenya," he added.

Bizimana's post followed an urgent meeting he held with representatives of the East African Community (EAC), an eight-member bloc which promotes economic integration in the region.

Both Kenya and Burundi are part of the group. Kenyan representatives attended the meeting called by Bizimana in Burundi.

Bizimana said he had asked the Kenyan ambassador to convey to his government Burundi's concerns and to ensure that no Burundian was subjected to abuse.

On Sunday, a top official in Kenya's foreign affairs ministry said foreigners, with the required documentation, including "work permits and licences", could continue their activities.

"Burundian nationals and all East Africans - and Africans for that matter - are free to live in Kenya as long as they conduct their businesses or work according to the requirements of our laws, Permanent Secretary Korir Sing'oei said.

The government's clarification, however, did little to ease concerns among some foreign traders.

Alexis Ntinanirwa, the head of the Association of Burundians living in Kenya, told the BBC Great Lakes service that he was unhappy with Ruto's decision, but was urging Burundians to remain patient.

He warned that the issue could have wider regional consequences because Kenyans are also involved in small-scale businesses in other East African countries.

"This issue is not only going to cause problems for Burundians working in Kenya, but it is also going to cause problems in the region because there are also Kenyans doing these small jobs in our countries in Burundi, Tanzania and Uganda."

Ntinanirwa advised Burundians involved in hawking and other small businesses to avoid confrontation with police.

Additional reporting by Akisa Wandera and Prime Ndikumagenge

Kenyan president orders crackdown on foreigners operating small businesses

Did a goat herder's lucky $200 nugget spark a gold rush in western Kenya?

Go to BBCAfrica.com, external for more news from the African continent.

title: UN agency accused of Hamas ties sees another European nation cut funding
excerpt: Speaking at the U.N. July 1, Ambassador Jeff Bartos said donors could continue supporting United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugee or choose a framework offering Gazans "peace, pro...
body_text:
Speaking at the U.N. July 1, Ambassador Jeff Bartos said donors could continue supporting United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugee or choose a framework offering Gazans "peace, prosperity and real durable change." (Credit: UNTV)

Another European nation has stopped funding the U.N. agency that aids the Palestinians. Finland has followed the U.S. and Sweden in halting donations to the terror-tainted agency.

The United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East (UNRWA), is presently being investigated for ties to the terrorist rulers of Gaza. Recently, organizations including the USAID Office of Inspector General (OIG) and NGO UN Watch have uncovered further evidence of what they allege is Hamas infiltration of UNRWA and its members’ participation in the Oct. 7, 2023 terror attacks in southern Israel.

Finland announced it would discontinue funding to the organization at the end of 2026. Finland’s Ministry for Foreign Affairs confirmed to Fox News Digital that the agreement with UNRWA would conclude at the end of 2026 but that "As of yet, no decision has been made on what are the international partners through which Finland’s support will be channeled next year to meet the acute needs in the region."

Finnish officials did not respond to Fox News Digital’s questions about what prompted the change to the country’s funding for UNRWA.

US URGES DONORS TO ABANDON UNRWA FUNDING AS UN DEFENDS AGENCY'S MISSION

This picture taken during a media tour organised by the Israeli army on February 8, 2024, shows Israeli soldiers inside an evacuated compound of the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees (UNRWA) in Gaza City. (Jack Guez/AFP via Getty Images)

While other nations still continue to fund UNRWA, President Donald Trump fully banned funding to the organization in February 2025 and Sweden ended funding to UNRWA in December 2024. Sweden redirected aid to other U.N. bodies for its Gaza response.

The future of aid provision in Gaza matters for the Trump administration-backed Board of Peace as it seeks to shape a conflict-free future for the region.

An official affiliated with the Board of Peace reconstruction effort told Fox News Digital that "the international community’s concern about UNRWA in Gaza continues to rise and is supported by damning evidence. The Board of Peace has been clear: New Gaza will be both demilitarized and deradicalized, and we will only be working with trusted, credible delivery partners to achieve our goals. We anticipate responsibly replacing UNRWA with vetted partners who will deliver for the people of Gaza."

WATCHDOG DEMANDS APOLOGY AFTER UN MEMORIAL ERRONEOUSLY HONORS HAMAS TERRORIST

United Nations Relief and Works Agency (UNRWA) building in Gaza, June, 2023. (Ahmed Zakot/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)

The USAID OIG is investigating about 1,500 members of UNRWA for terror participation, and has referred 108 UNRWA staff to the State Department to suggest they be suspended or excluded from further work with organizations in receipt of U.S. funds.

A senior U.S. official briefed on USAID OIG’s ongoing investigation told Fox News Digital that the USAID OIG’s "independent findings are prompting several other countries to reassess the stale and conventional thinking that UNRWA is the best and only option to provide aid to civilians in Gaza." The official said that the USAID OIG’s "findings also will prevent Hamas and October 7 affiliated staff from circulating across future, more responsible, aid organizations operating in Gaza."

WORLD'S HUMANITARIAN SYSTEM BUCKLING, 'NO LONGER FIT FOR PURPOSE,' US-BASED RESEARCHERS SAY

Hamas fighters secure an area before handing over an Israeli-American hostage Keith Siegel to a Red Cross team in Gaza City on Feb. 1, 2025, as part of the fourth hostage-prisoner exchange. Ranks of Hamas fighters formed up on Gaza's beachfront in a show of force against the dramatic backdrop of breaking waves. (SAEED JARAS/Middle East Images/AFP via Getty Images)

UN Watch’s Terror Network report claims that about 12% of UNRWA staff in Gaza are members of terror organizations, based on "cross-checking UNRWA employee rosters with Hamas records seized by the [Israel Defense Forces.]"

Executive director of UN Watch Hillel Neuer told Fox News Digital that "Finland’s principled decision to defund terror-infested UNRWA will not deprive Palestinians of aid, as it will be redirected through genuine humanitarian agencies such as the World Food Programme that are not systemically infiltrated by Hamas."

He said that "other democracies should follow" the examples of Finland, Sweden, and the U.S. "Contrary to what UNRWA supporters claim, the agency is not ‘indispensable’ — assistance can and must be delivered through responsible alternatives."

Displays featuring what organizers say are UNRWA facilities and personnel involved in terrorist activities. Displayed at the 'Return to October' exhibition in Israel. (Amelie Botbol for Fox News Digital)

Stéphane Dujarric, spokesperson for U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres, told Fox News Digital that "UNRWA has taken note of the announcement, and they are grateful to Finland for the disbursement of the 2023–2026 funds under the multi-year agreement. UNRWA looks forward to continuing our discussions with the government." He explained that "the Secretary-General continues to encourage member states to support UNRWA's vital work."

Finland's four-year funding was around $23.23 to UNRWA and will now end after this year. UNRWA did not respond to Fox News Digital questions about Finland’s decision.

Neuer said "defunding UNRWA is a prerequisite for deradicalization, the first step in the Gaza peace plan. Far from harming the prospects for peace, dismantling UNRWA is essential to achieving it. For decades, the agency has perpetuated the conflict by teaching generations of Palestinians that their future lies not in building their own society, but in a so-called ‘right of return’ that would eliminate Israel."

He concluded by noting that USAID OIG and UN Watch’s exposes on UNRWA prove that "the agency is unreformable. Nations that genuinely want peace should stop financing this machinery of hate, and invest instead in humanitarian relief, deradicalization and Palestinian self-reliance."

Beth Bailey writes on the United Nations, worldwide antisemitism, and regions in conflict for Fox News.

title: Next overturns equal pay ruling that raised basic wages for shop staff
excerpt:
Retailer wins appeal against 2024 decision forcing it to pay shop workers the same as warehouse employees

The UK retailer Next has overturned a 2024 court ruling forcing it to pay its shop staff the ...
body_text:
Retailer wins appeal against 2024 decision forcing it to pay shop workers the same as warehouse employees

The UK retailer Next has overturned a 2024 court ruling forcing it to pay its shop staff the same higher basic pay rates as its warehouse workers under equal pay rules.

The chain, led by the Conservative peer Simon Wolfson, said it had “won a landmark victory in its ongoing equal pay litigation”. It has succeeded in its appeal to the employment appeal tribunal “on the key issue of basic pay”, it said.

It comes two years after 3,540 claimants won a six-year legal fight for equal pay, which the fashion and homeware retailer then appealed against. Shop workers accused Next of paying its retail sales staff – who are predominantly female – lower hourly wages than its warehouse workers, the majority of whom are male.

Since that employment tribunal ruling in Leeds, several thousand more Next staff have brought equal pay claims, bringing the total number of claimants involved in the litigation to more than 6,400. Next employs more than 20,000 store staff across 458 stores in the UK and Ireland.

Next said the appeal judgment endorsed its position that it “should not have to pay shop assistants and warehouse operatives the same amount of basic pay, in circumstances where the market and working conditions are very different”.

The retailer argued that it had to pay a higher market rate to warehouse staff because of recruitment and retention pressures, which it said did not apply to the workforce in its stores. It added: “Next believes this element of the judgment is not only correct in law, but also a victory for common sense.”

The retailer said the judgment affirmed: “Employers must be able to pay what is necessary to recruit the people they need; and that doing so does not oblige them to raise the pay of other employees where there is no reason to do so.”

The law firm Leigh Day, which represents Next store workers, described it as a “mixed ruling” as it rejected Next’s challenge to the tribunal’s findings that it had failed to justify lower rates of night-time pay, overtime pay and the failure to provide paid rest breaks to store workers.

Next also failed to persuade the employment appeal tribunal that lower Sunday premium payments to store workers were justified. The appeal tribunal held that the issue remains to be determined and should return to the employment tribunal.

The Next case, which covered the period from 2012 and 2023, explained women made up almost 78% of retail sales jobs, while men made up about 53% of warehouse staff. During that time, some warehouse staff were able to earn between 38p and £3.13 more an hour than retail sales workers, according to Leigh Day.

Elizabeth George, a partner at Leigh Day representing the claimants, said: “I am pleased that the employment appeal tribunal rejected Next’s arguments that its pay practices do not disadvantage women. They plainly do and the appeal tribunal firmly recognised that. I am also pleased that the tribunal upheld the findings on night-time premiums, overtime premiums and paid rest breaks.

“The appeal tribunal’s conclusion on basic pay is disappointing. Next pays market rates in both its stores and its warehouses in order to recruit and retain staff. The market rate is higher in the predominantly male warehouse labour market, even though the work carried out in stores has already been found to be equal work.

“While the store staff and their legal team welcome many aspects of this appeal judgment, we respectfully disagree with this approach to justification. We remain confident in our clients’ position and intend to appeal.”

Next had argued that the equal pay ruling created a threat to the viability of many of its stores, and that it put retailers operating their own warehouses at a “material disadvantage” to rivals that contract out their warehouse operations.

The original employment tribunal and the appeal tribunal found that there was no direct discrimination. The employment tribunal found: “It was all about cost. Gender did not enter into the equation” when Next set pay rates.

Next said it had won the vast majority of the terms challenged in the equal pay litigation, including bonus pay to warehouse staff previously, and now basic pay. It intends to seek permission to appeal in relation to other terms.

“This judgment has come at the right time, the UK economy desperately needs jobs and the loss of this appeal would have represented a hammer blow to retail employment in the UK,” the company said.

title: NASCAR race turns ominous as driver delivers chilling warning, Hooters Gianna gets racy in the pool & Hocevar!
excerpt:
Carson Hocevar is currently 12th in the cup series

Monday Morning Pit-Stop is a weekly NASCAR column that runs on OutKick.com and Fox News Digital. If you're looking for a normal NASCAR recap, go che...
body_text:
Carson Hocevar is currently 12th in the cup series

Monday Morning Pit-Stop is a weekly NASCAR column that runs on OutKick.com and Fox News Digital. If you're looking for a normal NASCAR recap, go check out insufferable ESPN ... assuming they still know NASCAR exists.

Last week, Carson Hocevar told me he didn't expect any drama in The Chase.

I asked him, point blank, if he felt like he had any enemies on the track, or if he felt like he was driving around with a target on his back.

This, of course, came after months of NASCAR drama — all culminating in a recently launched relationship with a TikTok influencer who was starting to ruffle some feathers around the garage.

"I think it's good for TV and merch sales at times, but I don't think so," Hocevar told me when I asked him about other drivers coming after him.

NASCAR RACE INCLUDES HALF THE FIELD WRECKING, FURIOUS DRIVERS & HOLLYWOOD ACTOR RIPPING A 'LEFTIST, WOKE' MOVE

"You know, I've had people try to wreck me and they just end up wrecking themselves lately. So I don't foresee anybody really having to, you know, wanting to do anything like that that where I would have to really be worried about it.

"So, yeah, I mean, I'm not really worried about."

Brad Keselowski, driver of the #6 BuildSubmarines.com Ford, and Carson Hocevar, driver of the #77 Spectrum Chevrolet, race during the NASCAR Cup Series Cook Out Southern 500 at Darlington Raceway in Darlington, S.C., on Sept. 6, 2026. (Getty Images)

Carson, buddy, it's time to start worrying. If your head wasn't on a swivel before Darlington, it HAS to be on one now.

Welcome to a Labor Day edition of Monday Morning Pit-Stop! We're gonna keep this one brief today because A) it's a holiday, B) it's a holiday, and C) I've got meat to smoke ... because it's a holiday.

We're gonna dive into Carson's antics last night at Darlington here in just a minute.

We'll also get into Ryan Blaney putting another few dollars in NASCAR's new 'Swear Jar,' Dale Jarrett got a nice little Sunday night wakeup call, and Hooters Gianna Blaney gave us one final summer photo dump from the pool.

Four tires, enough fuel to get us to Gateway, and maybe some secret service protection for Carson ... Monday Morning Pit-Stop — the 'Watch Out, Carson' edition — is LIVE!

Look, I'm not gonna break down the race. It's a holiday, and it was a relatively "meh" finish.

OK, we all caught up? Good! Now, let's check in with Carson and Brad Keselowski:

First of all, Brad didn't just spin, as Hocevar says with a s–tgrin on his face 14 times. That's obviously false. Hocevar washed up the track and got into Brad, which caused the spin.

Now, here's where I veer a bit with the rest of the pitchfork crowd today ...

He barely — and I mean barely — tapped him. You have to squint to see it. If anything, it looks like he really just got Brad loose enough to spin him out. I don't think it was intentional. I think it was a mistake on Carson's part, and he's too embarrassed/proud to admit it.

"His day’s coming and it’s coming hard. Watch out, Carson."

Brad Keselowski, driver of the #6 BuildSubmarines.com Ford, and Carson Hocevar, driver of the #77 Zeigler Auto Group Chevrolet, talk on the grid during practice for the NASCAR Cup Series Coca-Cola 600 at Charlotte Motor Speedway in Concord, N.C., on May 25, 2024. (Getty Images)

You don't hear Brad Keselowski talk like that often — not this version of Brad, at least. He was hot, and I get it. At some point over the next few weeks, he's going to end Carson Hocevar's day. This sport has a way of policing itself, and you will see it unfold.

Now, the question becomes ... is this good for NASCAR?

The series desperately needs a villain, and they have one in Carson Hocevar. He's also an extremely popular villain, given he LEADS the series in merchandise sales right now.

Hocevar talked to me a lot last week about the state of the sport, and even compared it, to a degree, to WWE.

"They don't understand the new guys," Hocevar said when asked about balancing old and new NASCAR fans. "'This guy is popular, and I don't understand why.' A lot of my friends, some of them love WWE and all the intricacies of that world. But the casuals of it, they're like, 'Man, I loved Stone Cold when he walked out. I never even watched him wrestle, but I liked him, and the Undertaker and their shticks.

"It's very similar to how NASCAR fans describe everything and become negative to everything. A lot of times, they're not sure what they're looking for."

That's an actual social media post from Brad Keselowski's RFK racing team, if you were wondering how the rest of the garage felt about Carson Hocevar.

By the way, they also hated Kyle Busch and Brad Keselowski back in the day. I can remember a time when those two were HATED. Kyle especially.

Carson Hocevar is young and stupid. He's got a hot TikTok influencer girlfriend. He was just told he's the most popular driver on the circuit. He won at Talladega earlier this year, and he's in the Chase.

He's good for NASCAR. He also needs some humbling. Both things can be true.

PS: Massive sale going on over at Carson's pro shop right now!

Amazing. The kid doesn't care. Can't wait to see the fight in a few weeks!

OK, let's put the pedal to the floor and get on outta here ... it's a HOLIDAY.

First up? NASCAR has a new initiative where they are going to put $5 in a swear jar over these next 10 weeks every time a driver cusses over the radio.

Ryan Blaney and Gianna Tulio kiss after Blaney won the 2023 NASCAR Cup Series Championship race at Phoenix Raceway in Avondale, Ariz., on Nov. 5, 2023. (Getty Images)

That's A LOT, by the way. These guys are disgusting over the radio in the heat of battle. Trust me.

Anyway, if you can guess how much money is in the jar by the end, you, apparently, get ALL of it!

Hat's off to NASCAR. I give them a bunch of crap (rightfully so), but this is a smart promotion. Perhaps they took a page out of Carson's WWE playbook?

Also ... what a liner there from Angry Ryan Blaney!

Next? Let's check in with Dale Jarrett on the way out:

Amazing. That gif, I assume, will get some good play this football season. It's not often that 40 stock cars can sneak up on you, but Dale was genuinely taken aback here.

No clue what he was doing, but I'm glad the cameras were rolling. Well done.

OK, that's it for today. Some solid laboring on Labor Day, everyone. Let's go have a big week.

title: Opposition parties accuse Healey of offering ‘more of the same’ in his first major speech as chancellor – UK politics live
excerpt:
Chancellor accused of being ‘continuity Rachel Reeves’ and giving ‘dire and dreary speech’ as JLR announced 4,000 job losses

Chancellor to argue UK economy can ‘turn corner’ despite bond market turmo...
body_text:
Chancellor accused of being ‘continuity Rachel Reeves’ and giving ‘dire and dreary speech’ as JLR announced 4,000 job losses

Chancellor to argue UK economy can ‘turn corner’ despite bond market turmoil

Opposition parties have criticised John Healey for sounding too much like Rachel Reeves in his speech.

This is from Andrew Griffith, the new shadow chancellor.

double quotation markJohn Healey sounds increasingly like continuity Rachel Reeves. Warm words about growth will not make growth a reality or cover up the enormous damage Labour have done to businesses and family finances.

Healey failed to end uncertainty by ruling out more tax rises, failed to set out a serious plan to reform welfare, and failed to commit to funding defence properly – the very issue he resigned over as defence secretary. Even as Jaguar Land Rover cuts jobs, he offered no pause to Labour’s job-destroying employment red tape and no measures to get ruinously high energy bills down.

This is from Robert Jenrick, the Reform UK Treasury spokesperson.

double quotation markOn the day 4,000 people are losing their jobs, Healey gave a dire and dreary speech that will change absolutely nothing. John Healey is beginning to make even Rachel Reeves seem inspiring.

And this is from Ellie Chowns, the Green party’s Treasury spokesperson.

double quotation markOnce again Britain is promised a new economic vision for the future – and once again we are delivered more of the same, from another government unwilling to truly grasp the nettle on wealth inequality and deliver for our communities.

The Green party is clear that the biggest priority must be building economic prosperity that is sustainable, equitable, and genuinely meaningful – not simply chasing ever-more growth for its own sake, regardless of impact.

Chris Osuh is a Guardian community affairs correspondent.

A proposal to ban anyone who is not a healthcare professional from performing circumcisions has been launched in parliament after the deaths of baby boys in the UK.

Sam Carling, Labour MP for North West Cambridgeshire, has tabled an amendment to the government’s health bill.

At present, anyone can legally circumcise in the UK. The amendment calls for non-therapeutic male circumcision to become a “regulated activity,” and follows coroner’s inquests and criminal prosecutions drawing attention to the risk of unregulated circumcisers.

Circumcision is routinely performed for religious and cultural reasons in some Black, Jewish and Muslim communities in Britain. Community organisations have been warning of the risks of the lack of regulation.

In a prevention of future deaths report published in January, the government was urged by a coroner to take action to avoid similar tragedies to the death of Mohamed Abdisamad, a baby who died of a streptococcus infection in February 2023, a week after being circumcised.

Since 2001, circumcision has been a factor in the deaths of seven boys.

double quotation markThe need to strengthen the regulation of non-therapeutic male circumcision could not be clearer. The tragic death of Mohamed Abdisamad in 2023, and other tragic deaths and serious injuries in recent years, have shown that the legal framework in this space is simply not good enough.

My amendment would enact the recommendations of the coroner in Mohamed’s case, who was clear that the status quo, in which anyone can perform a circumcision with no requirements on infection control measures or aftercare, would lead to future deaths.

Carling’s amendment would require circumcision to come under the inspection regime of the Care Quality Commission, and for integrated care boards to produce annual data on prevalence and complications of non- therapeutic male circumcision.

MPs will be debating report stage amendments to the health bill this evening, and it will get its third reading tomorrow.

Yvette Cooper, the new health secretary, is tabling a series of government amendments to the bill intended to strengthen local accountability and increase support for maternity services. Explaining the changes, a government source said:

double quotation markMandatory local government representation will be restored on the integrated care boards which manage health services around the country, reflecting Andy Burnham’s devolution agenda.
  And a new role of maternity and neonatal commissioner will be created by the bill, reflecting Cooper’s personal prioritisation of maternity services and developed alongside the government’s maternity advisor Michelle Welsh (MP for Sherwood Forest).

Peter Walker is a senior Guardian political correspondent.

Zack Polanski is facing unexpected internal opposition in his bid to fight the Holborn and St Pancras byelection for the Greens, with a local councillor saying he is also seeking the nomination and that the seat needs a local MP, not “a politician you’ll only see on a leaflet”.

Hamza Chowdhury, a Green councillor on Camden council in north London, said in a post that he had received nomination from six other Greens, meaning seven of the 10 Greens on the council oppose Polanski being selected.

Among those backing him is Lorna Russell, the group leader in Camden for the Greens, who are the official opposition to Labour.

Polanski, the leader of the Greens in England and Wales, announced on Thursday that he would seek the nomination to fight the seat vacated by Keir Starmer, setting up a high-stakes byelection against Labour.

Local party members will vote later this week to select a candidate, and the Guardian has been told that they are broadly supportive of Polanski standing.

But such high-profile opposition is notable, especially given Chowdhury argued that Polanski, who currently lives in east London, would be unable to properly represent the area if he won.

double quotation markI know Camden because I live it every day. I know the challenges facing our communities, our estates, our broken lifts, our unpicked bins, our unclean roads and endless housing register waiting list because these are the places I have grown up and continue to call home.

We don’t need another MP who arrives during an election campaign, puts out a few leaflets, makes a few promises and disappears once the votes are counted. We need an MP who is present, accessible and visibly part of the community all year round.

I am asking Green party members for the opportunity to represent your home truly and properly. I’m not asking you to vote for a politician you’ll only see on a leaflet. I’m asking you to choose someone who is already here.

The Sarah Jones statement about Portsmouth (see 1.18pm) will be the second of three ministerial statements this afternoon. There are no urgent questions.

At 3.30pm, before Jones, Angela Rayner, the communities secretary, will make a statement about local government reorganisation. That should last about an hour, and after Jones finishes, at about 5.30pm, Emma Reynolds, the chief secretary to the Treasury, will make a statement about economic growth.

At the Downing Street lobby briefing the PM’s spokesperson condemned the behaviour of anti-migrant protesters who blocked roads in Portsmouth yesterday. He said: “Thuggish behaviour is unacceptable, we condemn it unreservedly.”

This was stronger than the initial response released by the Home Office yesterday, but in line with what Emma Reynolds, the chief secretary to the Treasury, said in interviews this morning. (See 8.59am.)

Sarah Jones, the policing minister, will give a statement to MPs on the disruption later this afternoon.

Asked if the government regarded the protests as “far-right”, the PM’s spokesperson said that dealing with them was an operational matter for the police, but that “any behaviour that is intimidatory and a cause of disruption to passengers and travellers is unacceptable”.

At the weekend Mike Huckabee, the US ambassador to Israel, posted this on social media about the UK.

double quotation markThe Brits have lost it. The Jew hate of their government knows no boundaries and knows no facts

Huckabee was commenting on a tweet from the Israeli government criticising Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, for comments about Israel’s record in Gaza.

Asked about Huckabee’s comment at the Downing Street lobby briefing, the PM’s spokesperson said:

double quotation markWe completely reject that assertion. We’re committed to protecting Jewish communities in the UK and continue to engage with community leaders and groups.

The government is investing almost £380m over three years, to protect Jewish communities, crack down on antisemitic extremism and hostile state activity, and tackle antisemitism in schools, universities and local communities.

The spokesperson would not say if the government had formally complained to the US authorities about Huckabee’s remark.

Jaguar Land Rover has announced thousands of job cuts in a “body blow for workers” as it grapples with tough trading conditions, Donald Trump’s tariff wars and the fallout from a cyber-attack. Rob Davies and Alex Daniel have the story.

Asked about this at the No 10 lobby briefing, the PM’s spokesperson said:

double quotation markWe understand that this will be an uncertain and concerning time for affected workers, their families and the wider communities.

And we know that current market conditions are challenging for the automotive sector globally. That’s why we’ve taken significant action to back the UK’s automotive industry by lowering electricity bills for manufacturers, providing £4bn of capital R and D funding to manufacture zero-emission vehicles and launching a £2bn electric car grant to encourage people to buy Evs.

The business secretary [Jonathan Reynolds] is in close contact with JLR and he will be meeting them early this week.

The spokesperson also confirmed that Reynolds has been “clear on his ruling out of any form of bailout”.

Hamish Falconer, appointed by Andy Burnham as minister for EU relations, has had his first official meeting with his EU opposite number, Maroš Šefčovič. In a social media post, Falconer says he wants “a more ambitious partnership”.

Opposition parties have criticised John Healey for sounding too much like Rachel Reeves in his speech.

This is from Andrew Griffith, the new shadow chancellor.

double quotation markJohn Healey sounds increasingly like continuity Rachel Reeves. Warm words about growth will not make growth a reality or cover up the enormous damage Labour have done to businesses and family finances.

Healey failed to end uncertainty by ruling out more tax rises, failed to set out a serious plan to reform welfare, and failed to commit to funding defence properly – the very issue he resigned over as defence secretary. Even as Jaguar Land Rover cuts jobs, he offered no pause to Labour’s job-destroying employment red tape and no measures to get ruinously high energy bills down.

This is from Robert Jenrick, the Reform UK Treasury spokesperson.

double quotation markOn the day 4,000 people are losing their jobs, Healey gave a dire and dreary speech that will change absolutely nothing. John Healey is beginning to make even Rachel Reeves seem inspiring.

And this is from Ellie Chowns, the Green party’s Treasury spokesperson.

double quotation markOnce again Britain is promised a new economic vision for the future – and once again we are delivered more of the same, from another government unwilling to truly grasp the nettle on wealth inequality and deliver for our communities.

The Green party is clear that the biggest priority must be building economic prosperity that is sustainable, equitable, and genuinely meaningful – not simply chasing ever-more growth for its own sake, regardless of impact.

There is nothing unusual about a chancellor refusing to rule out tax rises before a budget. It is normal for a chancellor not to comment on what is in the budget until it is delivered (apart from when they do rule out specific measures in advance, which happens more often than you might think). But, in his column in the Sunday Times yesterday, Rishi Sunak, the Conservative former PM and chancellor, argued on this occasion John Healey should rule out tax cuts now. Sunak argued that the rise in government borrowing costs means that the government’s headroom has been slashed, that Healey already has to find £4.7bn to fund the defence investment plan, and that as a result the country faces weeks of speculation about possible tax rises.

double quotation markThe uncertainty will deter investment and chill economic activity, the last thing needed if we are to foster the sense of optimism that Burnham rightly wants and the growth the country so urgently needs.

Chancellors are loath to tie their hands before a budget. I spent weeks before each fiscal event answering almost every question with, “You wouldn’t expect me to comment on that ahead of the budget.”

Yet Healey should reject such reticence. He should make clear that he’ll not increase taxes in the budget and that if adjustments need to be made, he’ll cut spending. That would provide the certainty needed in an increasingly uncertain world. Research shows that improving the budgetary position by spending cuts rather than tax rises is both more durable and better for growth.

When Kemi Badenoch keeps challenging the government to rule out tax rises in the budget, she is trying to cause trouble by generating a negative headline for the PM when he ignores her. By contrast, in his column, Sunak sounded like someone trying to constructive advice based on what might be good for the country.

If so, Healey did not take it. To be fair, in his speech today the chancellor clearly signalled that he is not about to embark on a big, tax-raising spree. (See 9.57am.) This was consistent with the message the Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary (in the audience for the speech) gave in an interview on Sky News yesterday. “There is no taxation answer that will meet the British people’s expectations on social care or defense or public services,” Reynolds said. But a hint about controlling spending is not the same as a firm commitment not to put up tax, and so Healey’s refusal to rule out tax rises is a story. (It is already the lead on the Telegraph’s website.)

That would not matter much if there were other big stories in the speech. But there weren’t; it was quite dull, and while it conveyed seriousness, it did not project authority. Most of it not only could have been said by Rachel Reeves, the previous chancellor, but actually was said by her (in terms of the arguments being made, if not the words and phrases). As new PM, Burnham has successfully signalled that he is a change from his predecessor. Healey hasn’t.

In his speech, towards the end, John Healey gave a bit more detail of how he intends to cut the burden of business regulation by 25%. (See 10.25am.)

He said that, as well as taking forward the recommendations of the Fingleton review to speed up the construction of nuclear power stations, he would apply those findings to some other sectors. He said there would be a review of the costs involved in rail infrastructure projects.

And he said he wanted to “end the consultation culture at the Treasury and beyond” by getting ministers to speed up decision making. He said new guidance has gone out today to ministers on this from the Treasury and the attorney general, Ellie Reeves.

The Treasury has now published this guidance, which has been sent to ministers as a letter from Healey, Reeves and Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state. It is potentially quite radical.

It starts by saying that in the past “administrative frictions” have stopped the government acting on behalf of the British public.

double quotation markWe want to be clear that the government will act with the full agency that sits with the executive, and which flows from our command of a majority in the House of Commons … We are also determined to overcome the administrative frictions that past administrations have allowed to accumulate, often with good intentions but which have served to slow the work of government, and which we must not allow to frustrate the speed of change.

Healey, Reeves and Haigh then go on to propose three changes.

Ministers are being told to reduce the amount of consultations they hold before decisions are taken and implemented. The letter says that “habitual, box-ticking consultation” has become a problem, and it says that “thousands” of unnecessary consultation requirements should be scrapped. It also implies formal consultation should be the exception, rather than the norm.

double quotation markConsultation culture has turned a sensible mechanism for sourcing external input into an industry of dither and delay, which too often fails to hear from those whose perspectives are most relevant to the issue under consideration, and can drag policies to a lowest common denominator outcome.

We will end this trend by reasserting that there is no general duty of consultation, and that the default position should be that ministers reach decisions and proceed to act on them …

Habitual, box-ticking consultation does not serve people or business and is a distraction to government …

New general guidance will be circulated by officials and more detailed guidance on approaches to public participation will follow in due course. Within this parliament, we will then go further and seek to unwind the thousands of unnecessary consultation and reporting requirements that have come to litter the statute book.

Ministers are being told that a “high” risk of a policy being ruled unlawful should not necessarily stop a policy being implemented. The letter says No 10 wants ministers to feel that they are “trusted” to take decisions even when there is a legal risk, and advice to government lawyers is being changed accordingly. It says:

double quotation markIn support of this approach, we will this week update the legal risk guidance that is used by government lawyers, and which amongst other changes will be clear that it is wholly proper for ministers to take decisions where there is a tenable legal argument even where there is a high legal risk, as well as encouraging lawyers proactively to suggest alternative options where there is a significant barrier or risk to a proposed policy.

Ministers are being told that the government will extend the list of projects exempt from judicial review (JR), building on decisions already taken to stop infrastructure projects being blocked by JR.

The arguments in the letter echo complaints about Whitehall and the civil service more usually heard on the right. When Suella Braverman was attorney general, she also encouraged government lawyers to worry a bit less about the risk of government decisions being found unlawful in the courts. Braverman is now a Reform UK MP, and at its party conference last week Reform also suggested elected politicians were being obstructed by officials – but using much more extreme language.

Q: [From Katherine Forster from GB News] It sounds from what you are saying taxes are going to go up in the budget. And what do you think of the British Chambers of Commerce today saying the pension triple lock should be scrapped so that more money can be spent on Neets (young people not in education, employment or training)?

On tax, Healey said Labour would stick to the promises it made in its manifesto. He repeated his point about not wanting to fuel more speculation by commenting on the budget.

double quotation markI agree with them what they were saying about youth unemployment. You heard me talk about it today -a scar, a blight on the future of those million young people … It cannot be right that we write off a young generation in that way. And so Alan Milburn is doing important work. We’ll base our plans on his full recommendations. But as the prime minister has said, there is a need to bring down welfare costs.

Q: [From Helia Ebrahimi, Channel 4 News] How are you going to deliver change on defence, the cost of living and social care. And would you devolve responsibility for corporation tax to local government.

Healey say he won’s speculate on what will be in the budget.

Addressing Ebrahimi, and also Beth Rigby, given her question a moment ago, he says:

double quotation markIf I respond to speculation now, that will only fuel more speculation. And it’s quite right, and every chancellor would say, that’s for the budget.

I’ll set out my plans and the future route for government for this country at that budget.

Q: [From Sky’s Beth Rigby] The markets expect interest rates to go up. So is the government really turning the corner? And can you assure people you won’t put taxes up in the budget?

Healey says global problems are making “our task in government harder”.

double quotation markWhat I am doing today is setting out plans, a direction for growth … that will see growth in more places in future.

I want to be the chancellor that gets things done, and I want to see growth driven from more places across the UK.

I want to be the chancellor also that recognises, tough as it is, Britain has huge resilience, great latent potential and relative strengths in relation to the way that we are dealing with the fiscal challenges we face.

He does not address the tax question directly.

Healey says he wants to cut the burden of business regulation by 25%.

double quotation markI will take an axe to the thicket of consultation, litigation and administration that has a stranglehold too often on private investment.

So I confirm today my commitment to reducing the burden of business regulation by 25% by the end of this parliament.

And today I announce this [the extension of] the reforms of judicial review from energy to all major infrastructure so that vexatious legislation and vexatious litigation and challenge can’t block economic growth.

Healey says he will change the Treasury’s green book rules to enable to back more regional investement.

double quotation markInvestment has increased by 4.9% since the election alone.

But we need to do more. So first, I’m making changes to the Treasury green book, reducing the discount rate from 3.5% to 3%, and that will skew investment towards projects with more long-term potential, meaning that more places across the UK will get a fair hearing.

This builds on a process that started when Rachel Reeves was chancellor.

Healey says he is also announcing that the I’m announcing today that South Yorkshire and Liverpool cityregions, the North East England. region and the Cardiff Capital Region will all become the latest strategic partners of the National Wealth Fund.

Healey confirms he is announcing an allocation of £150m from the British Business Bank, £150 million for scale-ups in the north of England.

In its news release, the Treasury has given a bit more detail about what this will do.

double quotation markThe new fund, from money already allocated to the British Business Bank, will provide larger investments of between £5m and £15m and is expected to back university spinouts and other ambitious businesses across the North, from Liverpool and Manchester to Leeds, Sheffield, Hull and Newcastle.

The British Business Bank will commit up to £150m, with the proposed fund intended to attract additional private investment. By bringing public and private capital together, it will give some of the north’s most promising companies the backing to grow, create jobs and build their future in the communities where they started.

title: Beverly Vance calls daughter-in-law Usha humble: 'One of the nicest people I've ever met'

"She's one of the nicest people I've ever met"
